payload.author: Manny7717
payload.body:
Verified locally (head 6b73a8f):

- **10/10 new tests pass** in tests/test_login_redirect_when_authenticated.py (file is new — no such tests on base). Coverage is thorough: trusted-header redirect with safe `next` (+ session cookie flushed so the target doesn't bounce back), no-`next` → `/`, three unsafe-`next` shapes fall back to `/`, cookie-authenticated redirect, unauthenticated still renders the form, spoofed header from a non-proxy peer still renders the form, expired cookie still renders the form, and auth-disabled still renders the form.
- **Adjacent suites green:** test_auth.py + test_auth_sessions.py + test_auth_oidc.py + test_issue5578_login_next_nesting.py + test_1038_pwa_auth_redirect.py = 83 passed; test_login_locale.py + test_issue1910_login_attempt_persistence.py = 6 passed.
- **Helpers confirmed:** `ensure_trusted_auth_session` (api/auth.py:885) reconciles trusted-header + cookie identity and returns a session dict (or None); `flush_pending_auth_cookies` (api/helpers.py:204) emits the queued session cookie; `_safe_login_redirect_path` (api/routes.py:10995) rejects non-root-relative paths, control chars, and nested login-route chains (per #5578) — so the redirect can't become an open redirect.
- **Lint:** ruff on api/routes.py = identical 17 pre-existing errors on base and head (zero new); the new test file is ruff-clean.

Logic is sound: `/login` is in PUBLIC_PATHS so `check_auth()` returns before identity reconciliation, and this route-level check is the right place to do it. Redirect only fires when auth is enabled AND a real session/trusted identity exists; every other path renders the form exactly as before. The iOS installed-web-app relaunch-at-last-URL motivation is real and this fixes the parked-on-/login dead end.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete three-file diff at `6b73a8f80`, the full route and regression files at the PR head and on `origin/master`, plus the trusted-session reconciliation and cookie-flush helpers, this fixes the public-route gap at the correct boundary. `/login` bypasses `check_auth()`, so the route itself must reconcile either a valid ordinary cookie or a trusted-header identity before deciding whether to render the form. I found no blocker.

## Code reference

The new branch at `api/routes.py:12931-12955` reuses the existing redirect validator and flushes a session minted during trusted-header reconciliation:

```python
if is_auth_enabled() and ensure_trusted_auth_session(handler):
    handler.send_response(302)
    handler.send_header(
        "Location",
        _safe_login_redirect_path(
            parse_qs(parsed.query or "").get("next", [""])[0]
        ),
    )
```

The remaining response setup at `api/routes.py:12950-12954` matches the neighboring OIDC redirect contract: no-store caching, zero body length, standard security headers, pending auth cookies before `end_headers()`. That ordering matters because `api/auth.py:885-924` can create a trusted session and queue both the auth cookie and a profile-bound cookie during this request. `api/helpers.py:204-210` confirms that `flush_pending_auth_cookies()` emits those queued values without changing other response state.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

No product-code change requested. The use of `ensure_trusted_auth_session()` is narrower than duplicating cookie or proxy checks in the route. It accepts an already-valid non-trusted session at `api/auth.py:888-891`, while trusted-header creation still requires the existing trusted-peer and identity checks at `api/auth.py:897-923`. A spoofed header from an ordinary peer therefore remains on the login form.

The redirect target continues through `_safe_login_redirect_path()` at `api/routes.py:10994-11035`, which rejects external, scheme-relative, control-character, overlong, and login-recursive targets.

## Test plan / verification

`tests/test_login_redirect_when_authenticated.py:86-147` covers the minted-cookie redirect, safe and unsafe destinations, an existing cookie session, and the unauthenticated form path. Lines 150-186 cover an untrusted peer, invalidated cookie, and auth-disabled behavior. The manual checks in `TESTING.md:1929-1930` match the user-visible change.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: merge-ready on inspection, subject to hosted CI.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete three-file diff at `e305d7154`, the new resolver matrix, and the surrounding custom-provider helpers on `origin/master`, the Nous/static-provider branch is pointed at the right shared boundary. I found one blocker in the named-custom branch: every `custom:<slug>` value is treated as known and routable, even when that slug is absent or ambiguous. That contradicts both the PR description and the negative-control policy in the new comment.

## Code reference

The new condition at `api/config.py:3311-3322` is broader than its comment:

```python
if "/" in model:
    if (
        provider in _PROVIDER_MODELS
        or provider in _PROVIDER_DISPLAY
        or provider.startswith("custom:")
    ):
        return f"@{provider}:{model}"
    return model
```

The static-provider checks prove registry membership. `startswith("custom:")` proves only syntax. The codebase already has the config-aware primitives needed to distinguish these cases: `_named_custom_provider_slugs()` at `api/config.py:1420-1428` and `_unique_custom_provider_entry()` at `api/config.py:2664-2695`.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

A stale session provider such as `custom:removed` now becomes an explicit `@custom:removed:vendor/model` route. That prevents the documented bare passthrough and sends `resolve_model_provider()` down a named-provider lane with no matching endpoint. It is the custom-provider version of the unknown slug that the patch says must remain untouched.

Gate the custom case on a real unique entry, for example by checking membership in `_named_custom_provider_slugs(cfg)` or by using `_unique_custom_provider_entry()` and preserving its ambiguity failure. Do not make every `custom:` prefix routable.

## Test plan

`tests/test_issue7333_slash_id_provider_hint.py:216-245` covers an unknown ordinary provider and bare `custom`, but not an unknown named custom provider. Add a case with a foreign profile default, `model_provider="custom:missing"`, and a slash-bearing model. Assert that `model_with_provider_context()` returns the bare model. Also add an ambiguous normalized-slug case if ambiguity is expected to fail closed.

The Nous case and the configured named-custom cases otherwise read correctly. Verdict: block only on the overbroad `custom:` predicate.

payload.author: Manny7717
payload.body:
Thanks for the careful review - you're right that startswith("custom:") was broader than the comment promised. Fixed in 1a31003.

**Change:** the named-custom branch now gates on a real, unique custom_providers[] entry via _unique_custom_provider_entry(custom_providers, _custom_provider_slug_key(provider)):
- Unknown slug (custom:missing, no config entry) -> returns None -> bare passthrough (stale session provider no longer minted into an @custom:missing:... route).
- 2+ entries normalizing to the same slug -> raises AmbiguousCustomProviderError, matching the point-of-return collision guard in resolve_model_provider (fail closed).
- Known unique slug -> @custom:<slug>:model as before.

**Tests added** (per your test plan):
- test_unknown_named_custom_slug_slash_id_stays_bare - foreign profile default (custom:proxy-main), model_provider=custom:missing, slash-bearing model -> asserts bare upstage/solar-pro4:free. Fails on the previous head (returned @custom:missing:upstage/solar-pro4:free), passes on 1a31003.
- test_ambiguous_named_custom_slug_fails_closed - entries proxy-main and Proxy Main (both normalize to slug proxy-main) with a foreign default -> asserts AmbiguousCustomProviderError. Fails on previous head (no raise), passes now.

**Verification:** 281/281 tests across 15 resolver/provider/routing suites (incl. the full #7333 matrix and test_provider_mismatch.py); ruff_lint.py --diff origin/master = 0 new violations; compileall clean. The positive paths (known unique custom slugs, legacy providers: map shape) are unchanged and still covered by the existing #7346 tests.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Re-reading the current head `1a31003e9` after the contributor follow-up, the blocker from my previous review is resolved. Named custom hints are now emitted only when the slug maps to one real, unique `custom_providers[]` entry. Unknown stale slugs retain the documented bare passthrough, while normalized collisions fail closed through the same ambiguity primitive used by final provider resolution. I found no new blocker.

## Code reference

The corrected gate at `api/config.py:3323-3343` now proves custom-provider membership rather than accepting syntax alone:

```python
if provider.startswith("custom:"):
    custom_providers = cfg.get("custom_providers") if isinstance(cfg, dict) else []
    if (
        _unique_custom_provider_entry(
            custom_providers, _custom_provider_slug_key(provider)
        )
        is not None
    ):
        return f"@{provider}:{model}"
```

This composes correctly with `_unique_custom_provider_entry()` at `api/config.py:2664-2695`: no match returns `None`, and two entries sharing the normalized slug raise `AmbiguousCustomProviderError`. The same guard already runs at the `resolve_model_provider()` return boundary at `api/config.py:2751-2770`, so the encoding and resolution sides now agree on what a routable named provider means.

The original portal/static-provider fix remains intact at `api/config.py:3323-3325`. A known non-default provider keeps the explicit hint, while same-provider picks still return bare at `api/config.py:3290-3293` and plugin, ACP, OpenRouter, and configured-provider branches retain their earlier precedence.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

No further product-code change requested. The custom runtime paths already backfill endpoint and credentials from the named entry after resolving the explicit provider: embedded streaming does this at `api/streaming.py:10043-10053`, and the route-side construction does the same at `api/routes.py:24470-24475`. The follow-up therefore fixes the stale-slug lane without weakening valid named-provider routing.

## Test plan / verification

The added cases at `tests/test_issue7333_slash_id_provider_hint.py:248-301` directly cover both requested controls: `custom:missing` stays bare, and two names normalizing to `custom:proxy-main` raise. The positive named-custom and legacy-map cases remain at lines 141-216, while lines 39-138 retain the Nous, same-provider, OpenRouter, and configured-provider matrix. The updated assertion in `tests/test_provider_mismatch.py:556-591` now pins the corrected portal behavior against a foreign default.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: previous feedback addressed; merge-ready on inspection, subject to hosted CI.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body: ## Summary Reading both changed files at `77958aea0` and the full Kanban rendering and localization files on `origin/master`, the escaped diagnostic values and blocked-card placement look safe. The PR has one visible blocker: the five translation keys named in the body do not exist in `static/i18n.js`. Missing keys are returned verbatim, so the card and detail panel render implementation identifiers instead of user-facing labels. ## Code reference The new card path at `static/panels.js:2547-2555` has no fallback for the badge: ```javascript const blocked = task.status === "blocked" || status === "blocked"; const blockBadge = blocked ? `⛔ ${esc(t("kanban_task_blocked"))}` : ""; ``` The detail helper at `static/panels.js:3713-3726` also calls `kanban_block_reason`, `kanban_block_kind`, `kanban_consecutive_failures`, and `kanban_last_failure`. On current `static/i18n.js`, searches for all five return no matches. The translation fallback at `static/i18n.js:26314-26316` is explicit: ```javascript function t(key, ...args) { const val = resolveKey(key); if (val === undefined) return key; } ``` That means users will see text such as `kanban_task_blocked` and `kanban_block_reason`. The existing `kanban_block` and `kanban_unblock` keys are different strings and do not cover these calls. ## Diagnosis / recommendation Add all five keys to every locale in `static/i18n.js`, following the repository localization contract. If complete translations are not available, use clear English fallbacks consistently rather than relying on missing-key behavior. The `|| "Block diagnostics"` expressions in the detail helper do not work as fallbacks because `t()` returns the truthy key name. ## Test plan This PR has no test file. Extend `tests/test_kanban_ui_static.py` to assert every new key is present for every locale and add a small renderer check proving a blocked card and detail panel contain translated labels, escaped diagnostic values, and no raw key names. The CSS addition at `static/style.css:6994-6997` otherwise fits the existing badge rules.

payload.author: samfoy
payload.title: fix(streaming): bind the turn workspace as the agent session cwd

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I pulled this branch into a read-only worktree and read the full two-file diff, the complete regression file, the corresponding `origin/master` code, and the Agent working-directory contract in `agent/runtime_cwd.py`. The diagnosis is correct. The in-process WebUI currently stamps `TERMINAL_CWD`, but that value is process-global; binding the selected workspace to the Agent ContextVar gives concurrent turns independent cwd authority. Reset-token restoration is also the right choice for reused worker threads.

## Code reference

The production bind at `api/streaming.py:2799-2808` is narrow and fail-soft:

```python
if workspace:
    try:
        from agent.runtime_cwd import _SESSION_CWD as _SCWD
        tokens["session_cwd"] = _SCWD.set(str(workspace))
    except Exception:
        logger.debug("per-turn _SESSION_CWD bind failed", exc_info=True)
```

The matching reset at `api/streaming.py:2823-2830` restores the previous context value rather than assigning an empty string. That matters because an empty assignment would suppress the Agent fallback for a later CLI or cron use on the same worker. At the call site, `api/streaming.py:9177-9189` resolves the same `workspace` argument used immediately afterward for `s.workspace`, then binds it before any Agent work starts.

The Agent-side resolver checks its session cwd before `TERMINAL_CWD`, so this is the correct WebUI/Agent contract boundary. A WebUI-only environment-variable change would leave the concurrent-turn race intact.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

I found no blocking issue. The production lifecycle is paired: `_turn_session_identity_tokens` is initialized before the outer try and reset in the existing outer finally, so exceptions after binding do not leak cwd state. Omitting a workspace still leaves the ContextVar untouched for other callers.

The direct private-ContextVar import is consistent with the three neighboring identity bindings. A future Agent API could expose a token-reset helper and remove that private coupling, but that is not a reason to block this patch.

## Verification

`tests/test_xsession_wakeup_misroute.py:318-398` covers bind, no-workspace behavior, reset to the Agent sentinel, and two concurrent turns with distinct workspaces. The assertions exercise the real Agent resolver rather than a duplicate WebUI implementation. One useful non-blocking follow-up would pin the `_run_agent_streaming` call-site wiring itself, so a later refactor cannot keep the helper tests green while forgetting to pass `workspace` in production.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: no blocker found.

payload.author: nrlcode
payload.title: feat: add default-off WebUI Kanban wake activation

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full wake consumer, activation routes, all three new regression files, and the Agent claim/list symbols, the ownership filter and claim-before-wake contract are coherent. I found one liveness blocker in the integration with the existing completion drain: Kanban polling runs only after the completion queue times out. A continuously non-empty background-completion queue can starve the Kanban consumer forever, despite the advertised one-second poll cadence.

## Code reference

At `api/background_process.py:2172-2204`, the poll launch exists only in the missing-queue and `queue.Empty` branches:

```python
try:
    evt = q.get(timeout=1.0)
except queue.Empty:
    now = time.monotonic()
    if now >= next_kanban_poll and not _DRAIN_STOP.is_set():
        next_kanban_poll = now + _KANBAN_POLL_INTERVAL_SECS
        threading.Thread(target=_poll_webui_kanban_wakeups, ...).start()
    continue
```

When `q.get()` succeeds, execution proceeds directly to the normal completion handling. There is no cadence check on that path. If process completions arrive at least once per second, `queue.Empty` never occurs and no WebUI Kanban subscription is polled.

The Agent-side claim primitive at `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:11766` makes each poll safe to attempt; the WebUI should not make queue idleness a prerequisite for reaching it. The existing test `tests/test_kanban_webui_wakeup.py:test_drain_runs_kanban_poll_off_completion_drain_thread` covers one timeout followed by one completion, so it does not expose sustained queue activity.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Move the `now >= next_kanban_poll` check to a shared point in each drain-loop iteration, independent of whether `q.get()` returned an event or timed out. Keep the poll itself on its daemon thread and retain `_KANBAN_POLL_LOCK`, so completion processing remains non-blocking and overlapping polls still collapse.

## Test plan

Add a drain-loop regression whose fake completion queue returns several events without ever raising `queue.Empty`. Set a short bounded stop condition, then assert that all completion events are processed and at least one Kanban poll thread starts. Also retain the current test proving a slow poll cannot block completion draining.

The default-off sidecar, hosted-profile filtering at `api/background_process.py:711-1000`, and exact claim rewind behavior otherwise read as intentionally scoped. Verdict: block on the busy-queue starvation path.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Re-reading the current head `bd7152f46`, the focused follow-up diff from `36ffb37e5`, and the complete drain-loop and regression context, the busy-queue starvation blocker from my previous review is fixed. Kanban cadence is now checked at the start of every drain iteration, independent of whether the completion queue returns an event, is absent, or times out. I found no new blocker in this update.

## Code reference

The corrected placement is at `api/background_process.py:2167-2185`:

```python
while not _DRAIN_STOP.is_set():
    now = time.monotonic()
    if now >= next_kanban_poll and not _DRAIN_STOP.is_set():
        next_kanban_poll = now + _KANBAN_POLL_INTERVAL_SECS
        threading.Thread(
            target=_poll_webui_kanban_wakeups,
            name="hermes-webui-kanban-wakeup-poll",
            daemon=True,
        ).start()
```

The queue read now begins afterward at `api/background_process.py:2192-2213`. A successful `q.get()` therefore cannot bypass the cadence check, and completion processing remains unchanged. The missing-queue and `queue.Empty` branches no longer duplicate scheduling logic.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

No further product-code change requested for the prior blocker. Poll work still runs off the completion-drain thread, while `_poll_webui_kanban_wakeups()` retains `_KANBAN_POLL_LOCK` at `api/background_process.py:887-889`; if one poll lasts beyond the one-second interval, later launch attempts collapse instead of overlapping claims. `_DRAIN_STOP` is checked before launch and again inside the poll path, preserving shutdown behavior.

This also keeps completion handling responsive. The drain thread only starts a daemon poll worker, then continues directly to `q.get()` and `_process_one()`.

## Test plan / verification

The new regression at `tests/test_kanban_webui_wakeup.py:638-679` supplies five completion events without ever raising `queue.Empty`. It asserts every event is processed and at least one Kanban poll starts. The neighboring test at lines 594-635 still proves a slow poll does not block completion draining, so together they cover busy and idle queue shapes.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: the starvation feedback is addressed; the PR is merge-ready on inspection, subject to hosted CI.

payload.title: fix(session): reconcile one turn held by both stores in messaging display merge

payload.author: mekx
payload.body:
Fresh reproduction on a turn taken *after* this PR was opened, same deployment, stock `exp-v0.52.264`. Worth adding because it shows the user-visible shape is not always "the answer appears twice".

`GET /api/session?...&messages=1` for one browser turn (text elided, it is a personal conversation):

```
274  user       id=9      ts=…824.983
275  user       id=None   ts=…826.880     <- same prompt, agent-store copy
…
283  assistant  id=None   ts=…857.189     <- same answer, agent-store copy
284  assistant  id=10     ts=…857.350
```

Both the prompt and the answer are served twice, exactly the identified/unidentified key-shape split this PR fixes. But in the rendered transcript only the **prompt** visibly duplicated: the id-less assistant copy sits adjacent to the turn's tool rows and gets folded into the collapsed activity block, so it never appears as a second answer bubble.

That is probably worth knowing for triage — the same defect can be reported as "my question is duplicated" with no mention of the reply, depending on where the unidentified copy lands relative to the tool rows.

Running the patched `_merged_session_messages_for_display` against this session's real store contents:

```
before: 285 rows, prompt at 274+275, answer at 283+284
after:  275 rows, prompt once (id=9), answer once (id=10)
```

Unrelated note in case it reaches someone who knows the agent side: the same runs also end with `token × N → reasoning(text == the entire reply, byte-identical) → done`, which is [NousResearch/hermes-agent#13007](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/13007) and is a separate cause of duplicate-looking output. It is not what this PR addresses.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I pulled this branch into a read-only worktree and read the complete `api/routes.py` and new regression file at the PR head, their `origin/master` context, plus the full merge helpers in `api/models.py` and the Gateway writeback path. The duplicate-turn diagnosis is correct: the chronological-union branch cannot compare an identified sidecar key with an unidentified Agent key. Keeping the stable sidecar row is also necessary for frontend coordinates. There is one blocking data-preservation issue, though: the newly discarded Agent row can carry semantic payload that is not copied into the survivor.

## Code reference

At `api/routes.py:9797-9807`, the idless row is removed after only a display-metadata merge:

```python
elif unmatched_identified.get(visible_key, 0) > 0:
    unmatched_identified[visible_key] -= 1
    _merge_session_display_metadata(
        identified_by_visible_key.get(visible_key), msg
    )
    continue
```

That helper is intentionally narrow. Its allowlist at `api/models.py:8961-8978` contains turn timing, usage, status-card, routing, anchor, and media-snapshot fields. It does not contain `reasoning`, `reasoning_content`, `reasoning_details`, `codex_reasoning_items`, or `codex_message_items`.

The new fixture demonstrates the gap itself. `tests/test_gateway_dual_store_duplicate_turn.py:55-66` puts `reasoning` and `codex_message_items` only on the unidentified Agent assistant row, while the identified sidecar assistant has only id, role, content, and timestamp. The assertions check that one answer survives and that stable ids remain, but never assert preservation of those Agent-only fields. With this implementation, both fields disappear from the returned transcript.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

This matters for the reported production shape, not only a synthetic edge. The PR description says the Agent copy owns the real reasoning and Codex payload while the sidecar copy may have unreliable reasoning. Reconciliation should not fix duplicate bubbles by silently deleting the better semantic record.

Keep the sidecar row as the coordinate owner, but define an explicit semantic-payload reconciliation policy. Copy safe Agent-owned fields when the identified target lacks them. When both sides contain conflicting non-empty values, fail closed or choose authority through a documented field-specific rule. Do not fold `api_content` through a generic dictionary merge; its existing identity rules in `api/models.py` are stricter for good reason.

The visible-key buckets also need one-to-one pairing for repeated identical text. `identified_by_visible_key.setdefault(...)` points every match in a bucket at the first identified row, so two equal assistant answers with different reasoning payloads can cross-wire metadata even when row counts remain correct. A per-key queue in transcript order, separated by store, would make the cross-store match explicit.

## Test plan

Please add regressions that assert:

1. the reported single turn keeps the sidecar id and the Agent-only reasoning/Codex fields;
2. two identical assistant texts with distinct ids and distinct reasoning payloads pair one-to-one in chronological order;
3. conflicting non-empty semantic fields follow the documented authority rule;
4. the existing distinct-identified and idless-repeat contracts still hold.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: block until duplicate reconciliation preserves the semantic payload of the removed row.

payload.author: mekx
payload.body:
Thanks for the thorough read — both findings are real and fixed in `20eb3f05`.

## Semantic payload preservation

Added `_AGENT_SEMANTIC_PAYLOAD_KEYS` + `_adopt_agent_semantic_payload` (`api/models.py`), a second, narrow, explicitly-named allowlist covering exactly `reasoning`, `reasoning_content`, `reasoning_details`, `codex_reasoning_items`, `codex_message_items`. Deliberately **not** folded into `_SESSION_MESSAGE_DISPLAY_METADATA_KEYS` / `_merge_session_display_metadata` — that allowlist is shared by other merge call sites that never asked for reasoning/Codex semantics, and widening it would change their behavior too. `api_content` stays excluded from both, per your note about its stricter identity rules.

Policy: fill-only-if-absent, same as the existing display-metadata helper — the identified survivor's own non-empty value always wins, so agent-store data never silently overwrites a sidecar-authored one. New test `test_conflicting_semantic_payload_keeps_survivors_own_value` pins that explicitly.

## One-to-one pairing

Replaced `identified_by_visible_key.setdefault(visible_key, msg)` (which pointed every match at whichever identified row was seen first) with a per-visible-key FIFO queue built in transcript order — pass 1 enqueues identified rows, pass 2 pops the oldest still-unmatched entry on each unidentified match. Repeats now pair up one-to-one in the order they actually occurred, as you suggested. New test `test_repeated_identical_answers_pair_one_to_one_in_order` covers two identical-text assistant answers with distinct ids and distinct reasoning payloads, asserting each recovers its own.

## Test plan

Added exactly the three regressions you asked for, plus re-ran the fourth (existing contracts):

1. `test_gateway_reconciliation_preserves_agent_semantic_payload` — the reported single-turn shape keeps the sidecar id and the agent-only reasoning/Codex fields.
2. `test_repeated_identical_answers_pair_one_to_one_in_order` — two identical assistant texts with distinct ids/reasoning pair 1:1 in chronological order.
3. `test_conflicting_semantic_payload_keeps_survivors_own_value` — conflicting non-empty semantic fields keep the survivor's own value.
4. `test_identified_rows_with_matching_text_stay_distinct` / `test_unidentified_repeats_within_one_store_are_not_collapsed` (existing) — still pass unchanged.

All three new tests fail against the prior commit on this branch except (3), which has no prior behavior to regress (it pins the new mechanism's policy, not a fix to an old one) — confirmed by reverting to `62e51fd5` and re-running.

Full suite: `14872 passed, 310 skipped, 2 xfailed, 1 xpassed, 2 errors` (same two pre-existing `test_issue2695_packaged_runtime_layout` errors as `master`, unrelated to this change).

Re-verified against the live deployment once more: 0 duplicated assistant answers, all stable ids preserved, and the reported production session's `reasoning` field now round-trips through this reconciliation instead of being silently dropped.

payload.author: Alextechgamer
payload.title: fix(api): stop /api/session wedging the server on huge sessions

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Pulled the branch into a read-only worktree and read both backend changes plus the redactor internals on master. Two independent bounds on the `GET /api/session` path: (1) a per-string length cap on the agent redact pass in `api/helpers.py`, and (2) an auto-window that forces a 30-row tail on huge sidecars in `api/routes.py` unless `?full=1`. Both are correctly gated so normal-size sessions are unchanged, and the redaction safety boundary holds. Nice incident write-up — the ~117s field number is consistent with the root cause below.

## Why the redact pass explodes (confirmed at the agent layer)

I traced why a URL-heavy dump is catastrophic. The agent redactor gates each regex behind a cheap substring pre-check, and for URL/DB/JWT patterns that gate is `"://" in text` / `"eyJ" in text` (`agent/redact.py:812`). A multi-MB blob of `http://example.com/...` passes the `://` gate trivially, so the full `_DB_CONNSTR_RE` / `_URL_BARE_TOKEN_RE` scan runs across the entire megabyte string — the pre-check that makes this fast on log lines does nothing here. That's the GIL wedge. So the length cap is the right lever; you can't lean on the agent's own guards for this input shape.

## The per-string cap is complementary to the window (worth stating explicitly)

The redactor is applied per-field, not once over the whole transcript — `_redact_value` recurses the payload and calls `_redact_text` → `_redact_fn_cached` on each individual string (`api/helpers.py:966-977`). So `_REDACT_AGENT_MAX_TEXT_LEN = 16384` bounds a *single huge field* (one giant tool dump), while the routes.py auto-window bounds *many messages*. A session can hit either axis independently, which is why you correctly need both changes rather than one.

## Redaction safety when the agent pass is skipped

This is the part that matters for the security boundary, so I read `_fallback_redact` (`api/helpers.py:433-439`) directly:

```python
text = _CRED_RE.sub(lambda m: _mask(m.group(1)), text)
text = _EMBEDDED_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_RE.sub(lambda m: _mask(m.group(0)), text)
text = _AUTH_HDR_RE.sub(lambda m: m.group(1) + _mask(m.group(2)), text)
text = _ENV_RE.sub(_env_replacement, text)
text = _PRIVKEY_RE.sub("[REDACTED PRIVATE KEY]", text)
```

`_CRED_RE` (`api/helpers.py:320-357`) is actually much broader than the PR body claims — beyond ghp_/sk-/hf_/AKIA it also covers Stripe `sk_live_`/`rk_live_`, Google `AIza`, Slack `xox[baprs]-`, SendGrid, Groq `gsk_`, and ~25 other prefixes. Plus auth headers, `*_TOKEN=`/`*_SECRET=` env assignments, and PEM private keys. So above the cap the residual gap is only the **prefix-less** agent patterns: JWTs (`eyJ…`, `_JWT_RE` at `agent/redact.py:402`), Telegram bot tokens (`<digits>:<token>`, :354), and DB connection-string passwords (`postgres://user:PASSWORD@`, :374). Worth a one-line note in the code comment that JWT/Telegram/DB-connstr are the specific shapes that leak above 16KB, since "the local fallback covers the common shapes" undersells what's actually dropped.

## routes.py windowing

`_auto_msg_limit_for_huge_sidecar` (`api/routes.py:8850`) only fires when `msg_limit is None and not full and _sidecar_file_exceeds_threshold(...)` — so it's a no-op for explicit limits, for `?full=1`, and for normal-size sidecars. The `?full=1` opt-out is correctly plumbed into `outline.js`/`sessions.js` for the absolute-index paths (jump-to-message, load-older) that genuinely need the whole array. `_messages_truncated`/`_messages_offset` are set so the client knows more rows exist — the tests assert `offset==10`, `truncated is True` on a 40-row session windowed to 30.

## Test plan

The three routes tests + the `< 2s` redact timing test (`test_huge_tool_dump_skips_agent_pass_but_still_masks_secrets`) cover both axes and the security assertion (`secret not in out`). Only suggestion: add a fixture asserting a `postgres://u:pw@h` or a bare `eyJ…` JWT in a >16KB field **is** leaked past the cap — not to change behavior, but to pin the known residua

payload.title: fix: preserve compacted context across cancellation

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Pulled the branch into a read-only worktree, read the new `_adopt_cancelled_in_place_compaction` helper (`api/streaming.py:2099-2225`) end to end, and cross-checked the agent contract it depends on. The failure mode is real and the fix is a careful, fail-closed adoption gate. This is the right layer: the WebUI owns the sidecar writeback, so recovering a committed-but-cancelled in-place compaction has to happen here, not in the agent.

## Agent contract check (this is the part that matters)

The helper keys on two agent signals, and both are genuine:

- `agent._last_compaction_in_place` is set at `agent/conversation_compression.py:3899` (`agent._last_compaction_in_place = compacted_in_place`) and reset per-turn at `agent/conversation_loop.py:1819` (`agent._last_compaction_in_place = False`) precisely because "the gateway caches agents across user turns."
- `context_compressor.compression_count` is a real monotonically-advancing counter (`conversation_compression.py:254`).

The per-turn reset is the subtle risk — a cached agent could carry a stale-true flag into a later uncompressed turn. The PR defends against exactly that with the count-advance requirement:

```python
bool(getattr(agent, "_last_compaction_in_place", False))
and getattr(compressor, "compression_count", 0) > pre_compression_count
```

`_pre_compression_count` is captured before the run at `api/streaming.py:10742`, so `count > pre_count` proves *this* turn compressed — even if the flag were stale, the gate holds. Good defense in depth.

## Fail-closed boundary verification

The strongest design choice: the boundary is verified against the Agent's **unmodified** `result["messages"]` before any settlement helper runs, with an explicit comment that `_settle_result_messages` can synthesize the missing current-turn row and thereby "turn absent commit evidence into apparent evidence." That ordering is correct and easy to get wrong. The projection is then truncated to `[:verified_turn_idx + 1]`, so assistant/tool output produced after the compaction boundary on a cancelled turn stays rejected. The `test_cancelled_compaction_adoption_rejects_missing_result_user_boundary` test pins exactly this — a result with a compaction marker but no committed user boundary is refused and the session stays on `prior_messages`.

## Ownership guards + concurrency

All three insertion points (`api/streaming.py:10893`, `:10956`, `:11024`) sit inside `with _agent_lock:` blocks, and the helper re-reads `session_writeback_owner(session_id) != stream_id` plus `active_stream_id` before adopting, so a rotated stream or superseded worker fails closed independent of lock scope. Solid.

## Cancel provenance / log-injection

`boot.js` interpolates `_reason` (correctly defined as `reason || 'explicit-cancel'` at the top of `cancelStream`), and `api/routes.py:14345-14350` sanitizes it before logging:

```python
cancel_reason = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9._:-]+", "_", cancel_reason)[:80]
```

Character-class allowlist + 80-char cap closes the obvious log-forging vector. Good.

## One suggestion

`test_cancel_provenance.py` asserts on source *strings* (`"reason=${encodeURIComponent(_reason)}" in boot`) rather than behavior. That's brittle — a harmless refactor (renaming `_reason`, reformatting the fetch) breaks the test without any regression. Consider asserting the route's runtime behavior (feed a `reason=` with metacharacters, assert the logged value is sanitized) instead of pinning the literal template. Not blocking; the compaction tests carry the real coverage.

Overall: well-scoped, correctly fail-closed, contract-accurate. LGTM on a read-through.

Closing this PR in favour of a broader refactor.

The two review findings on this PR (root-profile scopes bypassing hydration, and the thread-local-only publication missing raw `os.getenv()` readers) turned out to be two instances of a deeper problem: profile-scoped secret hydration has no single chokepoint, so every new credential reader is a chance for the next divergence. payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete six-file diff at `04be6002c`, the full new comparator and audit CLI, both regression files, the corresponding `origin/master` config/documentation, and the canonical continuation helper in `api/agent_sessions.py`, I found one aggregate-accounting blocker. Rejected sidecar evidence is counted once as an inventory-level ambiguity and then counted again when its identity anchor reaches the lineage loop. The resulting diagnostic can report more blocked/classified lineages than `total_lineages`, which makes the only user-facing output unreliable.

## Code reference

The first count is established at `api/session_metadata_sync.py:677` and copied into the result accumulator at `api/session_metadata_sync.py:851`:

```python
inv_blocked_total = sum(inv_blocked.values()) + invalid_core_blocked
...
blocked_ambiguous = inv_blocked_total
```

The same rejected sidecar identities are also placed in `blocked_anchor_ids`, expanded, and grouped into `lineage_roots`. The lineage loop at `api/session_metadata_sync.py:884-886` then counts them again:

```python
if any(mid in blocked_expanded for mid in members):
    blocked_ambiguous += 1
    continue
```

For the fixture at `tests/test_issue498_session_lifecycle_shadow.py:369-381`, `bad.json` increments `inv_blocked["malformed"]` and contributes its filename stem to `inv_blocked_ids`. It therefore adds one to the initial accumulator and one more through its blocked lineage. Together with the valid matched row, the report has two lineages but three classified counts (`matched=1`, `blocked.ambiguous=2`). The ID-mismatch path at `tests/test_issue498_session_lifecycle_shadow.py:383-410` is worse: one rejected file can create two blocked anchors plus the initial inventory count. Both tests use `>= 1`, so they do not detect the overcount.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Choose one unit for `blocked.ambiguous`. Since the surrounding schema is lineage-based, count identity-bearing rejected records only when their anchored lineage is visited. Seed the accumulator only with records that cannot be represented by an anchor (for example, a malformed core ID with no admissible string identity), or expose malformed-record counts under a separate field instead of mixing records and lineages.

## Test plan

Add exact-count regressions for:

1. one valid matched row plus one malformed sidecar: `total_lineages=2`, `matched=1`, `blocked.ambiguous=1`;
2. one filename/payload ID mismatch: assert the chosen two-anchor grouping explicitly and ensure no third inventory count appears;
3. a profile-mismatch anchor and an invalid core ID, covering anchored and unanchorable cases separately.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: block on aggregate double-counting; the read-only and no-runtime-wiring boundaries otherwise match the stated slice.

payload.title: fix(streaming): lock-disciplined STREAMS reads via peek_stream()

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Pulled the branch into a read-only worktree and diffed against `origin/master`. The change is exactly what the description says: one lock-disciplined helper `peek_stream()` in `api/config.py`, and four bare `STREAMS.get()` read sites migrated to it with identical None-guard logic after the call. No behavioral change, just centralizing the read discipline.

I verified the RED claim directly on master — all four call sites exist at the exact lines cited, and `peek_stream` does not yet exist:

```
api/streaming.py:8683:    q = STREAMS.get(stream_id)
api/routes.py:18769:    stream = STREAMS.get(stream_id)
api/routes.py:18912:        stream = STREAMS.get(stream_id) if stream_id else None
api/gateway_chat.py:922:    q = STREAMS.get(stream_id)
```

## Code reference

The helper itself (`api/config.py`, placed right after the `STREAMS`/`STREAMS_LOCK` definitions at :9154-9155):

```python
def peek_stream(stream_id):
    """Lock-disciplined stream queue lookup. ..."""
    with STREAMS_LOCK:
        return STREAMS.get(stream_id)
```

Each site is a clean one-liner swap, e.g. `api/gateway_chat.py:922` `q = STREAMS.get(stream_id)` → `q = peek_stream(stream_id)`, with `STREAMS` kept imported in all three files (they still do locked pops/lists directly).

## Reentrancy check (the one thing worth confirming)

`STREAMS_LOCK` is a plain `threading.Lock` (non-reentrant), so the real risk in a change like this is migrating a read site that is *already inside* a `with STREAMS_LOCK:` block — that would self-deadlock. I checked all four: none sit under a held lock. The nearest acquires in `gateway_chat.py` are at :951/:1478 (after the `peek_stream` at :920), and in `routes.py` the SSE attach paths at :18767/:18910 are well clear of the `with STREAMS_LOCK` blocks (:2996, :12309, :22336+). So all four migrations are deadlock-safe. Good.

## Guard test

`tests/test_streams_locked_reads.py` is the right shape — a structural pin (`test_no_bare_streams_get_outside_config`) that greps every `api/*.py` except `config.py` for `STREAMS.get(` and fails if any reappear. That's what prevents the bare-read pattern from getting copy-pasted back in. The `test_peek_stream_acquires_streams_lock` recording-lock monkeypatch is a nice touch to prove the lock is actually taken rather than just trusting the `with`.

One note on the test-seam fixups (the `dual-patch config.STREAMS alongside routes.STREAMS` commit): because the SSE tests previously monkeypatched `routes.STREAMS` but the read now resolves through `config.peek_stream`, each affected test had to also patch `config.STREAMS`. That's correct and unavoidable given the indirection, but it's a reminder that `routes.STREAMS` and `config.STREAMS` are now two names for the same registry — future tests should patch `config.STREAMS` (or `peek_stream` directly) rather than the re-exported `routes.STREAMS`, otherwise the read path silently ignores the patch.

## Verdict

Correct, minimal, well-tested, no behavior change. The lock traffic added is an uncontended acquire on already-hot paths, negligible. LGTM from a read-through — the check-then-act windows (get → `register_active_run`, get → subscribe) are the real motivation and centralizing the read is the right first step even if the compound operations still aren't atomic end-to-end.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Read `read_body()` in `api/helpers.py` and the four dispatchers (`handle_post`, `handle_patch`, `handle_delete`, `handle_put`) in `api/routes.py` on both `origin/master` and this branch. The two lenient failure modes are real: malformed JSON returned `{}` (turning into a misleading `Missing required field` 400), and non-object JSON (`[1,2,3]`) flowed into `body.get(...)` and surfaced as a generic 500. The fix is correct and the mapping is consistent with what already existed.

## Code reference

Master's `read_body()` (`api/helpers.py:1269`) swallowed both cases:

```python
raw = handler.rfile.read(length) if length else b'{}'
try:
    return _json.loads(raw)
except Exception:
    return {}
```

This branch raises `ValueError('Invalid JSON body')` on parse failure and `ValueError('JSON body must be an object')` when the result isn't a dict, while keeping the empty-body `b'{}'` default. That's the right layering because `handle_post` at `api/routes.py:14982` already maps a `read_body` `ValueError` to a clean 400/413:

```python
status = 413 if "too large" in str(exc).lower() else 400
return bad(handler, str(exc), status=status)
```

The PATCH/DELETE/PUT wrappers (`api/routes.py:17630/17658/17694` on master) called `read_body` bare and previously had no such mapping — this PR gives them the identical block. Verbatim match, good.

## Diagnosis / Recommendation

I checked the non-object rejection for regressions by enumerating every `read_body` caller. There are five: the four dispatchers plus `_handle_tts` (`api/routes.py:19890`), which already wraps the call in `except Exception → 400`. None of them iterate the body as a list — every consumer uses `body.get(...)`, so rejecting arrays/scalars breaks no existing handler. The webhook ingestion paths use their own lenient parse-and-discard helper and are correctly left untouched.

One thing worth stating in the PR for reviewers: this is a **behavior change** for any client that was relying on malformed JSON silently becoming `{}`. In practice that only ever produced a misleading downstream 400, so the new explicit `Invalid JSON body` 400 is strictly more informative — but it's a contract change worth a CHANGELOG line if the project tracks API-error semantics.

## Verification

`tests/test_read_body_json_validation.py` covers both the unit contract (7 cases) and HTTP-level behavior across POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE, including the `[1,2,3]` → 500 crash that motivated this. The empty-body `{}` default and valid-dict passthrough are both asserted, so the safe paths are pinned. Reads clean and ready.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Read the `jsArg()` helper in `static/ui.js`, all of the converted call sites in `static/panels.js`, `static/sessions.js`, `static/onboarding.js`, plus the new guard test and the kanban-static sandbox stub. The core change is correct and the mechanism-promotion approach (one shared `jsArg()` instead of copies of `_kanbanJsArg`) is the right call. One out-of-scope artifact should be dropped before merge — see below.

## Code reference

The promoted helper at `static/ui.js:281` is exactly the old `_kanbanJsArg` body, which is what makes this a safe cutover:

```js
function jsArg(s){
  // JSON.stringify quotes/escapes for the JS context; esc() then makes the
  // result safe inside the HTML attribute.
  return esc(JSON.stringify(String(s == null ? '' : s)));
}
```

The important detail every converted site gets right: because `JSON.stringify` supplies its own quotes, the surrounding `'…'` must be dropped. Spot-checking the trickiest ones, all are correct — e.g. `_loadCronDetailRuns` at `panels.js:1370`:

```js
onclick="_loadRunContent(${jsArg(jobId)},${jsArg(run.filename)},${jsArg(rid)})"
```

and the hoisted-esc variant in `_kanbanCardQuickActions` (`const id = esc(task.id)` → now `${jsArg(task.id)}`) which the inline sweep would have missed — good catch in self-review. The manual `.replace(/'/g,"\\'")` on the checkpoint-restore `msg` arg (`panels.js:13358`) is now uniformly `jsArg(msg)`, removing a bespoke escape.

## One issue: drop the uv.lock changes

The diff regenerates `uv.lock` (+232 lines: `cffi`, `cryptography`, `pyyaml`, `pycparser`, the `hermes-webui` self-entry). Master ships `uv.lock` as a deliberate 3-line stub:

```
version = 1
revision = 3
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

This is a JS-only escaping fix — none of those Python deps are relevant, and the lockfile expansion looks like a local `uv` side effect that got swept into the commit. Please `git checkout origin/master -- uv.lock` and drop it from the PR so the change stays scoped to the four JS files + tests.

## Verification

`tests/test_inline_handler_arg_escaping.py` has two layers: a source guard (`_ESC_ONLY_INLINE_ARG` regex) that fails if any `on*="…'${esc(x)}'…"` form comes back, and a real Chromium round-trip proving the esc()-only form executes `alert('pwned')` while `jsArg()` round-trips `"');alert('pwned');//"` byte-exact. The kanban-static stub in `tests/test_kanban_ui_static.py:866` correctly gains a `jsArg` mirror so the node VM run of `panels.js` resolves the new global. Solid coverage. The guard's known blind spots (hoisted-esc, percent-encoded transports) are honestly documented. Once uv.lock is reverted this is ready.

payload.author: angelusbr
payload.title: Fix download 404 when a MEDIA: token is wrapped in an inline-code span

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Confirmed the bug and the fix by reading `renderMd()` in `static/ui.js` and the streaming MEDIA tail helpers in `static/messages.js` on both `origin/master` and this branch. The diagnosis holds: the MEDIA stash runs *before* the inline-code / fence stash, so when the token sits inside a code span the closing backtick has not been stripped yet, and the path character class `[^\s\)\]]+` happily consumes it.

## Code reference

The ordering that makes this a real bug is documented in `renderMd()` at `static/ui.js:7588`:

```js
// ── MEDIA: token stash (must run first, before any other processing) ──
const media_stash=[];
s=s.replace(/MEDIA:([^\s\)\]]+)/g,(_,raw_ref)=>{
```

Because the fence/backtick stash is explicitly required to run *after* this, a `` `MEDIA:/workspace/report.md` `` span still has its trailing backtick when the regex runs, and `%60` leaks into `/api/media?path=…report.md%60` → 404.

## Diagnosis / Recommendation

The four URL-building call sites are the right and complete set. I swept master for the class:

```
static/ui.js:7594          renderMd stash
static/messages.js:4804    _smdMediaTailFlushEntry  (^MEDIA:…$ exact)
static/messages.js:4852    _smdMediaAwareAddText    (global)
static/messages.js:4878    tail matcher             (…$)
```

All four are patched here. There is a fifth MEDIA regex at `static/ui.js:8962` (`text.replace(/MEDIA:[^\s]+/g,'a file')`) which you correctly left alone — it collapses the token into a plaintext label rather than building a URL, so a swallowed backtick is harmless there. Good call not touching it.

The `\x60` (hex) escape instead of a literal backtick is the right choice given the char-by-char source scanners in `test_smooth_text_fade` / `test_issue342`, and the rationale is worth the inline comment you added. Excluding backtick from a filesystem path class is safe — a backtick is not a valid path terminator in any of these contexts, and a genuine file with a trailing backtick in its name is not a case worth preserving over the 404.

## Verification

The new `test_media_token_in_code_span_does_not_capture_backtick` in `tests/test_renderer_js_behaviour.py` drives the real `renderMd()` via node and asserts `%60` never reaches the URL — a tight regression guard for exactly the reported symptom. This looks ready; only the four URL sites changed, behavior is otherwise identical.

## Summary

Reading the complete product diff at `b07bb4510`, the full new OPS-359 regression file, the changed fast-path and provider-repair tests, and the surrounding cache and send-path code, I found no blocking issue. The change fixes both halves of the split-state failure: the browser no longer carries a provider across a model change, and the server repairs an explicit pair only when an immediately available catalog gives complete, unique ownership evidence. The Agent runtime consumes model and provider as separate initialization inputs, so repairing the tuple before streaming is the correct WebUI boundary.

## Code reference

The server decision at `api/routes.py:6504-6553` is conservative:

```python
if any(_catalog_group_owns_exact_model(group, model) for group in requested_groups):
    return requested_provider, False
owners = {
    provider
    for group in groups
    if _catalog_group_owns_exact_model(group, model)
}
if len(owners) != 1:
    return requested_provider, False
```

`api/config.py:8633-8657` obtains memory evidence with `blocking=False`, releases the cache lock in `finally`, and falls back only to the validated disk snapshot. It never enters the live catalog builder. `static/ui.js:3091-3117` also fixes the initiating state transition: selected option metadata and matching persisted picker state now outrank the session provider, while the session provider remains usable when `session.model` exactly matches the model being sent.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The fail-closed rules are appropriate. A missing requested-provider group, any per-group endpoint error, ambiguous owners, a failed snapshot, or no snapshot preserves the submitted pair. That avoids turning an incomplete fallback catalog into routing authority. Exact custom-provider identities are also preserved, and the existing qualified-model slow path receives the same nonblocking snapshot through `catalog_override`.

The regression matrix is unusually good. `tests/test_ops359_model_provider_atomic.py:25-238` covers Terra, Luna, Sol, shared IDs, alias ambiguity, persistence, and lock contention. `tests/test_chat_start_provider_fallback.py:157-298` covers same-model collisions plus stale session transitions in the browser helper. I would keep the 0.2 second contention assertion focused on proving lock independence rather than treating it as a general performance budget, which is how it is currently written.

## Verification

The exact-head CI test, lint, browser-smoke, and conversation-lifecycle checks are green. No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: no blocker found.

payload.body:
## Summary

Reading both changed files in full at `bb5347e1c`, their `origin/master` versions, and the surrounding trusted-header binding flow, the parser change is at the right layer and I found no blocking issue. `_trusted_groups_header_value()` is the sole normalization point before group membership becomes a set, so supporting the proxy serialization there fixes both initial trusted-session creation and later identity reconciliation without changing profile precedence.

## Code reference

The functional change at `api/auth.py:714-741` is small and remains bounded to the configured groups header:

```python
normalized = str(raw).replace("\n", ",").replace("|", ",")
for part in normalized.split(","):
    part = part.strip()
    if part:
        values.append(part)
```

The result is consumed at `api/auth.py:753-761`, where `_trusted_auth_bound_profile()` converts the list to a set and still iterates the configured mapping in declaration order. That preserves the existing deterministic precedence pinned by `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py:202-212`; header order does not gain authority from this change.

The new regression at `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py:215-246` exercises the reported failure through `ensure_trusted_auth_session()`, not just the parser helper. It proves that a pipe-joined multi-group identity binds to `devops` and remains allowed by the active-profile guard.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The behavior is consistent with the existing comma and newline normalization. Empty segments and surrounding whitespace remain ignored, while a lone group is unchanged. The scope note around wildcard mapping is also accurate: this patch changes tokenization only and does not alter mapping precedence.

I recommend adding one compact parameterized parser regression before merge for comma, pipe, newline, mixed separators, repeated separators, and surrounding whitespace. The end-to-end test covers the main symptom, but a direct table would make the accepted wire formats explicit and prevent a later refactor from accidentally dropping one delimiter. If deployments can use literal pipe characters inside a group name, that compatibility tradeoff should also be documented; with the proposed contract, pipe is always structural.

The diff is two files and the new assertion matches the implementation. No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: no blocker found; add the delimiter table as a useful follow-up.

payload.title: feat(#7303): show cron responses before run diagnostics

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full parser, all route and browser changes, the changed regression files, and the Agent cron artifact contract, I found one blocking historical-run bug. The parser itself is conservative about fences, quotes, duplicate markers, errors, and malformed artifacts. The problem is how the route chooses `job_mode`: it uses the current job record rather than metadata for the historical run being opened. Since cron jobs can be edited between runs, an old script run can later be treated as an agent run, or an old agent run can be forced to raw mode.

## Code reference

`api/routes.py:21733-21766` resolves the current job and passes its present mode into the projection:

```python
get_job = getattr(cron_jobs, "get_job", None)
job = get_job(job_id) if get_job else None
job_mode = "unknown" if job is None else (
    "script" if job.get("no_agent") else "agent"
)
projection = parse_cron_output_artifact(content, job_mode=job_mode)
```

The same current-state lookup is repeated for history and output windows at `api/routes.py:21714-21725` and `api/routes.py:21877-21891`. Meanwhile, `static/panels.js:1596-1676` carries `no_agent` through the edit form, so mode is not immutable for the lifetime of files already under run history.

`api/cron_output.py:32-68` correctly refuses script and unknown modes, but that safety only works when the supplied mode belongs to this artifact. `tests/test_issue7303_cron_response_first.py:120-141` fixes `get_job()` to `no_agent=False`; it does not cover a historical mode change.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Do not derive historical presentation from the mutable current job definition. Persist the run mode beside each output filename, or derive it from an immutable field in the saved artifact contract and use the current job only as a fallback for legacy files. Deleted jobs should remain unknown/raw unless their own run metadata proves agent mode.

A minimal regression should create or fixture two historical artifacts under one job, change the current job from script to agent and then from agent to script, and verify that each artifact keeps its original projection. Also cover a deleted job and a script payload containing marker-like headings; both must remain raw.

The browser response-first hierarchy at `static/panels.js:1425-1506` looks sound once the API projection is trustworthy. Diagnostics and raw output use literal DOM text, expansion changes only the response cap, and the tests cover focus plus narrow layout.

## Verification

Exact-head CI is green, but the current tests do not exercise mode mutation. No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: block until historical run mode no longer depends on the current job record.

payload.author: rodboev
payload.body:

`api/routes.py` applies that resolution independently in history, detail, and bounded-output routes. Agent usage comes only from contiguous top-level metadata, script and unknown artifacts stay raw with no fabricated usage, and detail paths remain confined to the requested job directory.

The regressions cover both job-edit directions, deleted jobs, legacy Agent fallback, failed and silent scripts, fenced and marker-like payloads, platform-stable raw bytes, usage isolation, cross-job path traversal, and all three route consumers.

payload.author: rodboev
payload.title: fix(#7295): keep scheduled cron runs off the profile lock

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading all five changed files at `7ab6af748`, the complete new subprocess transport, both full regression files, and the current Agent scheduler lifecycle, I found a blocking contract break in the live-adapter path. The normal branch correctly sends the original `run_one_job` lifecycle into the child. When `adapters` or `loop` is present, however, the wrapper bypasses `run_one_job`, runs only `run_job` in the child, and reconstructs completion in WebUI. Those live handles are present on the ordinary gateway tick path, so this is not a rare compatibility branch.

## Code reference

The split occurs at `api/profiles.py:698-719`:

```python
if live_adapters is not None or live_loop is not None:
    ...
    if claim_dispatch is not None and not claim_dispatch(job["id"]):
        return True
    result = run_cron_in_profile_subprocess(
        job, execution_home, "run_job", args=args, kwargs=child_kwargs
    )
    return _complete_cron_run_with_live_handles(
        job, result, live_adapters, live_loop,
        verbose=bool(kwargs.get("verbose")),
    )
```

`api/profiles.py:767-805` then saves output, performs delivery, and calls `mark_job_run`. That is only a subset of the lifecycle currently owned by Agent `cron/scheduler.py:6270-6368` and `cron/scheduler.py:6373-6860`. The Agent path also owns the fire-claim heartbeat, execution-ledger completion, interruption settlement, fire-owner fencing, lost-claim behavior, and delivery outcome. A WebUI-side replacement cannot safely omit or duplicate those steps.

The failure fallback at `api/profiles.py:754-764` is particularly risky because it calls `mark_job_run` without the expected fire owner. A child timeout or crash can therefore write terminal state after ownership has moved to a replacement worker.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Keep `run_one_job` as the sole lifecycle owner for every scheduled path. The non-serializable delivery handles need a narrow bridge, not a second lifecycle implementation. The safe design is an Agent-owned seam where `run_one_job` can request delivery through a serializable parent proxy or callback channel while claim heartbeat, fencing, execution records, save, and terminal settlement remain in the child lifecycle. If that seam does not exist yet, coordinate the Agent change first rather than copying private scheduler behavior into `api/profiles.py`.

`tests/test_scheduled_jobs_profile_isolation.py:580-621` currently mocks `_complete_cron_run_with_live_handles` and proves only that arguments are forwarded. Add an integration contract that exercises real live-handle execution and asserts one claim, active heartbeat during a blocked run, one fenced terminal mark, one execution-ledger finish, and one delivery. Add a takeover case where the old child returns after losing ownership and must not settle the replacement claim.

The shared transport at `api/cron_runtime.py:108-194` does solve the parent lock wait and drains the queue before joining. That part can remain once lifecycle ownership is corrected.

## Verification

Exact-head checks are green, but they do not cover the omitted Agent lifecycle state. No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: block the live-handle lifecycle split.

I removed the live un_job plus parent completion path. Scheduled and in-chat fires now execute Agent's existing un_one_job end to end in the profile-pinned child; WebUI no longer claims, saves, delivers, or marks those runs.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Re-reading the current head `bc27c15b7`, the previous lifecycle-ownership blocker is fixed: scheduled and in-chat fires now call Agent `run_one_job` end to end in the child, and the WebUI no longer performs its own save, delivery, or terminal mark. One blocking regression remains. The ordinary gateway path supplies live adapters and an event loop, but this revision deliberately drops both and changes those jobs to Agent standalone delivery. Adapter-dependent relay and encrypted destinations therefore lose working delivery behavior in exchange for releasing the profile lock.

## Code reference

The split is now explicit at `api/profiles.py:698-741`:

```python
live_context = [
    name for name in ("adapters", "loop")
    if child_kwargs.pop(name, None) is not None
]
cancel_event = child_kwargs.pop("cancel_event", None)
...
return run_cron_in_profile_subprocess(
    job, execution_home, "run_one_job",
    args=args, kwargs=child_kwargs, cancel_event=cancel_event,
)
```

`api/cron_runtime.py:35-43` strips the same process-local values defensively. The lifecycle side is now correct against `cron/scheduler.py:6373-6848`: claims, heartbeat, execution records, save, delivery outcome, fencing, and terminal settlement stay inside Agent `run_one_job`. The transport side is not equivalent, because Agent delivery in that function consumes `adapters` and `loop` when available.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The PR body already acknowledges that relay-fronted and encrypted delivery may record an error. That is a user-visible regression on the normal gateway tick path, not merely missing verification. A scheduled job that previously delivered through its live adapter can now complete its run but fail its configured destination.

Keep the corrected sole-owner lifecycle, but do not merge the live-handle downgrade as the final contract. The clean fix is the proposed Agent-owned serializable delivery bridge so the child retains claim and settlement ownership while delegating only transport I/O to the parent. If that seam cannot land with this PR, scope child isolation to invocations without live handles and preserve the existing path for adapter-backed jobs until the bridge exists. That is partial lock relief, but it avoids breaking delivery.

## Test plan

`tests/test_scheduled_jobs_profile_isolation.py:test_scheduler_live_gateway_handles_use_child_run_one_job_standalone_delivery` currently asserts that the handles are discarded; it proves the limitation rather than parity. Add a contract test with an adapter-only destination and assert one accepted delivery plus one Agent-owned fenced settlement. Also cover a child crash after parent transport acceptance so replay ownership is explicit.

Verdict: the lifecycle duplication blocker is resolved; block now on the admitted live-adapter delivery regression.

payload.author: rodboev
payload.title: feat(#7309): add built-in OpenCode Free provider

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full provider, onboarding, Settings, picker, and regression changes at `337a8194b`, I found a blocking availability bug. OpenCode Free is described as a built-in keyless entry point, but both catalog builders hide it for the most common existing-user state: another provider is active and there is no explicit `providers.opencode-free` config entry. Curiously, `providers.only_configured=true` later adds it unconditionally, so the stricter mode exposes the provider while the default mode can hide it.

## Code reference

The static path at `api/config.py:5644-5653` and live path at `api/config.py:7790-7799` use the same gate:

```python
if provider_is_keyless("opencode-free") and (
    not active_provider
    or active_provider == "opencode-free"
    or any(
        _canonicalise_provider_id(key) == "opencode-free"
        for key in (cfg.get("providers") or {})
    )
):
    detected_providers.add("opencode-free")
```

With a normal configuration such as active `openai-codex` and no free-provider stanza, every condition is false. The group therefore never reaches `_append_picker_group()` at `api/config.py:7862-7880`. By contrast, the `only_configured` branch at `api/config.py:7816-7820` adds it without that gate.

## Summary

Reading the new adapter in full at `746f38293`, the complete status regression file, the provider quota composition, browser rendering, styles, locale additions, and README contract, I found no blocking issue. The implementation keeps local account state authoritative, uses exact canonical provider slugs, and fails soft when the optional feed is disabled, malformed, stale, slow, oversized, or unavailable.

## Code reference

The composition boundary at `api/providers.py:2129-2141` preserves the existing local envelope and adds only optional context:

```python
provider = _canonicalise_provider_id(provider_id or _active_provider_id() or "")
local = _get_provider_quota_local(provider, refresh=refresh)
if not provider or not _is_known_model_provider(provider):
    return local
public = get_public_provider_statuses(
    known_slugs={provider}, refresh=refresh
).get(provider)
if public:
    local["public_status"] = public
```

`api/provider_status.py:38-60` rejects non-HTTP schemes, credentials, fragments, missing hosts, and malformed port syntax. `api/provider_status.py:71-121` then requires schema version 1, fresh timezone-aware timestamps, an allowed status, and exact row slugs; descriptions are whitespace-normalized and capped. The fetch path at `api/provider_status.py:168-210` denies redirects, sends fixed headers, applies the body sentinel, and returns no row on decode or schema failure.

The browser side at `static/panels.js:11218-11266` uses DOM-created nodes and `textContent` for external description and metadata. Source links are limited to normalized HTTP(S) values and receive `noopener noreferrer`, so the new feed does not enter the existing HTML template as markup.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The URL-keyed cache and per-URL in-flight event are a good fit. Freshness is checked against wall time even while the transport TTL remains valid, and unrelated feed URLs do not serialize behind one global fetch. Using a spawned, terminable process for the production network operation also gives the three-second bound meaning when a socket object cannot be reached to update read timeouts.

Two non-blocking follow-ups would improve confidence. First, add a product-path test for `_fetch_killable()` with a child that ignores normal completion, rather than testing most timeout cases through the monkeypatched thread fetcher. Assert that the child and queue are gone after the bound. Second, document that the feed URL is trusted operator configuration and must never become a request parameter or ordinary Settings field; the current environment-only surface has that property, but it is part of the security model.

## Verification

`tests/test_issue6805_provider_status.py:20-340` covers parsing, freshness, exact matching, coalescing, fixed headers, redirects, size, slow reads, rendering, and local-state precedence. Exact-head CI and docs checks are green. No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: no blocker found.

## Summary

I re-read the full adapter and regression file at the current head, then compared them with the accepted schema recorded on issue #6805 and the new contributor report. The contributor report is correct: this PR defines and tests a different flat feed contract, so the motivating aggregate endpoint produces zero usable rows. The fail-soft behavior prevents a crash, but it also makes the feature silently nonfunctional for the source whose contract was accepted before implementation.

## Code reference

`api/provider_status.py:70-84` requires this top-level shape:

```python
not isinstance(payload, dict)
or type(payload.get("version")) is not int
or payload.get("version") != 1
or not isinstance(payload.get("providers"), list)
```

The parser then reads `payload["generatedAt"]` and each row as `row["status"]`, `row["checkedAt"]`, and `row["url"]` at `api/provider_status.py:85-112`. The accepted issue contract is nested instead: version and generation metadata live under `meta`, rows live under `data.providers`, status is under `currentStatus.code`, freshness is under `source.checkedAt`, and source links are under `source.statusPageUrl` or `source.officialUrl`.

The mismatch is also baked into `tests/test_issue6805_provider_status.py:12-14`, whose `_payload()` fixture constructs only the flat schema, and into the README contract added near `README.md:380`. No test uses the accepted nested envelope. On the browser side, `static/panels.js:11233-11266` accepts only `operational`, `degraded`, and `outage`, so `partial_outage`, `major_outage`, and `maintenance` also need an explicit mapping before rendering.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

This is blocking for the stated feature. Keep the transport bounds, redirect denial, URL-keyed cache, exact-slug lookup, local-state precedence, and DOM-safe rendering. Replace the invented flat parser contract with the accepted generic nested version-1 contract:

- require `meta.version == "v1"` and validate `meta.generatedAt`;
- read rows only from `data.providers`;
- map `currentStatus.code` deliberately, for example partial and major outage into the local outage severity, while deciding how maintenance appears;
- take bounded description text from `currentStatus.summary`;
- validate freshness from `source.checkedAt` and normalize the selected source URL;
- keep `unknown`, stale, malformed, absent, and unsupported rows hidden.

Do not special-case a hostname or vendor name. The schema itself is the generic integration boundary.

## Test plan

Replace the flat helper fixture with the exact nested envelope from #6805. Add every accepted status code, malformed `meta` and `data` containers, source URL precedence, stale source timestamps, exact-slug collisions, and one route-level composition assertion proving a compatible payload reaches `public_status`. Keep the existing timeout, size, redirect, cache, local-authority, and textContent safety tests.

No contributor-authored code was executed during this read-only review. Verdict: block until the parser and documentation implement the accepted nested contract.

## Summary

Reading `api/streaming.py` and both changed test files at `5b9d60ee2`, plus their `origin/master` versions, the new-candidate path correctly rejects the structural menu and the unresolved path correctly switches to the latest completed exchange. I found one recovery gap: a session that already persisted this exact malformed title before the patch remains permanently classified as successfully titled. The new matcher exists only in `_is_bad_new_title()`, while existing-title self-heal still uses `_looks_invalid_generated_title()`, which does not recognize title-option menus.

## Code reference

The early gate at `api/streaming.py:4703-4720` is decisive:

```python
_invalid_existing = _looks_invalid_generated_title(s.title)
if getattr(s, 'llm_title_generated', False) and not _invalid_existing:
    _put_title_status(put_event, session_id, 'skipped', 'already_generated', str(s.title or ''))
    return
```

The structural menu matcher added at `api/streaming.py:3727-3742` is called only while sanitizing a fresh candidate. It is absent from `_looks_invalid_generated_title()` at `api/streaming.py:3685-3705`. Consequently, an existing title beginning with `Good title options:` has `llm_title_generated=True`, produces `_invalid_existing=False`, and exits above before the later exchange-selection logic can run. The turn-end scheduling gate at `api/streaming.py:11568-11578` has the same dependency on `_invalid_existing_title`.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

## Summary

Re-reading the complete current diff at `14aeb6940`, the focused follow-up from `5b9d60ee2`, the full streaming/model files, and both changed regression files, the persisted-menu recovery gap from my previous review is fixed. The shared matcher now reaches both fresh and stored titles, and the new persisted-title case proves that an old generated menu can re-enter self-heal. The follow-up introduces a deterministic deadlock, however: the initial eligibility block acquires the global non-reentrant session lock and then calls `get_session()`, whose canonical resolver acquires the same lock.

## Code reference

The new ordering at `api/streaming.py:4710-4718` is the blocker:

```python
with LOCK:
    s = get_session(session_id)
    cached_session = SESSIONS.get(session_id)
    if cached_session is not None:
        s = cached_session
```

`LOCK` is a plain `threading.Lock` at `api/config.py:8839`, not an `RLock`. The production `get_session()` entry point at `api/models.py:4915-4917` delegates to `_resolve_session()`, and `_resolve_session_once()` immediately enters `with LOCK` at `api/models.py:4737` to inspect the cache. On every real background-title call, the thread therefore blocks trying to reacquire the lock it already owns. Title generation never begins and no title-status event is emitted.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Move the canonical load outside the explicit critical section, then rebind and snapshot under the lock:

```python
s = get_session(session_id)
with LOCK:
    cached_session = SESSIONS.get(session_id)
    if cached_session is not None and cached_session.session_id == session_id:
        s = cached_session
    # snapshot title eligibility fields here
```

This keeps the intended race defense. `get_session()` performs its own cache/load synchronization, and the second locked lookup observes any canonical object replacement or manual rename that happened between the load and eligibility snapshot. Keep the later write-side `_get_session_agent_lock` plus `LOCK` recheck unchanged.

The new test at `tests/test_2235_initial_aux_title.py:194-225` patches both `api.streaming.get_session` and `api.streaming.LOCK`, so its mock loader never tries to acquire the patched lock and cannot expose the production recursion. ## Summary

Reading the full `server.py` at `cbfe0ce43` and on `origin/master`, plus the shutdown route that sends SIGINT, this five-line change closes the reported daemon gap. The existing shutdown machinery at `server.py:697-729` already has the necessary deadlock avoidance and idempotency:

_shutdown_requested = threading.Event()

def _request_shutdown(signum, _frame):
    if _shutdown_requested.is_set():

No functional change requested. One small cleanup would be to rename the helper thread to a signal-neutral value such as `webui-signal-shutdown`, since it now handles both signals, but that is not blocking.
