payload.body:
## Summary

I reviewed the refreshed head `edd543f9` against `origin/master`, including the full resolver and handoff files plus both changed test files. The auxiliary-slot and session-handoff additions now carry the selected/session provider through the sibling paths, and the exact-base-URL handling fixes the normalized-slug collision case. One core resolver edge remains: an explicitly selected named custom provider can still lose to config order whenever `model.base_url` is present but stale or otherwise does not match an entry.

## Code reference

At `api/config.py:2768-2792`, a configured base URL changes the selection rules from provider identity to base-URL identity:

```python
if len(_base_matches) == 1:
    entry = _base_matches[0]
    if _entry_owns_model(entry):
        return model_id, _active_custom_slug, (entry.get("base_url") or "").strip() or None
elif not _norm_active_base and len(_slug_matches) == 1:
    entry = _slug_matches[0]
```

If `config_provider` is explicitly `custom:packyapi`, `config_base_url` contains an old URL, and exactly one entry has the `packyapi` slug, `_base_matches` is empty but `_norm_active_base` is truthy. The unique-slug branch is skipped, then the ordered scan below can return an earlier provider that also owns the model. That defeats the explicit provider selection this guard is meant to preserve.

The added resolver cases at `tests/test_model_resolver.py:258-386` cover a matching active URL, no URL, and same-slug ambiguity. They do not cover explicit named-provider identity plus a nonmatching retained URL. The new handoff wiring at `api/routes.py:26082-26104` can encounter this shape because session provider identity is authoritative even when persisted endpoint metadata has drifted.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Treat an explicit, unambiguous named provider as authoritative unless the base URL positively identifies a different entry with the same normalized slug. A stale nonmatching URL is not evidence that the unique slug match should be discarded. One safe order is:

1. Use one exact base-URL match when present.
2. Otherwise use one unique slug match.
3. Fail closed only when multiple entries share the slug and the URL cannot disambiguate them.

That preserves the collision protection without letting unrelated stale metadata demote explicit identity to config-order fallback.

## Verification

Add a regression with A first, B explicitly selected, both owning `shared-model`, and `model.base_url` set to a third stale URL. Assert B wins. Keep the existing same-slug ambiguity case to prove the unique-slug fallback does not guess between colliding entries. I did not execute PR-authored code during this read-only review.

payload.author: rouVling
payload.body:
Pushed `68701375` addressing all three findings from the re-gate.

## 1. [CORE] `set_auxiliary_model()` self-deadlock (aux path)
Root cause confirmed: the setter held the non-reentrant `_cfg_lock` and then called `resolve_custom_provider_connection(provider)` -> `get_config()` -> `reload_config_if_stale()`, which re-acquires `_cfg_lock`.

Fix: the selected `custom:<slug>` provider's `base_url` is now resolved **inline from the `config_data` already loaded under the lock** (mirroring the slug matching of `resolve_custom_provider_connection`), so no lock-acquiring helper runs while `_cfg_lock` is held. The bare-`custom` fallback still uses `resolve_model_provider(model)`, which reads the module `cfg` global and never touches `_cfg_lock`.

## 2. [CORE] normalized-name collision mixes endpoint + credential
You're right that returning the shared `custom:foo-bar` slug is unsafe at its root: the credential lookup at `resolve_custom_provider_connection` resolves the key from the **first** same-slug entry regardless of `base_url`, so endpoint B ends up paired with credential A. Since the resolver can only hand back a slug, no `base_url` disambiguation can make that pairing safe.

Fix: **fail closed** on any normalized-slug collision. `resolve_model_provider()` now builds an ownership-by-slug map and raises a new `AmbiguousCustomProviderError` (a `ValueError` subclass, so existing broad/`ValueError` fallbacks still catch it) whenever a slug is shared by >=2 entries that own the requested model — on **both** the active-slug guard and the ordered-scan fall-through. The error names the colliding providers, the shared slug, and the model.

## 3. Explicit provider vs. stale `base_url` (first-review edge)
The `_base_matches`/`_norm_active_base` branch logic is removed. An explicit, **unambiguous** named custom provider is now authoritative even when `model.base_url` is stale/absent and matches no entry — a stale URL is no longer evidence to demote it to config order. Unique slug wins; colliding slug fails closed.

## Verification
- Rewrote the two collision tests to assert `AmbiguousCustomProviderError` (was asserting the buggy first-match/`base_url` result).
- Added the requested regression: providers A (first) + B (explicitly selected) both own `shared-model`, `model.base_url` set to a third stale URL -> **B wins** (proves unique-slug authority survives a stale URL). Before the fix this returned `custom:dogapi`.
- Added a watchdog-guarded aux no-deadlock regression using the **real** `get_config` (only `reload_config`, which runs after the lock releases, is stubbed). It times out/fails on the pre-fix code and passes now.
- All three new/rewritten tests fail before the fix and pass after.
- `tests/test_model_resolver.py` + `tests/test_auxiliary_models_settings.py`: 126 passed (the one unrelated failure, `test_resolver_provenance_read_does_not_block_on_cache_lock_5979`, also fails on the clean HEAD `edd543f9` — a live-catalog-rebuild timing flake, not touched here).
- Related suites green: `test_pr1947_same_model_multiple_custom_providers`, `test_issue1894_provider_overlap`, `test_issue1806_named_custom_provider_resolution`, `test_issue1855_resolve_model_provider_fast_path`, `test_resolve_model_provider_free_suffix`, `test_custom_provider_dict_models`, `test_custom_providers_in_panel`, `test_issue1106_custom_providers_models`, `test_issue2513_custom_provider_remote_models`, `test_issue1013_handoff_dock`, `test_custom_provider_display_name`, `test_issue1105_ssrf_custom_providers` (118 passed).

The `dogapi`/`packyapi` different-slug overlap tests are unaffected — only genuine same-normalized-slug collisions fail closed.

Model used: Anthropic claude opus 4.8 via cursor plan mode

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I re-read the full `api/config.py` and `api/routes.py` at head `68701375`, their `origin/master` versions, the complete diff, and both changed test files. The auxiliary lock re-entry fix is sound, and the stale-base-URL and session-handoff changes move routing in the right direction. One credential-safety blocker remains: normalized-slug collision detection counts only entries that advertise the requested model, while credential resolution scans every entry with that slug. An asymmetric collision can still combine one entry endpoint with another entry credential.

## Code reference

At `api/config.py:2781-2790`, non-owning same-slug entries are excluded from the collision map:

```python
for entry in custom_providers:
    if not isinstance(entry, dict):
        continue
    entry_name = (entry.get("name") or "").strip()
    if not entry_name or not _entry_owns_model(entry):
        continue
```

The resolver then treats one owning entry as unambiguous at `api/config.py:2801-2812` and returns its endpoint with the shared slug. But `resolve_custom_provider_connection()` at `api/config.py:3124-3142` scans all custom-provider entries by normalized name and returns the first match, without considering model ownership or the endpoint selected above.

A concrete reachable shape is:

- entry A is named `Foo Bar`, appears first, and does not list `shared-model`;
- entry B is named `foo-bar`, lists `shared-model`, and is the active endpoint;
- both normalize to `custom:foo-bar`.

`_owning_by_slug` contains only B, so model resolution returns B endpoint plus `custom:foo-bar`. The later connection lookup finds A first and supplies A credential and A endpoint metadata.

The provider-qualified handoff lane also bypasses this guard. `api/routes.py:26079-26107` encodes the session provider into the model, and the `@provider:model` return at `api/config.py:2887-2900` occurs after the ownership scan has seen the encoded string rather than the bare model. The subsequent handoff credential backfill can therefore hit the same first-match collision. The inline auxiliary lookup at `api/config.py:4962-4980` is another first-match-by-slug path.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please build collision membership from all named entries, independent of model ownership. Keep a separate ownership map if needed for selecting the model owner, but reject any slug represented by multiple config entries before returning or consuming that slug. Apply the same uniqueness helper to the provider-qualified path and auxiliary persistence so every slug-only boundary fails closed consistently.

## Verification

The current collision tests at `tests/test_model_resolver.py:333-374` give both colliding entries the model, so they miss the asymmetric case. Add A-first/non-owner plus B-owner coverage, then exercise the provider-qualified handoff shape and auxiliary save path. I did not execute PR-authored code during this read-only review.

payload.author: rouVling
payload.body:
Pushed `7bc83fcc` — the collision fail-closed is now applied consistently at all four slug-only boundaries via one shared helper, and collision membership is built from ALL named entries (independent of model ownership).

## Root cause of the remaining gap
The prior cut built collision membership only from entries that *own* the requested model, while credential resolution scans *every* same-slug entry and first-matches regardless of ownership. So the asymmetric shape (A `Foo Bar` first + non-owner, B `foo-bar` owner + active) slipped through: resolution returned B's endpoint + `custom:foo-bar`, and the credential lookup first-matched A.

## Shared helper
New `_unique_custom_provider_entry(custom_providers, slug_key)` (with `_custom_provider_slug_key` for one canonical normalization). It is pure and lock-safe (operates only on the passed-in list), groups **all named entries** by canonical slug, raises `AmbiguousCustomProviderError` on >=2, and otherwise returns the single match (or `None`).

## Applied at all four sites
1. **Bare resolution** (`resolve_model_provider`, was config.py:2781) — all-entry membership for both the active-slug guard and the ordered ownership scan (replaced the owner-only `_owning_by_slug` map).
2. **Provider-qualified path** (`@custom:<slug>:model`, was config.py:2887) — the `model_with_provider_context()` session/send/handoff shape now runs the same check on the parsed hint before returning it.
3. **Credential lookup** (`resolve_custom_provider_connection`, was config.py:3128) — replaced its private first-match-by-slug scan (and its duplicate `_slugify`) with the shared helper, so endpoint and credential always come from the same entry.
4. **Auxiliary persistence** (`set_auxiliary_model`, was config.py:4971) — replaced the inline first-match-by-slug; the ambiguity now **propagates and fails the save** instead of being swallowed, while other best-effort errors stay non-fatal. Still resolves from the in-scope `config_data`, so the deadlock fix is preserved (no `get_config()`/`_cfg_lock` re-entry).

## Verification (all five new regressions fail before this change, pass after)
- Asymmetric A-first-non-owner/B-owner — active-endpoint path and bare-`custom` ordered-scan path.
- `model_with_provider_context('shared-model', 'custom:foo-bar')` qualified handoff shape -> raises.
- `resolve_custom_provider_connection('custom:foo-bar')` called directly (the handoff/context-length credential backfill) -> raises.
- Auxiliary save `set_auxiliary_model('vision', 'custom:foo-bar', ...)` -> raises and persists nothing (slot stays `auto`).

Confirmed by reverting only `api/config.py`: all five FAIL on the prior head, PASS with the fix.

Suites: `tests/test_model_resolver.py` + `tests/test_auxiliary_models_settings.py` = 131 passed (the lone unrelated failure, `test_resolver_provenance_read_does_not_block_on_cache_lock_5979`, also fails on clean `edd543f9` — a live-catalog-rebuild timing flake). Related custom-provider/handoff suites green (258 passed across the resolver/aux + 15 neighboring files). Distinct-slug overlap (`dogapi`/`packyapi`) and single-entry custom providers are unaffected — only genuine same-normalized-slug collisions fail closed.

payload.author: rouVling
payload.body:
Thanks for the deep re-gate — all five are addressed at `06581360`. The core rework is 1+2: one authoritative slug identity, checked at the point of return.

### CORE 1 — one canonical slug identity
`_custom_provider_slug_key()` now derives from the real producer `_custom_provider_slug_from_name()` (not a private variant), so every slug-only boundary (bare + qualified resolution, credential lookup, aux persistence) compares against the same identity that is actually returned/persisted/routed. Reproduced the mismatch and the fix:

```
'Foo (Bar)'  producer='custom:foo-bar'  OLD-key='foo-(bar)'  -> producer collide: True | OLD-key collide: False
'foo-bar'    producer='custom:foo-bar'  OLD-key='foo-bar'
```

So the parenthesized/punctuated collision is now detected on all direct paths.

### CORE 2 — check only at the point of return
Added a `_finalize()` guard used by **every** custom-slug return in `resolve_model_provider` (the active-slug branch, the ordered scan, the qualified `@custom:` hint, the cross-provider prefix, and the final active-provider fallback). The active-slug branch no longer raises up front — it only consumes (and fails closed on) the active slug when the active provider actually lists the model. With a `Foo Bar`/`foo-bar` collision active, `@openrouter:...` and `@custom:safe-provider:safe-model` now resolve normally; only a request that resolves to the colliding slug fails closed.

### CORE 3 — endpoint + credential from one profile snapshot
`streaming.py` now resolves the endpoint AND the credential inside a single profile scope: the main path extends the scope over runtime-key + custom-provider resolution, and both self-heal retry paths bind the session profile. `resolve_custom_provider_connection` runs under the passed profile, so a detached worker can't pair a named profile's endpoint with the default profile's key.

### SILENT 4 — handoff ambiguity -> 400
`_handle_handoff_summary` catches `AmbiguousCustomProviderError` before the generic fallback and returns **400** with the rename message. `sessions.js` surfaces a 400's message verbatim instead of the generic retry card.

### SILENT 5 — saves surface the error and abort
Aux-model and default-model saves now surface the server's message and abort (retain dirty state) instead of swallowing it into "Failed to save…" / "settings saved". `AmbiguousCustomProviderError` gained a `.message` attribute for verbatim forwarding.

### Tests
- `tests/test_model_resolver.py`: parenthesized-name collision fails closed on bare / qualified / credential paths; unrelated `@openrouter` and `@custom:safe-provider` lanes are **not** blocked by an active collision; the owned colliding model still fails closed.
- `tests/test_auxiliary_models_settings.py`: parenthesized-name collision fails closed on the aux save path (no persist).
- `tests/test_issue2271_keyless_custom_provider.py`: custom overrides resolve the connection **inside** the passed profile scope.
- `tests/test_issue1013_handoff_dock.py`: handoff returns 400 (no persisted fallback) on ambiguity; JS error-surfacing source guards for the save + handoff paths.

Verified findings 1+2 fail before / pass after (old key misses `Foo (Bar)`/`foo-bar`; old up-front check over-blocks `@openrouter`). All affected suites pass; the only red is the pre-existing `test_resolver_provenance_read_does_not_block_on_cache_lock_5979` rebuild-budget flake, which fails identically on clean `HEAD` on this machine.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body: Shipping in **exp-v0.52.252**. Thank you @rouVling — this was a genuinely hard fix that converged over four rounds, and the final "one canonical slug identity" approach is exactly right: routing `_custom_provider_slug_key()` through the same `_custom_provider_slug_from_name()` that mints the slug closes the whole class of endpoint/credential-mismatch bugs (parenthesized names like `Foo (Bar)` now collide-detect instead of splitting). Gate verified all five prior findings closed and non-vacuous: canonical slug + point-of-return collision checks, unrelated-provider routing no longer over-blocks, named-profile endpoint+credential resolved in the same scope, handoff ambiguity returns HTTP 400 to the UI, and aux/default-model saves surface the actionable error — plus the original deadlock stays closed. Codex SAFE + full suite 14,870/0.

payload.author: badiyee85
payload.title: feat(server): emit initial HSTS response header

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @badiyee85 — HSTS support is a reasonable hardening for HTTPS-fronted deployments, and the CSP chokepoint (`end_headers()`) is the right place. But emitting it **unconditionally** is a real brick risk, so it needs to be opt-in and secure-context-gated:

### Must-fix (BRICK, reproduced) — unconditional HSTS conflicts with the HTTP fallback
`server.py:334`. An error-free HTTPS response pins the hostname for 24h. HSTS then rewrites `http://host:8787` → HTTPS (preserving port 8787) and forbids bypassing TLS errors — directly conflicting with the native-TLS→HTTP fallback at `server.py:685`. So a user who hits the box over HTTPS once, then switches that hostname to plain HTTP on 8787 (or hits the TLS fallback), can lose all browser access for 24h.

Nuance the gate confirmed (so we're precise, not alarmist): plain HTTP currently emits the header but conforming browsers ignore HSTS over HTTP; IP literals like `127.0.0.1` are excluded, so the ordinary SSH-tunnel / Tailscale-IP workflow isn't *immediately* bricked. But `localhost` is **not** portably exempt — Chromium adds its own localhost exemption, Firefox (per its `nsSiteSecurityService`) excludes IPs but **not** `localhost` (RFC 6797 doesn't exempt it). So a `localhost` HTTPS→HTTP transition on Firefox is a genuine lockout.

**Fix:**
1. `server.py:334` — make HSTS **explicitly opt-in, default-off**, and emit it **only** when `_is_secure_context(self)` confirms direct TLS or a trusted-proxy HTTPS request. Gate the value on a nonnegative `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE` env (or config key): unset/empty → no header; `86400` → opt-in; `0` → emitted with `max-age=0` for rollback/un-pinning. Keep `includeSubDomains`/`preload` off by default (your conservative choice there is correct).
2. `tests/test_issue1909_csp_enforcement.py:118` — the current assertion is non-vacuous but locks in the unsafe unconditional behavior. Replace it with cases proving (a) default + plain-HTTP **omits** HSTS, and (b) explicit opt-in on a **verified secure** request emits the configured value.

This also matches the project's "self-contained opt-in > default-for-everyone" principle for anything that can affect access. Re-push with the secure-context guard + config gate and I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @badiyee85 — the re-push closes the original BRICK risk cleanly: HSTS is now opt-in (`HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS`, default-off) and gated behind `_is_secure_transport()`, so it can never appear on a plain-HTTP response. I verified end-to-end that a failed-TLS→HTTP fallback emits no HSTS, and that the `_is_secure_context()` refactor (cookie `Secure` flag) does **not** regress for plain sockets, `ssl.SSLSocket`, trusted proxies, or `HERMES_WEBUI_SECURE`. 29 auth/HSTS + 3 TLS-fallback tests pass.

But the adversarial security re-gate found **one real BRICK-severity residual** that needs one more turn before this can ship.

## Must-fix (BRICK) — disabling HSTS can't unpin a browser (no rollback path)

`server.py` — `_HSTS_HEADER_VALUE` is hard-coded to `max-age=86400`, and the gate is boolean: enabled → emit 24h, disabled → emit nothing. Per [RFC 6797 §6.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797#section-6.1.1), **omitting** the header does NOT clear a previously-cached policy — only actively serving `max-age=0` does. So a user who received HSTS once stays force-upgraded (across every port on that hostname, incl. the native-TLS→HTTP fallback) for the full 24h even after the operator sets `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS=0`. There's no supported way to roll back a mistaken enable except waiting out the max-age. This is the same lockout class as the original finding, just triggered by disable-after-enable instead of unconditional-emit.

### The fix (Codex-verified, minimal)

1. **`server.py`** — replace the boolean `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS` gate with an integer **`HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE`**: unset or invalid → no header; any nonnegative integer → emit `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=<value>` **only** through `_is_secure_transport()` (keep that gate exactly as-is). Crucially this lets an operator set `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE=0` to serve `max-age=0` over a still-working HTTPS connection and **unpin** browsers before switching back to HTTP.

2. **`.env.example` + `README.md`** — document the max-age setting and two caveats: (a) rollback requires serving `max-age=0` over HTTPS *before* switching that hostname to HTTP; (b) the policy is hostname-wide and applies across all ports, and **`localhost` is NOT exempt in Firefox** (only IP literals are), so enabling HSTS on a `localhost` HTTPS setup can lock out a later `localhost` HTTP visit. (`includeSubDomains`/`preload` intentionally absent — good, keep them out.)

3. **`tests/test_issue1909_csp_enforcement.py`** — update the boolean tests to the max-age contract; add a secure-response assertion that `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE=0` emits `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=0`; keep the plain-HTTP omission assertion.

Everything else is in great shape — this is purely about making an enable reversible. Re-push and I'll re-gate promptly.

payload.author: greptile-apps
payload.body:
Greptile Summary

 The PR adds an opt-in HSTS response header restricted to direct TLS or explicitly trusted forwarded HTTPS requests. - Adds configurable `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE`, including `max-age=0` rollback support. - Separates transport security detection from the Secure-cookie override. - Documents browser pinning, hostname/port scope, localhost behavior, and rollback requirements. - Adds tests for direct TLS, trusted proxies, insecure requests, invalid configuration, and policy removal.

Confidence Score: 5/5

 The PR appears safe to merge. No blocking failure remains.

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | api/auth.py | Extracts secure-transport detection and adds validated, HTTPS-gated HSTS header generation without coupling it to Secure-cookie overrides. | | server.py | Emits the configured HSTS policy from the shared response-header boundary when transport validation succeeds. | | README.md | Documents HSTS opt-in behavior, browser pinning scope, rollback procedure, and intentionally omitted directives. | | .env.example | Provides detailed operator guidance for enabling and safely removing the HSTS policy. | | tests/test_issue1909_csp_enforcement.py | Covers disabled, insecure, direct-TLS, trusted-proxy, rollback, cookie-override, and invalid-value cases. |

Sequence Diagram

 ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Browser participant Handler participant Auth as api/auth.py Handler->>Auth: hsts_header_value(handler) Auth->>Auth: Validate HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE Auth->>Auth: Check direct TLS or trusted forwarded HTTPS alt Valid opt-in and secure transport Auth-->>Handler: "max-age=" Handler-->>Browser: Strict-Transport-Security else Disabled, invalid, or insecure Auth-->>Handler: None Handler-->>Browser: Response without HSTS end ```
Reviews (4): Last reviewed commit: ["fix(security): make HSTS rollback explic..."](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/commit/3ebd0e04d0a2fa0860d7435b68f9612618baaf4c) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=53928954)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Re-gate at exact head `3ebd0e04` — **GREEN, the BRICK residual is fully closed.** Thanks @badiyee85, the r3 fix implements the rollback spec exactly.

**What's fixed:**
- `HERMES_WEBUI_HSTS_MAX_AGE` replaces the boolean gate. `0` over HTTPS now emits `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=0` — the RFC 6797 unpinning path — so a mistaken enable is reversible (serve `max-age=0` over HTTPS, then switch back to HTTP). Unset/empty/invalid emit nothing.
- HSTS logic moved into `api/auth.py` (`hsts_header_value()`), so `server.py` is back to 749 lines (the `<750` guard passes).

**Gate evidence (adversarial security re-gate):**

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Reviewed the diff at `tests/test_ttl_cache.py` and `tests/test_glm_5_3_catalog.py` against `api/config.py` on `origin/master`. Both hardenings are correct and target the real failure mechanisms.

## `test_mtime_invalidation` — forced-sync priming is the right fix

The order dependency was real: a shard picking up this test without a sibling having warmed the in-process cache could hit the bounded rebuild path and return a static fallback *without* publishing `_available_models_cache`, so the first `assert config._available_models_cache is not None` blew up. Setting `_LIVE_REBUILD_BUDGET_SECONDS = 0.0` routes the priming call through the legacy synchronous branch, which is the only path that unconditionally publishes before returning:

```python
# api/config.py:8190-8222 (budget <= 0 branch)
if _LIVE_REBUILD_BUDGET_SECONDS <= 0:
    ...
    with _cache_build_cv:
        published_at = time.monotonic()
        _available_models_cache = result
        _available_models_cache_ts = published_at
```

So the two new precondition asserts (`_available_models_cache is not None`, `_ts > 0.0`) are guaranteed to hold under the forced-sync path. The `try/finally` restoring `_LIVE_REBUILD_BUDGET_SECONDS`, `_cfg_mtime`, and calling `invalidate_models_cache()` keeps global module state clean even on assertion failure — good hygiene given this is process-global.

## `test_glm_5_3` — stubbing `provider_model_ids` is effective because the import is lazy

The zai group flows through the generic branch, not a special-case, so it asks the installed core first:

```python
# api/config.py:7822-7828
else:
    raw_models = _models_from_live_provider_ids(
        pid, _read_live_provider_model_ids(pid),
    )
if not raw_models:
    raw_models = copy.deepcopy(_PROVIDER_MODELS.get(pid, []))
```

Worth calling out *why* `monkeypatch.setattr(hm, "provider_model_ids", lambda _pid: [])` actually works here: `_read_live_provider_model_ids` re-imports the symbol lazily on every call (`from hermes_cli.models import provider_model_ids as _provider_model_ids` at `config.py:6397`), so patching the module attribute is picked up. If the import had been bound at module load, the patch would have missed and the test would still read the installed core. With the stub returning `[]` for every candidate, `_read_live_provider_model_ids` returns `[]`, `raw_models` stays empty, and the `_PROVIDER_MODELS["zai"]` fallback (which carries `glm-5.3` at `config.py:1739`) is exercised deterministically — exactly the "test WebUI propagation, not installed core" intent.

CI is green (lint + browser-smoke + the sharded `test (3.x, N)` matrix). No concerns; this is a clean test-only change that removes real sharded-gate noise. LGTM.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I pulled HEAD (`51b55f26`) into a read-only worktree and read the full `static/style.css` + `static/panels.js` diff against `origin/master`. The core approach is clean: replace hardcoded `color:#fff` on accent-filled buttons with a per-skin `--btn-primary-text` token, defaulting `#fff` at `:root` (`style.css:16`) and `#111` at `.dark` (`style.css:123`), then overriding per skin whose dark-mode accent is light (mono, ares, slate, sisyphus, catppuccin, etc.). That fixes #7092. But one line in the diff is a **global** button rule, and it introduces a contrast regression on the neon skin family that the per-skin overrides don't cover.

## The regression: base `.send-btn` now flips neon skins to near-black text

The diff changes the shared send-button rule at `style.css:2766`:

```css
.send-btn{...background:var(--accent);border:none;color:var(--btn-primary-text);...}
```

On master this was `color:#fff` (old `style.css:2754`). Every dark skin that does **not** set its own `--btn-primary-text` now inherits the base `.dark` value `#111`. The neon family has saturated, genuinely-dark accents and sets no override:

- `:root.dark[data-skin="neon"]` → `--accent:#b347ff` (`style.css:1108`)
- `:root.dark[data-skin="neon-soft"]` → `--accent:#b347ff` (`style.css:1188`)
- `:root.dark[data-skin="neon-paint"]` → `--accent:#FF2D95` (`style.css:1254`)

I confirmed no neon block defines `--btn-primary-text` and none has a skin-specific `.send-btn` color override (only box-shadow, e.g. `style.css:1132`), so they all fall through to `style.css:2766`. Result: the send-button glyph goes from white → `#111` on vivid purple/hot-pink — the exact low-contrast failure this PR is meant to eliminate, just moved to a different skin.

It also creates an internal inconsistency: neon's `.new-chat-btn` still hardcodes `color:#fff` (`style.css:1135-1136`), so within one neon skin the New-chat button stays white while the send button turns black.

## Same class, lower severity

`poseidon` (`--accent:#0EA5E9`, `style.css:649`) and `charizard` (`--accent:#FB923C`, `style.css:655`) also lack the token and fall through to `#111`. Orange/charizard is arguably still legible; sky-blue/poseidon at `#111` is borderline. Worth a glance while you're in here.

## Recommended fix

Add an explicit white override to the three neon dark blocks (and decide on poseidon/charizard):

```css
:root.dark[data-skin="neon"]{ ... --btn-primary-text:#fff; }
:root.dark[data-skin="neon-soft"]{ ... --btn-primary-text:#fff; }
:root.dark[data-skin="neon-paint"]{ ... --btn-primary-text:#fff; }
```

That keeps the token approach and restores the pre-PR appearance on neon.

## Verification

Toggle each skin in dark mode with the composer focused and confirm the send-arrow contrast: mono/ares/slate/sisyphus should be dark-on-light (the fix), neon/neon-soft/neon-paint should be white-on-accent (the regression guard). The shard-1 CI failures on 3.11/3.12/3.13 are unrelated to this CSS diff — they match the intra-file test-order issue tracked in #7104.

payload.author: allenliang2022
payload.body:
Good catch — documented.

I added the contract to `docs/rfcs/webui-run-state-consistency-contract.md`, which is where the run-state invariants for streaming/recovery already live, rather than describing it only in code comments:

- **State Layers table** now lists `ACTIVE_RUNS` as the worker-lifecycle registry, with an explicit "must not do": be read directly as the set of runs a browser may attach to.
- **New invariant 9 — "Lifecycle-busy is not client-attachable."** Spells out that cancellation splits the two meanings, that recovery paths (session SSE recovery, hidden-tab status polling) must exclude cancelling rows while admission checks must keep counting them, and what goes wrong when a single meaning is used: the attach → terminal event → teardown → resubscribe loop.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I pulled HEAD (`aadf4d04`) into a read-only worktree and read the `server.py` diff against `origin/master`, plus the `/api/shutdown` path it's fixing. The core change is correct and minimal: master's `server.main()` only registers `_request_shutdown` for SIGTERM (`server.py:718`), while `/api/shutdown` terminates via `os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGINT)` at `api/routes.py:12081`. With SIGINT inheriting `SIG_IGN` from ctl.sh's non-interactive background-job spawn, that kill was a genuine no-op — the diagnosis holds. Routing SIGINT through the same handler is the right fix. Two things worth addressing before merge, one of which is the red `lint` gate.

## The lint failure is a real F401

The gate is `E9 + F + B` (`pyproject.toml:74`). In `tests/test_issue7078_shutdown_sigint.py`, `import signal` at line 17 is **never used outside string literals**:

```python
import signal   # line 17
...
snippet = textwrap.dedent("""
    import os, signal, sys           # <-- inside the string
    ... signal.getsignal(signal.SIGINT) ...
""")
...
assert "signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, _request_shutdown)" in src   # <-- string literal
```

Pyflakes doesn't look inside strings, so `signal` at module scope is an unused import → **F401**. That's almost certainly what the `lint` job is flagging (run 95242426189). Drop the module-level `import signal` and the gate should go green — the test doesn't reference `signal.*` as real code anywhere.

## Latent test-guard bug: `requires_bash` is defined but never applied

Line 28 defines the skip mark but neither test wears it:

```python
requires_bash = pytest.mark.skipif(BASH is None, reason="bash not on PATH")

def test_sigint_handler_override_fires_from_background_job():   # no @requires_bash
    ...
    proc = subprocess.run([BASH, "-c", ...])
```

If `bash` is not on PATH, `BASH` is `None` and `subprocess.run([None, "-c", ...])` raises `TypeError` instead of skipping cleanly — the exact case the mark was written to guard. Add `@requires_bash` above `test_sigint_handler_override_fires_from_background_job` (the second test doesn't spawn bash, so it doesn't need it).

## On the fix itself — no behavioral regression

I checked the `serve_forever()` block at `server.py:733-757` on this branch: it's a bare `try/finally` with **no** `except KeyboardInterrupt`. So before this PR, a foreground Ctrl-C would raise `KeyboardInterrupt` up through `serve_forever()` and still hit `finally`, but with a traceback and without the idempotent double-shutdown guard. Routing SIGINT through `_request_shutdown` is strictly better: clean `httpd.shutdown()` on a daemon thread, `serve_forever()` returns normally, and `drain_all_on_shutdown()` runs the same as the SIGTERM path. The `_shutdown_requested.set()` guard also makes a second SIGINT/SIGTERM idempotent. Good.

## Verification

Once F401 is fixed: `python3 scripts/ruff_lint.py --diff origin/master` should report 0 new violations, and CI `lint` should pass. The two shard-1 test failures across 3.11/3.12/3.13 look unrelated to this diff — they match the intra-file order dependency tracked in #7104, not anything this PR touches.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I reviewed head `85b7af7f` against `origin/master`, including the full `server.py`, the complete new regression file, and the unchanged `/api/shutdown` signal path in `api/routes.py`. The refreshed commit addresses both points from the earlier review: the unused import and unapplied bash marker are gone because the test now reproduces inherited `SIG_IGN` directly through the Python subprocess boundary. I do not see a remaining correctness blocker in this revision.

## Code reference

The production change is centralized at `server.py:547-587` and used from `server.py:735-737`:

```python
for _sig in (signal.SIGTERM, signal.SIGINT):
    try:
        signal.signal(_sig, _request_shutdown)
    except (ValueError, OSError):
        logger.debug("Could not install %s handler", _sig, exc_info=True)
```

That is the correct counterpart to `api/routes.py:12060-12081`, where the Settings endpoint still sends the process `SIGINT`. Explicitly registering the handler replaces the inherited ignore disposition, while the helper thread preserves the existing requirement that `httpd.shutdown()` not run on the `serve_forever()` thread. The shared `threading.Event` keeps repeated SIGTERM/SIGINT delivery idempotent.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The extraction into `_install_shutdown_signal_handlers()` is small and improves testability without changing the shutdown ordering. payload.author: nesquena
payload.body:
## Review — end-to-end ✅ (clean approval, no fixes needed) — independent review as requested

Independent review of the approval-mirror producer-match fix (#4948 local variant): on the local backend, a notified approval could never be reunited with its queued producer entry, so the mirror was created **without a token** → reconcile kept the orphan → `_session_has_pending_approval` stayed True after the entry dropped → the stale approval card dead-ended with "Approval response not accepted."

### What this ships

`api/route_approvals.py` (+23 production lines — one scoped fallback), `tests/test_approval_unblock.py` (payload-fidelity fix). Agent-authored (`nesquena-hermes`, release-manager). MERGEABLE, CI 23/23 green.

### Both core-behavior premises verified against the fresh agent tarball

1. **The core notifies with a COPY:** `notify_cb(dict(entry.data))` (`tools/approval.py:4056`) — so the existing identity match (`entry.data is approval`) can never hold for a real gateway head. ✓
2. **A local `_ApprovalEntry` carries `request_id`, not `approval_id`:** `self.data.setdefault("request_id", uuid.uuid4().hex)` (`:2596`) is stamped **on the source entry** before the copy is taken, so it survives `dict(entry.data)` and uniquely reunites copy↔entry; no local `approval_id` exists for the second fallback to hit. ✓ (The core itself keys `ack_gateway_approval` on `request_id` — same identity the fix adopts.)

### The fix — correctly scoped

A third fallback after identity + approval_id, **gated on `not run_id`** (local backend only — the gateway `run_id` path is untouched), guarded on a non-empty `request_id`, and matched only within this session's locked `live_gateway_queue`. Defensive `getattr(entry,"data")or{}` access. Minimal and in the right place. ✓

### The decisive verification — agent-present, which CI structurally cannot do

The PR's key claim is that this bug is invisible to CI (no agent core → `skipif` skips). I reproduced the full triangle with the fresh core on PYTHONPATH:

| Configuration | Result |
|---|---|
| Branch + agent core | **31/31 pass** ✅ |
| **Master's production code** + the fidelity-fixed tests + agent core | **exactly 8 fail** (the claimed regression; tests are non-vacuous — they detect the production revert) ✅ |
| Agent absent (CI-equivalent) | **all 31 skip** (confirming CI-invisibility) ✅ |

### Test fidelity change — verified assertion-preserving

The old `test_approval_unblock.py` submitted the **pre-stamp source** `approval` (which made the identity match hold — unfaithful to production, masking the bug). The diff changes only the submitted payload to `dict(entry_X.data)` (the stamped copy, matching `notify_cb`); **no assertion lines changed** (verified in the diff). The sibling `test_issue4948_local_stale_approval.py` already simulated the copy faithfully and passes on the production fix alone.

### Edge-case matrix

| Scenario | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Local notify (copy, request_id) | reunited via fallback → mirror gets token → reconcile clears ✅ |
| Gateway head (`run_id` set) | fallback skipped — path unchanged ✅ |
| Empty/missing request_id | fallback no-ops (guarded) ✅ |
| Cross-session collision / reverse callback ordering | probed by the Codex gate, pass ✅ |
| Entry without `.data` | defensive access, no throw ✅ |

### Tests

- Approval files agent-present — **31/31**; approval blast-radius — **337 passed, 6 skipped**.
- **Full suite: 14425 passed / 0 failed** (with the documented #7013 workarounds: TMPDIR under /tmp for the darwin media-root gap + ignoring the unguarded-playwright file — both pre-existing master issues unrelated to this PR). CI 23/23 green.
- The one flake the PR noted (`test_static_asset_resolver` shard-sensitivity) did not reproduce here.

### Recommendation

✅ **Approved clean.** Parked at approval — ready for the release agent's merge/tag pipeline.

A precise fix at the exact seam: the local notify boundary hands WebUI a copy, and `request_id` — stamped on the source pre

Thanks @kadiratesdev — the false-offline brick is a real problem worth fixing, but the gate reproduced three regressions in this approach that would make offline reliability worse, so this needs rework before it can ship:

### Must-fix (both CORE, reproduced)

1. **`static/sw.js:142` — hard-coded `/login` breaks supported subpath mounts.** Both the recovery link and the navigation target use root-absolute `/login`, so a `/hermes/`-mounted instance sends the user to the origin root (404 or an unrelated site). Derive the URL from the SW scope: `new URL('login', self.registration.scope)`. Same for any other recovery link.

2. **`static/sw.js:143` — a genuinely-offline navigation now loses the working offline page.** On a cache miss, the two expected offline fetch failures immediately unregister the worker and navigate away *even when `navigator.onLine === false`* — replacing your offline fallback with the browser's raw network-error page (verified with an executed worker probe). That's the opposite of the goal. Keep the offline fallback displayed and only recover (unregister/redirect) **after a scope-relative health probe succeeds** or the user explicitly taps retry — never on the offline failure itself.

### Must-fix (SILENT, reproduced)

3. **`static/sw.js:143` — you unregister unrelated same-origin PWAs.** `getRegistrations()` iterates *every* service-worker registration on the origin, so a co-hosted PWA gets unregistered too. Use `self.registration` (or `getRegistration(scope)`) and only ever touch Hermes's own registration — never iterate and unregister across all of them.

Also note: the new source-string test currently asserts the broken root-absolute `/login`, so it locks in bug #1 — update it to expect the scope-relative URL once you fix the source.

Everything else checked out (retry ordering correct, retry/offline responses not cached, `skipWaiting`/activation untouched, 87 focused PWA/subpath tests pass). Fix these three and re-push — I'll re-gate.

payload.author: VHSgunzo
payload.title: fix(approval): stamp mirror token for no-run legacy mirrors so the first click resolves

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @VHSgunzo — I reproduced this carefully and your diagnosis is **correct and the bug is real**: in legacy in-process mode (`HERMES_WEBUI_CHAT_BACKEND` unset), the no-run mirror was created without `_GATEWAY_MIRROR_TOKEN`, so `_resolve_approval_legacy()` can't link the mirror to the live `_ApprovalEntry` and the first click returns `ok:true` while the agent thread stays blocked. I verified your repro test **still fails on current master** (which already carries the separate `request_id` resolve-fallback from #7093), so this is a genuinely **distinct, complementary fix** — not a duplicate. Nice root-cause.

However, the current implementation **regresses two exact-producer isolation guarantees**, so it can't ship as-is. Both fail deterministically (verified: they pass on clean master, fail with this PR):

- `tests/test_approval_unblock.py::TestApprovalHTTPEndpoints::test_gateway_mirror_without_run_id_with_one_producer_resolves_exactly` → **409 instead of 200**
- `tests/test_approval_unblock.py::TestApprovalHTTPEndpoints::test_gateway_no_run_non_head_response_resolves_only_exact_producer` → **409 instead of 200**

### Root cause of the regression

At creation (`submit_gateway_pending_mirror`, the `elif not _gateway_pending_mirror_locked(...)` branch) the new code stamps the mirror token from **`_gateway_queues[session_key][0]`** — i.e. the *current live head* — unconditionally:

```python
live_queue_for_mirror = _gateway_queues.get(session_key) or []
live_head_for_mirror = live_queue_for_mirror[0] if live_queue_for_mirror else None
mirror_token = _gateway_mirror_entry_token(live_head_for_mirror) ...
```

That's wrong whenever the mirror being created is **not** the current head — e.g. multiple parked producers (`[entry, sibling_entry]`), or a non-head response. The mirror gets bound to the head's token, so when the *exact* producer for that mirror later resolves, the token-match in `_resolve_approval_legacy` (line ~191, `entry_token == live_token`) points at the wrong entry, the exact-producer match fails, and the respond path returns **409** instead of retiring only that producer. #7093 specifically hardened this exact-producer isolation (a no-run mirror must retire *only* after its own local producer resolves), and this stamp breaks it.

### Fix direction

Bind the token to **the mirror's own producer**, not to `_gateway_queues[...][0]`. The mirror you're appending corresponds to a specific parked `_ApprovalEntry` (matched by `approval_id` / position), so derive `mirror_token = _gateway_mirror_entry_token(<that producer entry>)` rather than the queue head. With that, the first-click-unblocks fix and the exact-producer isolation both hold. Please make all three green together:

- your `tests/test_issue_legacy_first_click_repro.py::test_legacy_no_run_mirror_first_click_unblocks_agent`
- the two `test_approval_unblock.py` exact-producer tests above

Once those three pass simultaneously, re-push and I'll re-gate. This is close and worth finishing — it's a real legacy-mode first-click fix.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @VHSgunzo — resolving non-head no-run mirrors is a real gap, and the gate confirms the good parts: correctly-identified non-head producers now resolve exactly, cross-session IDs stay scoped, and normal `_session_has_pending_approval` cleanup works. But the new "scan all live producers" **fallback** introduced a serious approval-integrity regression that must be closed before this can ship:

### Must-fix (CORE) — approving stale command A can silently execute a different live producer B
`api/route_approvals.py:597` → `api/routes.py:24595`. When `request_id=A` fails exact matching, the new fallback assigns B's unclaimed/head token, and the resolver then finds that token and resolves **B**. Verified at HEAD: **A was displayed to the user, but B received `result="once"` and its event was set** — a different command ran than the one approved. On `origin/master`, B remained untouched.

This is an approval-integrity violation (the whole point of the approval card is that the user authorizes *that specific* command), so it's a hard blocker regardless of the convenience it adds.

**Exact fix:** when no producer matches the authoritative identity (`request_id`/`approval_id`), **fail closed** — never infer ownership from "first unclaimed" or the queue head. If a live queue exists, don't bind the submitted copy; let reconciliation mirror the authoritative live head. Preserve a tokenless orphan only when *no* producer exists (the legitimate #7093 case).

### Test
`tests/test_issue_legacy_first_click_repro.py:92` — the new non-head test is non-vacuous for the `routes.py` scan, but its valid `request_id` bypasses the unsafe fallback entirely, so it misses the regression. Add adversarial cases: (a) stale `request_id=A` with only B live, and (b) a tokenless non-head copy with multiple producers. Assert the displayed command and the resolved producer are always the same one.

Context: this exact area had a master-bug fixed in #7093 (exp-v0.52.231) — the `request_id` fallback for a genuinely tokenless orphan. The safe boundary is: tokenless-orphan mirror when *no* producer exists → fall back; unmatched identity when producers *do* exist → fail closed and reconcile from the live head. Re-push with the fail-closed fallback + the two adversarial cases and I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @VHSgunzo — solid progress: the gate confirms the **critical A→B execution exploit is now closed** (approving stale command A no longer wakes/executes a different live producer B), exact non-head resolution and cross-session isolation both work, and the no-producer tokenless-orphan boundary (#7093) is intact. 52 focused tests pass. One CORE issue remains on the same boundary, though:

### Must-fix (CORE) — an unmatched tokenless mirror A still masks live producer B
`api/route_approvals.py:609`. When producer B is live, an unmatched tokenless mirror A is still *appended*; reconciliation (lines 153–176) suppresses B's token, and the retained handling at line 224 lets A mask B indefinitely. Verified: **gateway mode returns 409 and permanently retains A; local mode returns `ok:true` while resolving nothing** — so the real pending approval (B) can't surface or be actioned. The fix closed the wrong-execution but opened a liveness/masking hole in its place.

**Fix:** `api/route_approvals.py:153` — when `_gateway_queues[session_key]` has live producers, **always tokenize/reconcile from its authoritative head and discard** the unmatched tokenless or retained no-run mirror. Only B's authoritative mirror may survive when a producer exists. Preserve tokenless-orphan retention **only when no producer exists** (the #7093 boundary).

### Test gap
`tests/test_issue_legacy_first_click_repro.py:168` — the new adversarial tests pass but never assert *authoritative displayed head == resolved producer*, so they miss this. Add: stale A is not returned/displayed, B becomes the pending head, responding with A's stale ID fails **without** waking B, and approving the displayed B wakes exactly B. Add the equivalent displayed-vs-resolved assertion for the multiple-producer case.

You're one iteration away — the dangerous exploit is gone; this is now making sure the stale mirror can't *block* the legitimate one. Re-push with the discard-on-live-producer fix + the displayed-vs-resolved assertions and I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Reading `api/route_approvals.py:505-526` on `origin/master` next to the working `exact_local_entry` branch above it, the root cause in this PR checks out. The no-run branch builds its mirror without the mirror token that the resolver later needs, while the sibling branch stamps it.

## Code reference

On master the no-run branch (`elif not exact_local_entry:`) ends with:

```python
elif not _gateway_pending_mirror_locked(session_key, approval_id=approval_id):
    mirror_entry = dict(approval)
    mirror_entry["approval_id"] = approval_id
    mirror_entry[_GATEWAY_MIRROR_FLAG] = True
    _normalize_pending_queue_locked(session_key).append(mirror_entry)   # no _GATEWAY_MIRROR_TOKEN
```

Compare the `exact_local_entry` branch at `api/route_approvals.py:462-466`, which *does* stamp it:

```python
mirror_entry = dict(local_data)
mirror_entry["approval_id"] = entry_approval_id
mirror_entry[_GATEWAY_MIRROR_FLAG] = True
mirror_entry[_GATEWAY_MIRROR_TOKEN] = token
```

## Diagnosis

The resolver in `api/routes.py:24582-24586` is the consumer that makes the missing token fatal:

```python
elif not run_id and found_target and pending:
    pending_token = str(pending.get(_GATEWAY_MIRROR_TOKEN) or "").strip()
    gateway_token = str(gw_data.get("_webui_mirror_token") or "").strip()
    if pending_token and pending_token == gateway_token:
        gw_data["approval_id"] = approval_id
        local_gateway_approval_id = approval_id
```

With `pending_token` empty the guard short-circuits, `resolve_gateway_pending_local()` never runs, and the parked entry's `event.set()` never fires — but `_resolve_approval_legacy()` still returns `True` because the `_pending` entry was popped. That matches the reported "first click closes the card + returns ok, agent stays blocked, second click works" symptom exactly, and it is specific to legacy in-process mode (`HERMES_WEBUI_CHAT_BACKEND` unset).

## On the fix

Deriving the token from the live gateway head via `_gateway_mirror_entry_token(live_head_for_mirror)` is the right source: that helper (`api/route_approvals.py:112-127`) stamps `_GATEWAY_ENTRY_DATA_TOKEN_KEY` into the head's `.data`, which is the same value the exact-branch uses, so the mirror and the parked entry end up in the same token space the resolver compares against. Guarding with `if mirror_token:` also preserves today's behavior when there is no live head, which is correct — no head means nothing to bind back to.

## One thing worth confirming

The `elif not exact_local_entry:` branch can also be reached via the earlier `no_run_mirror` reuse path (lines 512-520), where an existing tokenless mirror is reused rather than recreated. Please confirm the regression test exercises the *fresh-mirror* path (no prior mirror in `_pending`) rather than the reuse path — otherwise a pre-existing tokenless mirror from a prior submit could still reach the resolver without a token. If `tests/test_issue_legacy_first_click_repro.py` starts from an empty pending queue, that's the path that matters and you're covered.

Root cause, layer (webui in-process approval relay, not an agent contract), and fix all look correct.

payload.author: VHSgunzo
payload.body:
@nesquena-hermes — confirmed and fixed in `9c2ca104`. You were right that failing closed traded the wrong-execution bug for a masking one.

### The masking fix
`reconcile_gateway_pending_mirror_locked()` no longer defers to a pre-existing no-run mirror. It now **always** tokenizes every live no-run producer and derives `live_token` from the authoritative head whenever `_gateway_queues[session_key]` holds producers. The two suppressions are gone:

- the `has_no_run_mirror` guard that skipped tokenizing a producer (and nulled `live_token`) whenever any no-run mirror sat in `_pending` — that's what let A suppress B;
- the unconditional retained early-return at the old line 224 — a retained missing-producer mirror now survives **only while `live_gateway_queue` is empty**, otherwise it falls through to normal matching (kept if it still matches a live token, discarded if not).

Net effect: while a producer exists, only its authoritative mirror survives, so the unmatched tokenless copy is discarded rather than parked in front of B. Tokenless-orphan retention for the genuine no-producer case (#7093) is untouched — that path arrives with an empty live queue and therefore a `None` `live_token` anyway.

### Tests — displayed == resolved
Both adversarial cases now assert the full invariant you asked for: the stale/identity-less copy is **not** in `_pending`, the authoritative producer **is** the head (`total == 1`), responding with the stale id returns `False` and wakes nothing, and approving the displayed head wakes exactly its own producer (leaving any non-head producer parked).

### Heads-up: three existing tests updated
`tests/test_gateway_approval_runs_api.py` had three cases from the same #6008 lineage (`6460c48c`) that encoded the old masking behavior — most explicitly `..._keeps_its_own_id_beside_local_gateway_head`, which asserted a foreign `remote-id` mirror survives beside a live producer carrying `local-id`. That's the exact state you flagged as unresolvable-and-masking, so I updated them to the new invariant rather than leave them asserting it:

- `..._gets_browser_visible_id` — now asserts the id in the polling queue matches the **returned head**, which is what both production callers actually forward to the browser (`{**(head or approval_data), "pending_count": total}` in `streaming.py` and `gateway_chat.py`), so the browser-visible id is still guaranteed resolvable.
- `..._keeps_its_own_id_beside_local_head` — keeps its real point (the mirror's id is distinct from the unrelated local entry's `local-id`) without asserting copy-identity.
- `..._keeps_its_own_id_beside_local_gateway_head` → renamed to `..._yields_to_live_local_gateway_head` and inverted, with the reasoning in its docstring.

Flagging these explicitly since changed assertions deserve your eyes, not just a green check.

### Verification
Full suite: **14693 passed, 2 failed**. Both remaining failures are in `test_tls_aware_probe.py` (`test_helper_self_signed_warns_and_succeeds`, `test_helper_insecure_optin_is_silent`), are pre-existing on the pristine tree at `63087a40`, and are a test-fixture issue rather than anything in this PR — that file does not reference approvals at all.

Root cause, since it will bite anyone on a recent OpenSSL: `_Server` in that test TLS-wraps a stdlib `http.server.HTTPServer`, and its handler writes the body **without a `Content-Length`**. So `curl` must read to EOF, while the wrapped socket is closed without a TLS `close_notify`. OpenSSL 3.6.3 rejects that truncation — `error:0A000126:SSL routines::unexpected eof while reading` — and `curl` exits 56 even though the body arrived. `health_probe.sh` then tries its plain-HTTP fallback against an HTTPS listener, which also fails, so the helper returns 1. Nothing wrong with the probe or the production server, which does send `Content-Length`; adding that one header to the test handler makes both cases pass. Out of scope here, so I left it alone — happy to send it separately if you want.

T

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the thorough implementation and lifecycle coverage. I found two objective current-head blockers in the cache/server authorization contract.

## 1. A cache hit does not preserve `/api/media`'s canonical-path authorization and snapshot-binding decision

`static/media-cache.js::_requestScope()` sends only `session_id` and the raw `path` (`static/media-cache.js:244-269`). The new `/api/media-cache/scope` route resolves that path and checks its suffix plus `_session_media_token_allows_path()` (`api/routes.py:13055-13109`), but it does not apply either of the decisions that make the normal media route safe:

- `_media_deny_reason(target)` (`api/routes.py:20674-20688`), or
- `snapshot_servable_for_path(snap_digest, target)` (`api/routes.py:20725-20746`).

The returned scope is session-scoped rather than canonical-resource-scoped (`api/auth.py:660-708`), and `_cachedBlob()` then looks up the original raw source URL under that unchanged scope (`static/media-cache.js:176-192`).

A deterministic failing schedule is:

1. A session contains `MEDIA:/path/link.mp4`, where `link.mp4` resolves to allowed target A and digest A is source-bound to A.
2. Load and persist the snapshot.
3. Retarget the same symlink-shaped raw path to video target B, either under a hard-denied Hermes state directory or to an allowed canonical path to which digest A is not bound.
4. Re-open the same raw URL.

The scope endpoint re-resolves the session token and raw request to B, returns the same session scope, and the browser returns cached bytes for A. The canonical `/api/media` path would instead deny B or reject digest A's source binding and omit the snapshot attestation. This makes the persistent-cache path disagree with the server's authorization result.

Please centralize one server-owned immutable-video eligibility check shared by `/api/media` and `/api/media-cache/scope`. It must apply the hard deny, current path authorization, valid snapshot existence, and exact canonical path-to-digest binding. Keep the authority partition separate, but return a resource fingerprint/capability bound to the canonical target plus digest and key cache/task/metadata entries by it. A canonical-path or binding change must produce a miss/fallback, never reuse the old raw-URL entry.

Add production-composed tests that cache A, retarget the same raw path to (a) a denied video path and (b) an allowed B with a mismatched digest binding, then prove that old A is not attached and the normal deny/fallback behavior wins.

## 2. `X-Hermes-Media-Snapshot` attests a requested filename, not the served bytes

`snapshot_path_for_digest()` accepts any regular `<digest>.snap` file without hashing it (`api/media_snapshots.py:219-228`). `capture_snapshot()` also treats an existing destination as a valid dedup hit without validating its contents (`api/media_snapshots.py:347-405`). The route then emits `X-Hermes-Media-Snapshot: <requested digest>` (`api/routes.py:20747-20763`), and the browser persists the Blob after comparing only that header (`static/media-cache.js:303-348`).

The new Chromium fixture cannot detect this boundary because it intentionally pairs `DIGEST = "a" * 64` with unrelated MP4 bytes (`tests/browser_persistent_video_cache.py:28-30`). A corrupt or replaced snapshot object is therefore given a valid-looking attestation and cached persistently under the wrong digest.

Please make attestation body-coherent: verify that the opened snapshot bytes hash to the requested digest before emitting the attestation, or verify the downloaded Blob against `snap` before use/storage. Existing-object dedup must repair or reject a mismatched destination rather than discard the newly hashed good temp file. Add tampered-`<digest>.snap` and wrong-body/right-header regressions proving the bytes are neither played nor cached.

## Execution note

The mandatory threat scan returned **SUSPICIOUS** because `tests/browser_persistent_video_cache.py` embeds a large base64 MP4 fixture. Policy therefore

payload.author: ruizanthony
payload.title: fix(sessions): isolate per-tab conversation state (reload restores the wrong chat with 2 tabs open)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @ruizanthony — this is a real bug worth fixing (three global localStorage keys bleeding conversation/inflight/reconnect state across same-origin tabs is a genuine cross-tab contamination problem), and the design instincts are good (per-tab id, duplicate-tab reclaim, orphan GC, legacy-key first paint). But a fresh gate reproduced **four CORE lifecycle defects** against the real helpers, and together they mean the ownership/GC model isn't safe yet — so this needs a redesign pass before re-gating.

### Must-fix (all CORE, all reproduced)

1. **`static/ui.js:9203` — a throttled/frozen tab is misread as "gone," so a duplicate regains the same id.** `_claimTabId()` treats a 45-second heartbeat gap as proof the owner is gone, but Chrome throttles hidden-tab timers to ~1/min and *freezes* (suspends timers entirely) discarded/frozen tabs ([page-lifecycle](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/page-lifecycle-api), [timer throttling](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/timer-throttling-in-chrome-88/)). Reproduced with one missed heartbeat: the duplicate retained the source id, so two documents share an id and overwrite each other's session/transcript/stream state. **Fix:** replace timestamp-only ownership with collision arbitration that revalidates on `resume`/`visibilitychange` and forces one document to re-mint *before* any scoped read/write; absence of a heartbeat must not mean "available."

2. **`static/ui.js:9252` — orphan GC deletes live tabs' recovery state.** After 24h without timer execution, `_readTabSeen()` drops the live owner and `_gcOrphanTabKeys()` deletes its active-session + inflight keys. Worse, malformed `seen` JSON makes `_touchTabSeen()` replace the registry with only the current tab, then GC deletes **every other tab's** keys. Both reproduced. **Fix:** parse failure must be a GC no-op; protect confirmed claims / current ids; stop GCing active-session keys on heartbeat absence — expire inflight data from its own timestamps instead.

3. **`static/ui.js:9365` — first-upgrade legacy state can't be forgotten.** `_rememberedActiveSession()` returns the legacy value without adopting it, and `_forgetActiveSession()` only clears the legacy key when a scoped value already exists. Reproduced: reading and forgetting a legacy-only `dead-session` leaves it stored, so stale-session self-heal retries forever and a `?profile=` switch can reload the old session and flip back to the old profile. **Fix:** persist an accepted legacy fallback into this tab's scoped key before returning it, or pass the expected SID to `_forgetActiveSession()` and clear a matching legacy-only value.

4. **`static/ui.js:9344` — existing single-tab inflight recovery is discarded on rollout.** All reads now use suffixed keys, but the pre-release `hermes-webui-inflight` / `hermes-webui-inflight-state` values are never read, migrated, or removed. Reproduced: populated legacy marker/state → empty scoped reads, stranded. So on the first reload after deploy, every existing user's reconnect marker + local live transcript vanish. **Fix:** when scoped state is absent, validate legacy data against the requested SID + stream id, migrate it with the new tab stamp, then remove the legacy keys.

The core tension is that the heartbeat/TTL model at 9203-9333 can't distinguish a closed tab from a throttled/frozen/discarded/restored one, and 9344-9388 lacks rollout migration. Both need addressing before this is safe on the crown-jewel session-recovery surface. The direction is worth finishing — once ownership uses resume-revalidated collision arbitration (not timeout) and the legacy migration lands, re-push and I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @ruizanthony — this is a serious, thorough rework and the direction (per-tab id in sessionStorage + scoped keys + a claim registry + GC) is the right architecture. But an adversarial re-gate that **executed the real helpers** from head `590debcfb` reproduced all four of the prior defects — they're mitigated in code but still fail under the actual race/upgrade conditions. 41 focused tests pass, but the tests don't exercise these adversarial paths. Each finding below was reproduced, not inferred:

### Must-fix (CORE) — duplicated tabs still collide after a heartbeat gap
`static/ui.js:9298`. Advancing one 45-second lease: the clone retained the original tab ID, and writing session B in the clone made the *original* tab restore B. Timeout-based ID reuse is the root problem — **a missed heartbeat must never make an ID reusable.** Replace timeout-based reuse with collision arbitration / revalidation *before* any scoped read or write.

### Must-fix (CORE) — orphan GC still deletes live tabs' keys
`static/ui.js:9330`. Reproduced two ways: (a) after the 24-hour seen-TTL, and (b) immediately after malformed registry JSON. **Parse failure must disable GC** (fail safe), and active-tab state must not be collected based solely on elapsed heartbeats — liveness + orphan reclamation need an authoritative ownership mechanism, not a timer.

### Must-fix (CORE) — legacy fallback still bleeds + can't be forgotten on upgrade
`static/ui.js:9441`. Tab A, after forgetting session A, restored tab B's legacy session; and a legacy-only `dead-session` survived `_forgetActiveSession()`, defeating the 404 / profile-switch self-heal. Fix: adopt legacy state **once** into scoped storage, persist an explicit per-tab "no session" tombstone, and let forget clear a matching *expected* legacy SID even when no scoped value existed.

### Must-fix (CORE) — rollout discards existing inflight recovery
`static/ui.js:9498`. Both readers use suffixed keys exclusively, so a populated legacy `hermes-webui-inflight` / `hermes-webui-inflight-state` produces empty scoped reads and stays unmigrated (existing mid-stream recovery is lost on upgrade). When scoped state is absent: validate the legacy SID/stream/age, migrate it under the new tab stamp, then remove/invalidate the legacy entries.

The common thread: the lease/GC ownership (`ui.js:9292-9412`) and the fallback/migration (`ui.js:9441-9503`) boundaries need an **authoritative ownership mechanism** rather than heartbeat timers + suffix-only reads. Recommend redesigning those two boundaries (a real claim/lease with arbitration, and a one-time legacy adoption + tombstone) and adding execution-level tests that cover: duplicated-tab-after-heartbeat-gap, GC-with-malformed-registry, forget-with-legacy-only-SID, and upgrade-with-populated-legacy-inflight. payload.author: ruizanthony
payload.body:
Both P1 findings were real — thanks. Fixed at `48d4a61f`:

**1. Tab registry updates lose ownership.** Every claim/seen mutation was a whole-object read-modify-write, so two tabs interleaving between the read and the write could drop each other's entry. Replaced with a single `_updateTabRegistry(key, id, ttl, drop)` helper that re-reads immediately before writing and only ever touches the caller's **own** id — every other tab's entry is carried over untouched (minus TTL expiry). The heartbeat, claim and release paths all go through it; the old `_writeTabClaims()` whole-object writer is gone.

**2. Per-tab cleanup deletes global fallback.** `_forgetActiveSession()` now clears the shared legacy key only when it still points at the session *this* tab is forgetting. A tab clearing conversation A no longer blanks the restore target of a tab on conversation B, and a brand-new tab still restores the last active session.

Both are covered by new probes in `tests/test_multi_tab_session_isolation.py` (`test_forget_does_not_strip_the_shared_fallback_of_other_tabs`, `test_registry_writes_do_not_clobber_a_concurrent_tab`) — 12/12 green, and the full suite shows no regressions against `origin/master`.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Reading `api/config.py:3545-3556` at this PR's HEAD against `origin/master`, plus the agent's GA'd 5.6 catalog, the capability contract this PR targets is real: the OpenAI-family lane genuinely strips `max` from everything matching `bare.startswith("gpt-5")`, and GPT-5.6 is a live family, so `max` was being hidden/downgraded for it. The scoping is clean and the regression coverage is thoughtful.

One concrete gap before this is complete: the allowlist is narrower than the agent's GA set.

## Code reference

The new gate matches by exact set membership:

```python
_GPT_5_6_REASONING_MODELS = frozenset({
    "gpt-5.6", "gpt-5.6-sol", "gpt-5.6-terra", "gpt-5.6-luna",
})

def _is_gpt_5_6_reasoning_model(bare_model: str) -> bool:
    return str(bare_model or "").strip().lower() in _GPT_5_6_REASONING_MODELS
```

used as `if bare.startswith("gpt-5") and not _is_gpt_5_6_reasoning_model(bare): return [eff for eff in normalized if eff != "max"]`.

But the agent GA'd **six** 5.6 slugs, not four. In `hermes_cli/codex_models.py:16-23`:

```python
# GPT-5.6 series (Sol/Terra/Luna + -pro high-effort modes) — GA 2026-07-09
"gpt-5.6-sol", "gpt-5.6-sol-pro",
"gpt-5.6-terra", "gpt-5.6-terra-pro",
"gpt-5.6-luna", "gpt-5.6-luna-pro",
```

and the same six appear in `hermes_cli/models.py:92-97`. There is no bare `gpt-5.6` slug in the agent catalog (that entry in the allowlist is harmless forward-compat), while the three `-pro` variants that *do* ship are the ones described as "high-effort modes."

## Diagnosis

For `gpt-5.6-sol-pro`: `bare.startswith("gpt-5")` is True, `_is_gpt_5_6_reasoning_model("gpt-5.6-sol-pro")` is False (exact-match miss), so `max` is stripped. That is precisely the capability mismatch this PR sets out to fix, just left in place for the highest-effort tier of the family. If the base `sol`/`terra`/`luna` accept `max`, the `-pro` "high-effort mode" almost certainly does too; excluding it needs either coverage or an explicit rationale in the comment.

## Recommendation

A family-prefix check is both more robust and self-covering for `-pro` and any future dated snapshot slug (e.g. `gpt-5.6-sol-2026-07-09`):

```python
def _is_gpt_5_6_reasoning_model(bare_model: str) -> bool:
    return str(bare_model or "").strip().lower().startswith("gpt-5.6")
```

This keeps the pre-5.6 `gpt-5` / `gpt-5.1` / `gpt-5.5` ceiling intact (they don't start with `gpt-5.6`) while covering all six GA slugs.

## Test plan

Extend `test_openai_family_gpt56_models_expose_and_preserve_max` to iterate the full GA set, including the `-pro` tier:

```python
GPT_5_6_MODELS = (
    "gpt-5.6-sol", "gpt-5.6-sol-pro",
    "gpt-5.6-terra", "gpt-5.6-terra-pro",
    "gpt-5.6-luna", "gpt-5.6-luna-pro",
)
```

That would fail today for the three `-pro` ids and pass with the prefix change, keeping the WebUI gate aligned with `hermes_cli/codex_models.py`.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Really solid fix, @ruizanthony — the root-cause analysis is exactly right and the gate confirms it. The regression is real and this restores the universal live-streaming convention (ChatGPT / Claude / Codex all keep a partially-streamed word in-flow; master tore it across the block boundary as `"Ces deu"` / `"x fichiers"`).

**Gate results:**
- **Codex: SAFE TO SHIP** — verified exact cursor behavior across ASCII/emoji/CJK, live-to-final + reattach paths, default-render isolation; no regression risk.
- **Non-vacuous proof:** your two regression tests FAIL on clean master (the tear is genuinely present) and PASS on the fix — confirmed by re-running them against `origin/master`. Plus 1028 focused stream/fade/transparent tests green.
- **Fable UX: SHIP-WITH-UX-FIXES** — confirms the fix is in the right layer (row reconciler, not a CSS band-aid), reuses the existing fade machinery, no regression to the fade animation / thinking rows / settled message, and correct under RTL. Caret unaffected (it's suppressed in fade mode).

One minor UX-polish fix before it ships, and it's in the app's own established pattern:

### Should-fix — mute the already-rendered prefix on the no-cursor rebuild branch

The no-cursor rebuild branch of `_refreshTransparentFadeProseRow` (the branch that now fires in exactly the scenario that used to tear, since incremental rows never set `data-stream-fade-text`) clears the body and re-wraps **all** words as `.is-new`. So the whole visible row dips to opacity 0 and fades back over ~620ms, and because every node is replaced, native scroll anchoring may pick a new anchor (the one-time vertical bounce the #6257 comment in `_bindTransparentFadeCleanup` warns about).

This is strictly better than the persistent torn word, it's one-time per row, and reduced-motion users never see it — but it contradicts the app's own #6783 standard, where `messages.js` (`_streamFadeMuteRenderedPrefix`, messages.js:4997) deliberately mutes exactly this "replay the fade on ALL visible words at once" defect. The `ui.js` rebuild branch has no such mute, and the helper is currently closure-private.

**Fix (~3 lines):** on the rebuild branch, snapshot `body.textContent` before clearing, then apply the `messages.js` `_streamFadeMuteRenderedPrefix` idiom so only genuinely-new tail words animate. Export it on `window` the same way `__anchorProseIncrementalNode` is exposed. This kills both the one-time whole-row fade flash and the all-new-nodes scroll-anchor bounce, and it also repairs the pre-existing rewind case where messages.js carefully mutes the fade on the new node only for the ui.js reconciler to rebuild it as all-`is-new`.

Once that lands, this is a clean ship on the crown-jewel streaming surface. Re-push and I'll re-gate + capture the before/after mid-stream proof for the maintainer. Nice work tracking this to the one-character parser lag.
