payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @starship-s — this is a genuinely valuable fix (unbounded terminal `done` payloads freezing large conversations on settle is a real problem), and the bulk of it is solid. I gated the current head `6a1dd7da` (Codex adversarial reproduction + full suite, 13,954 passed). Codex verified the core is sound — **480 same-session boundary combinations merged without loss or duplication, redaction is safe, and both the native and gateway terminal producers use the bounded redacted helper** (39 focused terminal/gateway/cancel/pagination/redaction tests pass).

Holding for one **CORE** fix:

### CORE — auto-compression settlement collapses an expanded transcript to the bounded tail (`static/messages.js:2029`)
The reconciler treats **every** session-ID change as unrelated and skips the merge:
```js
if (!currentSession || !Array.isArray(currentMessages) || !currentSid || incomingSid !== currentSid) {
    return { ...incoming, messages: incomingMessages };   // raw bounded window, no merge
}
```
But automatic compression **changes the session ID** and sets `parent_session_id` to the previous ID (`api/streaming.py:9816-9869`). So when compression settles, `incomingSid !== currentSid` is true, the merge is skipped, and the bounded 30-row tail replaces the whole loaded window. Verified reproduction: **loaded rows 910–971 were dropped**, leaving only the terminal window — a user who had scrolled back loses their expanded transcript on compression.

**Fix:** recognize `incoming.parent_session_id === currentSid` as the same coordinate lineage and run the normal validated merge for that case (not just exact-SID-match). Add a rotated `done`/`apperror` regression test asserting the expanded prefix, the new session ID, offsets, and tool indexes all survive a compression rotation.

### Merge-order note (not a blocker, but important)
This PR **moves** `_messages_for_limited_payload` from `api/routes.py` to `api/session_ops.py`, and PR #6815 (currently in review) **adds** to that same function (bounding oversized user/assistant rows in the paginated payload). The two aren't independent — whichever lands second needs a rebase that preserves the other's changes to that helper. Recommend shipping this one **solo** once the CORE fix lands, and rebasing whichever of the two goes second.

Everything else checks out — this is one reconciliation edge away from being a strong fix. Ping me when it's re-pushed and I'll re-gate the exact head.

<sub>Gate: Codex (full 22-file diff audit + real-probe reproduction of the compression-rotation collapse; verified same-session merge, redaction, and gateway parity intact) + full suite (13,954 passed). Verdict: SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES.</sub>

Fixed and re-pushed at `354a97b9`. `_applyEmbeddedTerminalSession` now treats a direct compression continuation (`incoming.parent_session_id === currentSid`) as the same coordinate lineage, so the existing validated merge preserves the expanded prefix while adopting the continuation session ID, offsets/count, and translated tool metadata. Unrelated rotations still use the existing raw-adoption path.

Added regression coverage for rotated `done` and `apperror` settlement, including expanded-prefix preservation, continuation metadata, tool indexes, and unrelated/missing-parent rejection. All 23 checks are green on the exact head, and Greptile reports 5/5 with no blocking finding.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @starship-s — the compression-rotation fix is spot on. I re-gated the new head `79546138` (adversarial Codex + full suite, 13,954 passed), and the CORE window-collapse from the last round is **fixed**: `messages.js` now treats `parent_session_id === currentSid` as same-coordinate lineage, so a compression rotation goes through the validated windowed merge instead of collapsing to the bounded tail. Same-session merges, redaction, and native/gateway parity all still hold.

One more edge — a **separate** cap that silently drops data, this time on **tool calls** rather than messages:

### SILENT — terminal settlement drops tool cards when a session has >300 tool calls (`api/streaming.py:136`)
The done-payload applies an independent tail slice:
```python
raw['tool_calls'] = terminal_tool_calls[-300:]
```
so only the final 300 tool summaries are sent, and `static/messages.js:2084-2091` then discards the already-loaded overlapping calls and installs the capped list. Reproduced with 301 calls: **`call-0` disappeared** on settle. It's the same unbounded→bounded truncation this PR correctly solves for the message window, but applied to `tool_calls` without the lineage-aware merge — so the earliest tool cards/results are silently lost for any long-running session that accumulates more than 300 calls.

**Exact fix:** remove the independent `[-300:]` slice and emit all projected tool calls until there's a lossless truncation protocol for them (mirroring the offset/count windowed-merge you built for messages), and add a 301-call merge regression test to lock it in.

Everything else on this head is clean — this is the last thin edge on the same "bound it without losing already-loaded data" theme. Ping me on re-push and I'll re-run the adversarial gate on the exact head.

## Gate at head `bfaa08b0b2dd`: the redesign introduces a Codex routing regression

Thanks @starship-s. The catalog-hygiene intent is right — the four genuinely-retired IDs (`gpt-5.2-codex`, `gpt-5.1-codex-max`, `gpt-5.1-codex-mini`, `codex-mini-latest`) and `gpt-5.5-mini` are correctly gone, and the entitlement concern that motivated the last review is real.

But the approach here diverges from the requested surgical fix: instead of restoring `gpt-5.3-codex` and dropping only Spark from the `openai-codex` static fallback, this **removes all Codex IDs from the static fallback and excludes `openai-codex` from `_seed_provider_models_from_core()`**, delegating the whole catalog to the live/cache path. I gated the redesign on its own merits (adversarial reproduction + full suite, exact head rebased onto current master), and it has one **CORE** regression that blocks it.

### CORE — live-discovered Codex models can be routed to the wrong backend (api/config.py:1948 → ownership set 2686–2726 → `model_with_provider_context()` :3134)

Excluding `openai-codex` from core-seeding removes those model IDs from the **ownership set** (`_provider_models_set`) that `model_with_provider_context()` relies on. When a Codex model then comes from the live catalog, it falls through to the bare-model passthrough at :3134 (`if provider == config_provider: return model`) instead of emitting an explicit `@openai-codex:<model>` routing hint. If an overlapping custom/configured provider's catalog carries the same model ID, the bare model gets **hijacked** — this is the exact `#5511`/`#5909` hijack class the surrounding code already guards against (see the comments at :3124–3131 and :2686–2693).

Reproduced: `gpt-5.3-codex` with `model_provider=openai-codex` resolved to `custom:shared-relay` on this branch, but correctly to `openai-codex` with the master catalog restored. A Codex turn can be sent to the wrong backend.

**Why the surgical fix avoids this:** keeping the Codex IDs in the `openai-codex` static catalog (minus the dead ones + Spark) keeps them in the ownership set, so the routing hint is preserved. That's the lower-risk path the earlier review asked for.

### Two ways forward
1. **Surgical (recommended, matches the prior review):** keep the four retired removals, **restore `gpt-5.3-codex`** to the `openai-codex` static list, **drop only `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`** (Pro-only, entitlement-unknown in a static list), and do NOT exclude `openai-codex` from core-seeding. This gets the hygiene win without touching routing.
2. **Keep the redesign** only if you also preserve Codex routing context: return `@openai-codex:<model>` in `model_with_provider_context()` before the same-provider bare return at :3134 for live-discovered Codex models, and add the overlapping-custom-provider hijack case as a regression test.

The degraded/offline picker behavior itself is safe (with discovery empty it shows the three static models and injects a configured removed default without crashing) — the blocker is purely the routing hijack. Re-push either path and I'll re-gate.


---

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @Andre-4711 — bounding oversized paginated message content is a real need, and the core byte-math is correct (persisted messages are never mutated, no-`msg_limit` retrieval stays canonical, exactly 65,536 chars unbounded while 65,537 reduces to 65,536, ordinary/synthesized pagination agree, 26 focused tests pass). But the gate found this is the same defect class as #7040 — the bounded preview leaks into the canonical-action paths, plus a render-safety cut bug. Seven to fix:

### Must-fix (CORE) — oversized messages aren't recoverable in the transcript UI
`static/ui.js:16935`. The renderer creates no expand/full-content control for `_content_truncated`; the only marker consumers are the loader and edit path, and session-jump buttons are disabled by default. Add a per-message full-content action that fetches the no-`msg_limit` canonical value and displays/downloads it.

### Must-fix (SILENT) — Copy copies the 64 KiB preview + truncation notice
`static/ui.js:8831`. `copyMsg()` reads only stale `data-raw-text` and never triggers authoritative loading. Capture session ID + absolute message index, load canonical content when marked (guard session switches), and copy the full normalized message.

### Must-fix (SILENT) — Listen/TTS speaks only the preview + truncation notice
`static/ui.js:9009`. `speakMessage()` has the same stale `data-raw-text` dependency. Resolve the full message via the same race-safe absolute-index helper before stripping Markdown and starting TTS.

### Must-fix (SILENT) — Markdown download exports bounded previews
`static/boot.js:2101`. `transcript()` serializes current `S.messages` (unlike JSON/HTML exports, which use the canonical server endpoint), so the Markdown contains the preview and omits the full value. Await authoritative loading with a session guard before building the blob, or add a canonical server-side Markdown export.

### Must-fix (CORE render-safety) — slicing can create DOM-breaking bounded content
`api/routes.py:8895`. Both string and structured-text paths cut without respecting HTML comments, safe tags, fences, or tables. Verified: a valid cutoff-crossing `<!-- … -->` becomes an unclosed `<!--` in actual `renderMd()` output → the HTML tokenizer eats the footer/actions. Build previews at safe structural boundaries, or neutralize unmatched comments/tags before rendering. Cover a cutoff-crossing actual-`renderMd()` case.

### Also
- `static/ui.js:19165` — preserve normalized edit text for ordinary messages and normalize authoritative text after a truncated-message reload.
- `static/sessions.js:3864` — remove the global "any truncated row" reload condition; scope content recovery to the specific message the caller requested.

The pattern (same as #7040): keep the persisted/canonical path authoritative, never let the bounded preview reach Copy/TTS/export/edit, resolve those by message identity, and cut only at safe structural boundaries. Re-push and I'll re-gate.

### 2. Regression — session-payload helper signature drift (`api/routes.py`)

Reproduced with a 60-row tail at offset 140: after `_ensureAllMessagesLoaded()` the full 200-row render mounts rows 0–10 and 150–199, **excluding target 140**, and line 18536 returns → the edit no-ops with no feedback. **Fix:** retain the clicked row after the reload and use `absoluteMsgIdx`; don't rerender/requery before opening the editor, or explicitly remount the target.

payload.title: feat(boot): ?workspace= query param — one-shot workspace routing at boot

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @Anto1neL — reusing server-side `resolve_trusted_workspace()` and failing closed around profile-switch failure are the right boundaries. Static exact-head review found three deterministic launch-contract gaps.

1. `_workspaceQueryIntentFromLocation()` decodes the query and then returns `path.trim()`. Trimming is not just validation: valid Unix directory names may end in spaces. `?workspace=%2Fhome%2Fu%2Fproject%20` can therefore silently route to a different directory. Use trimming only for the blank predicate and send the exact decoded string to the server authority.
2. Existing `action=new-chat` routing runs before the workspace block. With `?action=new-chat&workspace=...&q=...`, boot creates the first session without the requested workspace, preserves the unconsumed `workspace` query, and a hard reload creates a second session with it. Parse workspace intent first and make it own the single new-session creation; on success consume both launch intents and finalize the prompt once.
3. `workspace` is removed before `newSession()` succeeds. If auth expires between profile bootstrap and the POST, the login redirect's `next=` URL has already lost the intent. Preserve it through auth/network/5xx failures, consume it after accepted creation, and consume an objectively server-rejected path before documented fallback.

Please keep `resolve_trusted_workspace()` as the sole path trust/existence/system-root authority; do not replace it with browser path rules. Add composed production-order tests for significant trailing whitespace, `profile+workspace+action=new-chat+q`, one session across hard reload, failed/deferred profile switch, and a 401 between bootstrap and session creation.

Threat scan was SUSPICIOUS, so this was strict static-only; no PR code was executed.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Static re-gate at exact head `4feced19423c`

The force-pushed rewrite materially fixes all three findings from the August 14 review. It forwards the decoded workspace value verbatim, gives workspace routing ownership of the compound `action=new-chat` launch, and preserves the URL intent across profile/auth/transport failures. The later held-state, structured-error, post-create, and composer-lock repairs are also coherent.

One objective one-shot gap remains.

### Blocking: committed POST + lost response still creates a duplicate session

The client now distinguishes “session created” by observing whether `S.session` changed around `await newSession(...)` (`static/boot.js:3778-3804`). That only detects failures after the response reached the browser and `newSession()` assigned `S.session`.

`POST /api/session/new` is non-idempotent and carries no launch/request identity. If the server creates and saves the session, but the connection drops before the response reaches `api()` (or the response is otherwise lost), `S.session` remains unchanged. The catch path classifies this as transport failure, preserves `workspace`, enters the held state, and tells the user to reload. Reload submits the same non-idempotent POST and creates a second session. The first successful server-side session is orphaned.

This is the standard ambiguous-commit boundary: client memory cannot prove whether a mutating request committed when its response was lost. The current post-create tests throw only after `S.session` is assigned, so they do not exercise it.

### Required fix

Make the launch retry idempotent across a full reload.

- Mint a stable launch request ID before the first POST and retain it with the outstanding URL/sessionStorage intent.
- Send it to `/api/session/new`; deduplicate atomically within the active profile, returning the same session for a matching retry. Scope and bound the receipt, and reject a reused ID whose workspace/profile/material payload fingerprint differs.
- Consume the launch parameters only after the server returns the created-or-existing session.
- Add a production-path test that commits the first create but drops its response, then replays the launch as a fresh document and proves exactly one session exists, with the requested workspace/profile and the same returned session ID.

This is deterministic duplicate/orphan creation under an ordinary network failure, so the one-shot contract is not ready yet.

### Execution note

The exact-head Layer-1 scan could not complete because GitHub REST quota was exhausted (`gh pr diff` HTTP 403, scanner rc=3). Policy required static-only NO-RUN. No PR code, tests, imports, browser, server, compiler, or linter was executed; this finding follows the production POST/response-loss/reload path above.

Pushed befc57f9 addressing the residual mismatch:

**Length cap removed.** `_workspaceQueryIntentFromLocation()` now routes any nonempty trimmed value — the client predicate matches the one-shot transport contract exactly, and `resolve_trusted_workspace()` is the single authority. Agreed on the principle: if a request-size ceiling is ever warranted, it belongs on the API boundary as an explicit, documented error shared with the client, not a parser-only cap.

payload.author: Anto1neL
payload.body:
Pushed 5600d9da addressing all three points.

**1. The value is forwarded verbatim.** `_workspaceQueryIntentFromLocation()` no longer returns `path.trim()` — trimming is now only the blank predicate, and the decoded string reaches the server untouched. `?workspace=%2Fhome%2Fu%2Fproject%20` now routes to `/home/u/project ` rather than silently resolving to a different, possibly existing directory.

**2. Workspace routing runs first and owns the single session creation.** The block moved ahead of the `action=new-chat` branch, so `?action=new-chat&workspace=…&q=…` no longer creates a workspace-less session and returns early. Both launch intents are consumed together once the server accepts the session (a small `_consumeLaunchActionParamFromLocation()` mirrors the existing consumers), so the reload that previously minted a second session now finds nothing left to act on. When the path is rejected, the boot falls through to the `new-chat` branch, which still honours its own contract.

**3. The parameter is consumed after the create attempt, not before.** A `400` is `resolve_trusted_workspace()`'s objective verdict on the path, so it is consumed before the documented fallback — retrying that URL could only fail again. Everything else (401, network error, timeout, 5xx) is transport rather than a verdict, so the parameter stays in the URL and the `login?next=<pathname+search>` snapshot still carries the intent. This was the concrete failure you described: auth expiring between profile bootstrap and the POST.

`resolve_trusted_workspace()` remains the sole authority on trust, existence, directory type and system-root policy — no browser path rules were added.

**Test plan — all five composed cases added**, in production order:
- significant trailing/leading/interior whitespace, at the parser level and end-to-end into the session-create request;
- `?action=new-chat&workspace=…&q=…`: exactly one session, carrying the workspace, both intents consumed, `q=` preserved for the prefill;
- one session across a hard reload — the second boot replays against the URL the first one left behind and creates nothing;
- compound `profile+workspace` with the switch returning false and throwing (unchanged, still deferred), plus the successful case;
- `401` / `500` / `503` / status-less network error between bootstrap and creation: the parameter survives; `400`: it is consumed.

Two supporting changes to the harness: the boot runner now extracts the workspace block and the `new-chat` branch as one region and runs `_shouldStartFreshPwaChat()` verbatim, so the ordering between the two launch intents is exercised by the shipped code rather than asserted on source shape; and the `newSession` stub rejects with a real `err.status`, matching the error shape `api()` throws, so the consume/preserve policy is computed by the boot block itself.

Also kept the README deep-link entry in sync with the three behaviours.

36 tests, all passing via `scripts/test.sh`. I also ran the full suite: the failures I see locally (model catalog / provider / onboarding / ttl-cache) reproduce identically on a clean checkout without this branch, so they are environmental here rather than introduced by this change.

payload.author: Anto1neL
payload.body:
Pushed 688a5916 — both P1 findings were real, thanks.

**Deferred routing creating duplicate sessions.** Correct, and it was a regression I introduced on the failure path while removing the duplicate on the happy path. The `workspace` parameter is deliberately preserved when the launch is deferred (profile switch did not complete) or fails for a transport reason, so falling through into the `action=new-chat` branch created a workspace-less session now and let the successful retry create a second one from the same launch. While a workspace launch is still outstanding for the URL, the shortcut now stands down; the preserved parameter carries the intent to the next load, which produces the single session.

**Unrelated 400 discarding the workspace intent.** Also correct — `POST /api/session/new` returns 400 from several independent validators (`_validate_session_toolsets_shape`, the explicit-worktree path), and branching on the bare status treated any of them as a permanent verdict on the workspace.

Rather than widen the client-side guess, I added the discriminator at the API boundary, which is the shape you asked for in the earlier round: `bad()` takes an optional `code`, and the workspace branch tags its rejection `invalid_workspace`. The boot block now branches on that code, so only an actual path verdict consumes the parameter — every other 400 leaves the launch retryable. Defined once on the server, documented in the README, shared with the client, rather than a parser-only heuristic. The other 558 `bad()` call sites are untouched; `code` is optional and omitted everywhere else, and the existing positional `status` calls keep working.

Tests (41 total, all green via `scripts/test.sh`):
- server-side coverage asserting a rejected path really does return `400` with `code:"invalid_workspace"`, so the two halves of the contract cannot drift apart silently;
- an unrelated 400 — both with no code and with a different code — preserving the parameter;
- the new-chat shortcut suppressed in both outstanding-launch shapes: profile switch deferring the launch, and a transport failure preserving it.

One note while verifying: `tests/test_new_chat_default_model_frontend.py::test_pwa_new_chat_launch_does_not_block_first_paint_on_model_catalog` asserts on the literal source of the launch branch, so my first attempt at the guard broke it. The guard now sits inside the branch and that test passes unmodified — I did not touch it.

payload.author: Anto1neL
payload.body:
Pushed 3696875c — good catch, the code was too coarse.

`_workspace_access_error()` reports two genuinely different situations through the same exception: a path the server **inspected and refused** (untrusted, not a directory, system root), and a path it **could not inspect at all** (permission denied, transient stat failure). Only the first is a verdict. The second is the user's to fix — granting macOS Full Disk Access is literally what the error message asks for — and the identical request then succeeds. Tagging it `invalid_workspace` made the boot discard the parameter, so granting the permission and reloading restored the saved session instead of completing the deep link. Exactly as described.

`WorkspaceAccessError` now marks the uninspectable case and `POST /api/session/new` returns it without the code. It subclasses `ValueError`, so every existing `except ValueError` keeps catching it unchanged — the distinction is additive and no other call site had to move.

Worth noting this mirrors a distinction the module already drew: `resolve_implicit_workspace_with_recovery()` separates a genuinely missing path (recoverable, falls back) from an inaccessible one (preserves the original error). The two call sites now classify the same failure the same way, which is the invariant I should have looked for before reaching for the status code.

The client policy is unchanged — only `code:"invalid_workspace"` consumes the parameter — so everything else (transport failures, unrelated 400s, and now access failures) keeps the launch retryable.

Tests: a permission-denied directory returning `400` **without** the code, plus a guard that `WorkspaceAccessError` stays a `ValueError` subclass so the distinction cannot silently change who catches what. I verified the new test actually fails against the previous behaviour rather than merely passing against the new one. 43 tests, all green via `scripts/test.sh`; the workspace suite (532 tests) is green apart from one socket-timeout flake that reproduces identically on a clean checkout.

payload.author: Anto1neL
payload.body:
Pushed 44afe816 — right again, and this one was the more serious half of the problem I only half-fixed.

Suppressing the `action=new-chat` branch was necessary but not sufficient. Below it, boot continued into normal restoration, which destroys the very intent the previous commit went out of its way to preserve:

- `loadSession()` calls `_setActiveSessionUrl()`, which rebuilds the whole query string from `_sessionUrlForSid()`. The preserved `workspace` — and the `q=` prefill riding with it — is gone from the URL, so the reload that was supposed to complete the deep link no longer carries anything.
- With no saved session, `_maybeBindFreshDefaultWorkspaceSession()` can auto-bind a session on the profile default workspace: a second, wrong-workspace session from the same launch, created before the user even retries.

So the flag now short-circuits the entire boot rather than one branch. When a workspace launch is still outstanding, boot renders the empty state, touches nothing in the URL, and returns. The next load replays the identical URL and produces the one intended session. Holding is the only behaviour consistent with preserving the parameter in the first place — anything that renders a session in the meantime either drops the intent or duplicates it.

Tests:
- the held path asserted both with and without a saved session in `localStorage`, since those are the two distinct ways the restore destroyed the intent (URL rewrite vs. default-workspace auto-bind);
- a compound `profile+workspace+q` launch asserted to leave **every** launch parameter intact — the retry needs the whole launch, not just the workspace;
- the existing outstanding-launch cases now assert the held contract rather than falling through.

Both new tests verified to fail against the previous behaviour before being kept. 46 tests green via `scripts/test.sh`, plus the neighbouring boot/PWA/profile suites (99 tests) to confirm the early return does not strand any of the other boot paths.

Also rebased onto current master — the branch had gone stale and was showing a conflict in `api/routes.py` against the new `_resolve_new_session_workspace()` helper. Resolved in favour of the upstream refactor, with the `WorkspaceAccessError` branch layered on top of it rather than reverting it.

payload.author: Anto1neL
payload.body:
Pushed 833fd57c — all three were real.

**1. Malformed paths remain retryable.** Correct, and it exposed the actual weakness: I was deriving the classification from the message prefix. An embedded NUL makes `Path.stat()` raise `ValueError`, and that message also begins `Cannot access path:`, so a malformed path was labelled recoverable and boot would replay an intrinsically invalid intent on every reload.

Rather than special-case the NUL string, the classification now travels as a flag from the probe that actually knows which `stat()` outcome occurred: `_workspace_access_failure()` returns `(message, recoverable)`. Text parsing is gone. `_workspace_access_error()` stays as the message-only view — and `resolve_trusted_workspace()` deliberately still calls it first, because it is the seam `tests/test_remote_terminal_workspace.py` monkeypatches to override accessibility; the classifying probe is consulted only once that seam reports a failure, and an override that changes the message falls back to the permanent verdict. (I found that the hard way: my first version bypassed the seam and broke `test_var_home_workspaces_stay_allowed_before_system_root_blocklist`.)

**2. Post-create failures retry session creation.** Also correct. `newSession()` sets `S.session` before boot finishes rendering, so a throw from a later step meant the session existed while the catch treated the whole thing as retryable — the held branch then cleared `S.session`, and the reload created a second workspace session, orphaning the first. Creation is now tracked separately: once the server has accepted, a rendering failure consumes the parameter and lets the normal boot path finish drawing the UI. Anything that throws before acceptance keeps the existing preserve/retry policy.

**3. Held composer bypasses workspace routing.** The one I liked least, because the held branch was mine and I had put the bug in it myself. `_finalizeComposerPrefillOnBoot()` does two things that are both wrong while a launch is outstanding: it consumes `q=`, stripping the prefill from the URL the retry depends on, and it fills the composer — and a Send from that composer routes through plain `newSession()` with no workspace cue, creating a default-workspace session while the requested one is still pending. Exactly the duplicate the branch exists to prevent. The held path no longer finalizes the prefill; it stays in the URL and lands when the launch completes.

Tests: NUL and the other permanent verdicts asserted at the classifier level rather than through the message; the held boot asserted not to finalize the prefill; a post-create rendering failure asserted to keep its session, spend the intent, and not hold. All three verified to fail against the previous behaviour before being kept. 51 tests green via `scripts/test.sh`, plus the full workspace suite (581) and the boot/PWA/profile suites — the only red there is a socket-timeout flake in `test_workspace_git.py` that passes in isolation on this branch and reproduces on a clean checkout under load.

payload.author: Anto1neL
payload.body:
Pushed 3abe7c5f — correct again. The flag was set after `newSession()` returned, but `newSession()` keeps initializing client state after the server accepted and `S.session` is assigned (todo hydration, stream start, dropdown sync, the model-override cleanup). A throw from that tail propagated out before the flag flipped, so a session that exists server-side was classified as a failed creation — parameter preserved, reload creates a second session, first one orphaned. Exactly as described.

Creation is now detected by observing `S.session` across the call: unchanged reference means the POST never succeeded and the retry policy applies; changed reference means the launch is spent, regardless of where inside `newSession()` the throw came from. That signal is anchored to the same assignment that makes the session real to the client, so it cannot drift from the thing it is supposed to witness the way an after-the-fact flag can.

One companion hardening in `newSession()` itself: `_clearEmptyComposerModelOverride()` — the only local cleanup sitting between the accepted POST and the `S.session` assignment — is now guarded, so a purely cosmetic failure there cannot make an accepted creation look failed to any caller deciding retry policy on it.

Test: a throw from inside `newSession()` after `S.session` is set, asserting exactly one POST, the parameter consumed, no hold, and the boot falling through to finish rendering. Verified to fail against the previous flag-based detection before being kept. 52 tests green via `scripts/test.sh`, plus the boot/PWA/profile neighbours (88).

payload.body:
Pushed 4feced19 addressing the held-composer finding.

**Held composer bypasses workspace ownership** — correct: an empty-but-interactive composer was still an escape hatch out of the held state. A manually typed Send routes through plain `newSession()` and binds to the profile-default workspace while the requested one is still pending in the URL — the same duplicate as before, this time user-initiated.

The held state now locks the composer through `lockComposerForClarify()` — the mechanism this codebase already uses for exactly this shape (disable + explanatory placeholder) — with a placeholder telling the user to reload to retry opening the requested project. Reload was already the retry vehicle; the lock makes it the only available action instead of merely the intended one. Scoped strictly to the held state: successful launches, rejected paths and the normal restore never engage it. Tests assert both sides. 54 tests green via `scripts/test.sh`.

---

@nesquena-hermes — with this pushed, a status check on the review from Aug 14, since `CHANGES_REQUESTED` from that round is what formally blocks the PR:

1. **Trim narrowing the path language** → the client predicate routes any nonblank value; `resolve_trusted_workspace()` is the single authority (and the value now travels verbatim, whitespace included).
2. **Workspace routing gated on profile-switch completion** → gated, with the parameter preserved for retry; the compound cases run the real boot blocks in tests.
3. **The four requested test scenarios** → all present, plus the boundary cases from the follow-up round.

Since then, seven Greptile review rounds have each been addressed as well (launch-intent ordering with `action=new-chat`, transport-vs-verdict consumption policy with an explicit `code:"invalid_workspace"` at the API boundary, recoverable-vs-permanent access classification, post-create failure semantics, and the held-state hardening above). All fixes carry regression tests that were verified to fail against the prior behaviour, and the branch is rebased on current master.

Could you re-review when you get a chance? And a process question so this converges: for any further hardening findings of the held/edge-failure shape, would you prefer they continue to land pre-merge on this PR, or as a follow-up once the core one-shot contract is in? payload.body:
## Summary

Reading `static/index.html:282` and `static/style.css:2232-2234` on `origin/master`, then the complete files and the PR diff at HEAD, this is the right layer for the fix. The inline declaration duplicates the Insights sidebar select rule and prevents that shared rule from fully controlling the period selector. Moving the element to a class makes the intent clearer and keeps the current full-width layout. I do not see a functional blocker in the two-line patch.

## Code reference

The relevant shared rule already supplies width, colors, typography, border, radius, and the custom chevron at `static/style.css:2232`; the PR adds only the spacing override at `static/style.css:2234`:

```css
.insights-controls select{
  width:100%;
  background:var(--input-bg);
  border:1px solid var(--border2);
}
.insights-controls .insights-period-select{padding:6px 28px 6px 10px;}
```

At `static/index.html:282`, the replacement is correspondingly small:

```html
<select id="insightsPeriod" class="insights-period-select" onchange="loadInsights()">
```

That preserves `width:100%`; the PR is not reintroducing the earlier `width:auto` behavior discussed in #6768. The wider right padding also leaves room for the shared background-image chevron.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The implementation is sound, but the stated automated verification is not present in this branch. `tests/test_insights.py:163-169` currently checks only that `insightsPeriod`, its options, and `loadInsights()` exist. It would still pass if the class were removed or the inline style returned.

Please add a focused regression assertion in `test_insights_frontend_has_daily_chart_styles_and_range_switching_hooks`, for example:

```python
assert "insights-period-select" in INDEX_HTML
assert ".insights-controls .insights-period-select" in STYLE_CSS
assert "insightsPeriod\" onchange" not in INDEX_HTML
```

A DOM parser would be stronger than string matching, but this matches the existing test style and protects the actual contract introduced by the PR.

## Verification

I performed read-only review only, as required for untrusted PR worktrees, and did not execute branch code. The final browser check should cover dark and light themes, confirm the chevron does not overlap the selected value, and verify the control remains full width in the Insights sidebar.

payload.author: greptile-apps
payload.body:
Greptile Summary

 The PR moves reasoning-effort overrides from profile-wide configuration into persisted session metadata and threads the effective value through the UI, HTTP endpoints, local runtime, and gateway runtime. - Persists a three-state `reasoning_effort` value on `Session`. - Sends session identity with reasoning status reads and writes. - Applies the session override to both local and gateway chat execution. - Adds focused persistence, route, resolution, and gateway tests.

Confidence Score: 4/5

payload.body:
## Summary

Reading all seven changed files at PR HEAD and on `origin/master`, plus the Hermes reasoning-resolution contract, the persisted per-session override is wired correctly for existing sessions. One user-visible path still falls back to the old profile-global mutation: changing reasoning from a blank/new chat, before `S.session` exists. That breaks the isolation guarantee because every session whose new `reasoning_effort` field is still `None` continues to inherit the changed profile value.

## Code reference

`static/ui.js:4991-4997` only adds the session identifier conditionally:

```js
const ctx={};
if(S&&S.session&&S.session.session_id) ctx.session_id=S.session.session_id;
if(model) ctx.model=model;
if(provider) ctx.provider=provider;
```

At `api/routes.py:14593-14620`, the new scoped write runs only when `session_id` is present. Otherwise execution falls through to the existing `set_reasoning_effort(...)` call, which writes the profile config. Meanwhile `api/models.py:1189-1244` initializes new and legacy sessions with `reasoning_effort=None`, and both `api/streaming.py:9138-9150` and `api/gateway_chat.py:286-303` intentionally fall back to profile config for that value.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

On a blank chat, selecting Low can therefore modify the global default. Opening another existing session that has no explicit override will now also run at Low. The UI looks session-scoped, but the request took the global branch.

I would block the picker until a session exists, or materialize a session before posting the change. Another option is a pending new-chat value that is copied into the `Session` when the first message creates it. The route should also avoid treating an ordinary WebUI request without `session_id` as permission to mutate profile configuration; keeping a separate explicitly global endpoint or flag would make that boundary unambiguous.

## Test plan

The current tests cover two persisted sessions but not the blank-chat branch. Please add a route/UI regression that posts a reasoning change without an active session and verifies the profile setter is not called, then create the session and verify only its `reasoning_effort` changes. Also verify an older session with `reasoning_effort=None` retains the prior profile fallback. I did not execute PR code because review worktrees are read-only; this finding follows the exercised branches in the diff.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @samfoy — this is a real and well-diagnosed data-isolation bug (the chip looking per-session while all four paths shared one global key), and the core of the fix is solid. I gated the current head `f79da530` (Codex adversarial reproduction + full suite, 13,943 passed). Codex verified the core is correct — **legacy/global fallback, isolated writes, lock-held save, reload persistence, malformed-value rejection, explicit `none`/default behavior, XSS-safe `textContent`, and local↔gateway parity are all intact** (I confirmed the parity probe: a session set to `low` resolves `low` on both the streaming and gateway paths while the global default stays `high` for sessions without an override).

Holding for a revision — the scoping fix is **incomplete across three sibling paths** that still route through the old global behavior. All three were reproduced with real probes:

### 1. SILENT — session-switch race poisons another session's chip (`static/ui.js:5228`)
A late reasoning POST from session A completes *after* a switch to session B and overwrites B's chip + poisons B's cache. This is the same session-confusion class the PR set out to fix, just on the async-completion path. **Fix:** snapshot the dispatch key, increment `_reasoningFetchSeq`, and apply/toast only when both the sequence and the current `_reasoningEffortQuery()` still match.

### 2. SILENT — the `/reasoning` slash command still writes the global (`static/commands.js:1859`)
The chip POST was scoped, but `/reasoning high` still writes the global default, so a session with a persisted override keeps its old effort while the UI claims the new value applies. **Fix:** include `_reasoningEffortContext()` in the command's POST and apply the same stale-context guard as #1. Calls with no active session should remain global (that's correct).

### 3. SILENT — duplicate/branch/focused-continuation sessions drop the override (`api/routes.py:14432, 15266, 21927`)
The duplicate, branch, and focused-continuation session constructors don't carry `reasoning_effort` forward — a source session with `xhigh` produced `None` in all three children, silently falling back to the global. (I confirmed the duplicate-session `Session(...)` constructor omits it on the current head.) **Fix:** pass `reasoning_effort=getattr(source, "reasoning_effort", None)` in each of the three constructors, and test with a global default different from the source override so the drop is caught.

**Net:** the per-session storage + fallback + gateway parity are right; the gap is that three sibling write/copy paths weren't migrated with the primary one. Once those three carry the session scope (with the switch-race guard on the two frontend paths), this is a clean, genuinely valuable fix. Ping me when it's re-pushed and I'll re-gate the exact head.

<sub>Gate: Codex (real-probe reproduction of the three paths + verification that the core scoping/fallback/parity is intact) + full suite (13,943 passed). Verdict: SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES.</sub>

payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete `static/index.html` at PR HEAD and on `origin/master`, this one-line guard fixes the reported first-load state problem without changing the pre-paint result. An empty store still renders the existing dark/default appearance for the initial paint, but it no longer turns that fallback into a persisted user choice. Existing or legacy appearance values still enter the normalization path because either storage key makes `_hadAppearance` true.

## Code reference

The relevant change is at `static/index.html:20`:

```js
var _hadAppearance=localStorage.getItem('hermes-theme')!==null||
  localStorage.getItem('hermes-skin')!==null;
if(_hadAppearance){
  localStorage.setItem('hermes-theme',theme);
  localStorage.setItem('hermes-skin',skin);
}
```

That preserves the later paint logic on the same line (`theme` still resolves to `dark`, `skin` to `default`) while avoiding writes when both keys were absent. It also correctly keeps migration behavior when a legacy theme or only one half of the theme/skin pair exists.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The implementation looks correct. The remaining concern is regression coverage: the PR diff contains only `static/index.html`, despite the description saying the appearance tests were expanded. The current checks at `tests/test_1003_appearance_autosave.py:69-77` cover picker autosave behavior, and `tests/test_bugfix_sweep.py:116-124` checks guarded storage access, but neither pins the new distinction between absent and explicit appearance state.

Please include the described test before merge. A small JS harness or focused source assertion should cover all three states: both keys absent means no `setItem`; one key present means both values are normalized and persisted; both keys present keeps the existing migration behavior. It should also assert that the absent-key case still applies the dark class for the pre-paint fallback.

## Verification

I did not execute PR code because review worktrees are read-only. Static branch tracing confirms that the guard changes persistence only, not the computed theme or DOM class path. The existing release check is green, but it does not substitute for a committed regression test that would prevent this exact boot-script behavior from returning.

payload.author: tomtong2015
payload.body:
Thanks for the review — the guard analysis matches the intent exactly, including the point that either storage key is enough to make `_hadAppearance` true. That pair-vs-per-key distinction is load-bearing, so I'm glad it was checked explicitly.

One small correction for the record: the description didn't say the appearance tests were expanded. It says the change was *"Verified by driving the bootstrap in node against a stubbed localStorage"* — ad-hoc verification, run by hand and not committed. So a diff of `static/index.html` only was accurate rather than an omission against a stated claim.

The request itself was right, though, and it's now addressed in `0fc7e846`: that harness is committed as `tests/test_6808_appearance_bootstrap_no_fabricated_choice.py`. It lifts the real bootstrap out of `static/index.html` and executes it in node against a stubbed `localStorage` / `documentElement`, covering the three states you listed plus the pre-paint assertion:

- **both keys absent** → no `setItem` at all, and the `dark` class is still applied
- **either key present** → both values normalised and persisted
- **legacy names** (`solarized` / `slate` / `monokai` / `nord` / `oled`) → migration preserved, including the *derived* skin

That last group is the one that fails under a per-key guard: with `hermes-theme=solarized` and no `hermes-skin`, the write of the derived skin is the only thing persisting the mapping.

I checked it behaves as a regression test rather than a tautology. Against the pre-fix `static/index.html`, `test_fresh_browser_writes_nothing` and `test_guard_is_on_the_pair_not_per_key` both fail while the other nine still pass — the unfixed bootstrap does still paint dark and does still persist migrations, so only the buggy behaviour differs.

One further note in case it's useful downstream, since it's adjacent but out of scope for this PR. Stopping the client from fabricating a choice does not by itself make a server-side default reachable. `load_settings()` in `api/config.py` calls `_read_raw_settings_file()`, which returns `{}` for a missing `settings.json`; `{}` is a dict, so the `isinstance(stored, dict)` arms are taken, `stored.get("theme")` is `None`, and `_normalize_appearance(None, None)` falls through to its unknown-theme branch — `("dark", "default")` — discarding `_SETTINGS_DEFAULTS`. That is invisible upstream because the defaults there are already dark/default, but a deployment that changes them still lands on dark even with this PR merged. I have a fix for it that gates on the pair in the same way (behaviour-identical for every input carrying stored appearance, including all five legacy mappings); happy to raise it separately if that would be welcome.

payload.title: fix: drain queued messages when tab is re-shown after agent finished while hidden (#6790)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Deep-review gate: SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES — the stranded-queue bug is real, but "local EventSource is CLOSED" isn't a safe signal that the turn is actually done

Thanks for this — the underlying bug (#6790: a message queued while busy gets stranded when the agent finishes while the tab is hidden, because the SSE closed and `stream_end → setBusy(false) → drain` never fired) is real and worth fixing. But the adversarial gate (Codex, driving the real helper + queue functions + `setBusy()` + the recovery path) found the drain trigger is unsafe, and it reproduced a queue-reordering bug.

Housekeeping first: your branch had drifted onto an older `startSessionStream`, and the update-branch merge silently REPLACED master's newer visibility handler (dropping `_startHiddenActiveStreamPoll` + the `known_count` bridging → 3 CI failures). I re-integrated your `_drainQueuedMessagesOnTabReveal` onto master's current handler (+22/-0, master's paths preserved) so we're reviewing the fix on a clean base — that part is on the branch (`gate-rebase/6807`) for you to build on. The finding below is about the drain logic itself, not the merge.

### MUST-FIX (CORE) — `readyState !== 2` (CLOSED) describes only the LOCAL EventSource, not whether the backend turn is done
`static/messages.js:~7944`. The hidden-tab error path (`_deferStreamErrorIfPageHidden`, `static/messages.js:2634`) **intentionally closes the local `EventSource` while preserving `S.activeStreamId = streamId`** so the deferred recovery can reattach to a still-running backend stream. So on reveal, a `CLOSED` local source does **not** mean the agent finished — the backend may still be streaming. Consequences Codex reproduced with a real probe:
- The helper clears `S.activeStreamId` and calls `setBusy(false)` to drain. The deferred recovery then rewires with `S.activeStreamId === null`, so the ownership guard at `static/messages.js:2222` rejects the reattached stream's terminal events as **stale** → the live turn's completion is dropped.
- The premature drain-send races the backend, which still considers the turn active; its 409 guard rejects the send, and `static/messages.js:1850` re-appends the shifted first item **behind** later-queued items → FIFO reversal, reproduced as `[A,B] → [B,A]`.

So the fix both breaks an in-flight reattach and can reorder the user's queued messages.

### Required shape (Codex's spec) — make the drain server-authoritative, never transport-state-based
Serialize the reveal through one recovery path:
1. Query `/api/session/status` (or the equivalent authoritative source) for this sid.
2. **If the backend reports an ACTIVE stream:** preserve busy/owner state and reattach WITHOUT draining — let the reattached stream's real `stream_end` drive `setBusy(false)` and the drain, as it normally would.
3. **If the backend reports IDLE:** restore/canonicalize the settled session, revalidate the current SID + stream identity, remove the stale live source, reopen the session SSE, and *only then* `setBusy(false)` to drain.
4. Never clear `S.activeStreamId` or dequeue based solely on `readyState`. If an authoritative 409 still races the drain, preserve FIFO order (don't re-append the first item behind later ones).

The good news: this is exactly the kind of thing master's existing `_startHiddenActiveStreamPoll` (the hidden-tab status poll) already reaches for — the drain should hang off the authoritative status the poll/recovery establishes, not off the local transport state. Please also add a regression test that reproduces the two failure modes (dropped completion on reattach; `[A,B]→[B,A]` reorder) so this stays fixed.

Verified-good: `node --check` clean; the 28 focused streaming/hidden-tab tests pass; the re-integration preserves master's handler. The concept is right — it just needs to key off "is the turn actually done?" (server truth) instead of "is my local EventSource closed?" Happy to re-gate as soon as it's reworked.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @waterWang — this is a real bug worth fixing (#6790: a queued message stranded when the tab was hidden during agent completion), and the guarded-drain approach with the established `_queueDrainSid` pattern is a reasonable shape. I gated the current head `9ebad7f8` with a Codex adversarial review focused on the drain race. It reproduced **one CORE defect** that needs a rework before this is safe to ship:

### CORE — a queued next-turn message can silently become a **Steer** when the transport is CLOSED but the backend run is still active (`static/messages.js:7671`)
The guard infers "the agent has finished" from the **browser** EventSource being CLOSED (`readyState === 2`). But per the [HTML EventSource spec](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html#the-eventsource-interface), `2 = CLOSED` describes only the **browser connection** — **not** whether the backend run is still executing. When the tab was hidden, the browser closed the SSE, but the agent can still be running server-side.

So on reveal, the path can drain the queue **while the old run is still active**:
- `startSessionStream()` may return early on stale local state (`:7711`), and the newly-created session EventSource isn't yet registered in `LIVE_STREAMS`;
- its recovered `server_turn_started` arrives **asynchronously**, after the helper has already run;
- with the run still active, `send()` takes the **Steer** branch — so the user's queued *next-turn message* silently becomes an *interrupt* of the running agent, with no normal chat start.

Codex reproduced this with a probe executing the real `_drainQueuedMessagesOnTabReveal()`, `setBusy()`, and `send()`: queue removed, `_trySteer()` called, no normal turn started. That's a corruption of the user's intent (next-turn → interrupt), which is worse than the stranded-message bug it fixes.

**What checks out:** the numeric EventSource guard values are correct; there's **no literal double-drain** (`static/ui.js:7952` shifts the queue synchronously, so a later terminal drain sees an empty queue); wrong-session composer dispatch is already guarded (`ui.js:7951-7965`); lint passed; 13 focused tests passed (2 "failures" were only brittle source-window slice assertions shifted by the added lines — not real).

**Fix direction:**
1. `static/messages.js:7668-7682` — don't infer idle from transport state. Reconcile through **`/api/session/status`** before mutating anything. If `active_stream_id` exists, **reattach** it (`_attachServerInitiatedStream(sid, streamId, true)`) and do **not** drain. Only when the server confirms the session is idle should you clear stale local stream ownership, rearm the session stream, and call `setBusy(false)`. On fetch failure / ambiguity / session mismatch, **fail closed** and leave the queue untouched.
2. `static/ui.js:7955-7980` — immediately before the delayed send, re-check same-session ownership plus `S.busy` / `S.activeStreamId`. If a recovered run appeared, restore the shifted item to the **front** of that session's queue (preserving order) and return — never let this recovery drain fall into `send()`'s Steer branch.

Since this touches the message-send path, a small jsdom repro of the hidden-tab → reveal → still-active-run sequence (asserting the queued message starts a normal turn, not a Steer) would make the fix airtight. Ping me when it's re-pushed and I'll re-gate the exact head.

<sub>Gate: Codex (real-probe reproduction of the queue→Steer race, verified against the EventSource spec + session-status semantics). JS-only change — not exercised by the Python suite, so this adversarial review is the load-bearing gate.</sub>

payload.title: fix: avoid full transcript writes for pending WebUI state

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## First-pass review: the concept is right, but the implementation isn't ready — 5 reproduced races + ~20 regressions in the durability guarantees it must preserve

Thanks @aslater3 — this is a genuinely valuable direction, and the write-amplification problem you're solving is real. I ran a full adversarial gate (Codex concurrency pass + the 5-shard suite) as a first-pass characterization.

### Concept: endorsed ✅
Sidecar-ing transient composer/pending state is the **right architecture**. Confirmed the old draft path called `Session.save()` on every autosave — serializing the entire transcript on every keystroke — so the amplification you're removing is real and worth removing. The catch is the bar this sets: **draft/runtime sidecars are only safe if they are generation-bound to their owning transcript and preserve *every* durability guarantee of the former full save.** This branch doesn't meet that bar yet — and both Codex and the suite agree.

### The suite shows the durability gap concretely
The 5-shard run has ~20 failures, all clustered in exactly the guarantees the old full-save provided:
- `test_stage326_composer_draft_validation` (multiple: `...appears_before_persist`, `...skips_unchanged_payload_before_persist`, `...does_not_touch_session_updated_at`) — the new draft path
- `test_provider_mismatch::test_issue1734_chat_start_persists_repaired_codex_provider` — chat-start durable state (see finding #2)
- `test_profile_switch_1200::test_chat_start_retags_empty_session_to_request_profile` — chat-start retag persistence
- `test_session_index::test_metadata_only_get_session_does_not_poison_full_session_cache` — the load/cache path
- `test_regressions::test_server_delete_removes_session_bak_snapshot`, `test_stale_stream_cleanup::*` — deletion / stale-stream races (findings #1, #4)

(Two more — `test_ttl_cache::test_mtime_invalidation` and `test_issue2513_custom_provider_remote_models` — are known environment flakes unrelated to this PR.)

### 5 reproduced correctness findings (Codex probes)

1. **(CORE) `api/routes.py:22717` — deleted session resurrected after a 404.** When deletion wins the chat-start race, the ownership check correctly returns 404 without launching a worker — but `_restore_cleared_recovery()` then calls `s.save()`, recreating the deleted transcript and clearing its tombstone. A probe reproduced `404` **plus a recreated session**. Fix: on 404, do not restore/save recovery state — or revalidate ownership under the session/runtime locks immediately before any compensating save.

2. **(CORE) `api/session_runtime_state.py:24` — restart restores stale provider/compression state.** The sidecar persists model/provider but omits `model_explicit_pick_signature`, `compression_recovery`, `recommended_recovery_action`, and `post_compression_context_tokens_estimate` — all of which the former `s.save()` persisted at chat start. A reload probe restored the old signature, the old compression-recovery card, and the old token estimate. Fix: persist and overlay **every** chat-start mutation (or checkpoint metadata whenever these durable fields change). This is the durability-parity requirement the concept hinges on.

payload.body:
## Summary

I read the complete changed files at PR head `ad68fabbe`, their `origin/master` counterparts, both new regression files, and the route diff. Moving draft writes and deferred pending state out of the transcript is the right performance direction, and writing the submitted journal event before the runtime sidecar improves crash ordering. I found two lifecycle blockers before these new files can become session-owned state.

## Code reference

The load path at `api/models.py:1578-1587` always overlays the runtime sidecar after reading the transcript:

```python
data = json.loads(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
data["messages"], _collapsed_partials = _collapse_adjacent_duplicate_partials(data.get("messages"))
data["composer_draft"] = _load_composer_draft_sidecar(
    sid,
    fallback=data.get("composer_draft"),
)
data.update(_load_runtime_state_sidecar(sid))
session = cls(**data)
```

A terminal `Session.save()` publishes the new transcript and only afterward calls `_clear_runtime_state_sidecar_if_terminal()` at `api/models.py:1534-1540`. A concurrent load between those operations can therefore read the completed transcript, overlay the old pending fields, and construct a session that is busy again. `session_runtime_state.py:115-120` has a lock-aware context manager, but neither `Session.load()` nor the terminal save-and-clear publication uses it, so atomic replacement of each individual file does not make the two-file state atomic.

The second ownership gap is deletion. `api/draft_store.py:95-108` ends with `save_draft()` and has no delete primitive. The runtime module has `clear_runtime_state()` at `api/session_runtime_state.py:121-127`, but the session deletion paths are unchanged. Deleting a WebUI session therefore leaves both owned files behind; importing or recreating the same ID can inherit an old draft or pending turn.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please make transcript publication plus terminal runtime cleanup one coordinated operation with loads. One workable shape is a per-session publication lock held across transcript read plus overlay, and across terminal transcript replace plus runtime clear. The crash contract still needs care: a crash after transcript replace but before clear must be recognized as terminal on the next load, rather than allowing the stale overlay to win.

Add explicit `clear_draft()` and one shared sidecar-cleanup helper, then call it from every WebUI session deletion/ID-retirement path. Cleanup should be best-effort only where deletion already has retry semantics; otherwise a reported successful delete should not leave state that can attach to a reused ID.

## Test plan

Extend `tests/test_pending_runtime_state.py:11-190` with a controlled load-versus-terminal-save interleaving and a crash-window fixture containing a terminal transcript plus stale runtime sidecar. Extend `tests/test_composer_draft_sidecar.py:12-132` with delete plus same-ID recreate/import coverage, asserting neither draft nor runtime metadata survives. I reviewed PR-authored code statically and did not execute it.

payload.body:
## Summary

I re-read all seven changed files at head `8ed4407c5`, their `origin/master` counterparts, both regression files, and the Agent session-deletion contract after the four follow-up commits. The runtime publication lock and CLI cleanup coverage address the races from my earlier review. One ownership failure path remains: both sidecar delete primitives swallow unlink failures, so every higher-level delete helper can report success while old per-session data is still present and eligible to attach to a reused ID.

## Code reference

`api/draft_store.py:108-117` currently converts an unlink error into a debug log and success:

```python
def delete_draft(session_id: str) -> None:
    with draft_lock(session_id):
        try:
            draft_path(session_id).unlink(missing_ok=True)
        except OSError:
            logger.debug("Failed to delete composer draft sidecar for %s", session_id, exc_info=True)
```

`api/session_runtime_state.py:126-133` does the same for runtime state. The callers then swallow again: `_delete_session_sidecars()` at `api/routes.py:21930-21946` and `_delete_webui_sidecars_for_session()` at `api/models.py:9506-9528` have no failure result. The CLI path invokes the latter after the database commit at `api/models.py:9835-9838`, so `delete_cli_session()` can return successful even when either WebUI-owned file survives.

The happy-path assertions at `tests/test_pending_runtime_state.py:208-255` prove removal only when unlink succeeds. They do not exercise a permission or I/O failure, nor same-ID recreation/import. A stale draft is especially persistent because a terminal `Session.save()` clears runtime state but does not clear the draft sidecar; `Session.load()` then prefers that old draft at `api/models.py:1583-1590`.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Make `delete_draft()` and `clear_runtime_state()` report failure or raise after logging. Propagate that status through both deletion helpers. For the post-commit CLI path, add failed sidecar IDs to a retryable cleanup record rather than returning a false clean result. For the WebUI transcript-delete path, either fail the request before deleting the owner or retain a tombstone that causes stale sidecars to be ignored and retried until removal succeeds.

## Test plan

Inject an unlink failure independently for draft and runtime files. Assert the delete is not reported as fully clean, the failed ID remains retryable, and recreating/importing that same ID cannot observe the stale draft or pending turn. Then clear the failure and assert a retry removes both files. I reviewed PR-authored code statically and did not execute it.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I re-read the current seven-file diff at head `5f71cf41f`, including both new sidecar modules, the complete new regression files, and the changed session-load, save, delete, and chat-start paths. The tombstone and unlink-failure work addresses my previous deletion blocker, and the runtime sidecar avoids rewriting an existing transcript at deferred chat start. One new cache-refresh bug remains: a one-shot context-manager instance is reused in multiple branches.

## Code reference

`api/models.py:4722-4763` constructs `runtime_lock` once, then can enter that same object twice:

```python
runtime_lock = runtime_state_lock(sid)
...
if not metadata_only and _cached_session_lags_disk(cached):
    with runtime_lock:
        disk_session = Session.load(sid)
...
if not metadata_only and _inactive_cache_tail_needs_disk_check(cached):
    with runtime_lock:
```

`runtime_state_lock()` at `api/session_runtime_state.py:64-68` is decorated with `@contextmanager`, so it returns a generator-backed context manager. That object is consumed by the first `with`; it is not reusable for the second entry. If both cache predicates are true, the second branch raises while entering the context. Its surrounding broad handler catches the error and logs at debug level, so the inactive-tail reconciliation is silently skipped.

The new test at `tests/test_pending_runtime_state.py:253-270` forces `_cached_session_lags_disk()` true but explicitly forces `_inactive_cache_tail_needs_disk_check()` false, so it cannot catch this path.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Keep a context-manager factory, not an instance. For example, retain the imported `runtime_state_lock` callable and use `with runtime_state_lock(sid):` independently in each branch and on the cache-miss path. A small local function returning a fresh context manager also works. This preserves the publication lock without coupling mutually nonexclusive refresh checks.

## Test plan

Add a cached-session regression where both predicates return true. Stub the two disk loads and tail comparison, then assert both guarded sections run without an exception and the final cached projection is the expected one. Retain the existing assertion that cache publication occurs while the runtime lock is owned. I reviewed PR-authored code statically and did not execute it.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

The lightweight runtime/draft separation is well motivated, and the new overlay/cleanup tests cover the normal lifecycle. One concurrency blocker remains after the latest changes: chat start and direct/cascaded CLI deletion still use different lock domains. The second ownership check narrows the race, but it does not make the check-and-start operation atomic with sidecar tombstoning and deletion.

## Code reference

At `api/routes.py:21369-21407`, the final check and worker launch are protected only by the Agent session lock:

```python
with session_lock:
    if hasattr(s, "path") and not _session_owner_present(s.session_id):
        return {"error": "Session not found", "_status": 404}
    ...
    register_stream_owner(stream_id, s.session_id)
    ...
    thr.start()
```

The deletion path uses a different lock. `api/models.py:9531-9545` acquires `runtime_state_lock(session_id)`, evicts the cache entry, records the tombstone, and clears both sidecars. `delete_cli_session()` at `api/models.py:9572` can invoke that cleanup for every cascaded `removed_id`, without acquiring the route-level `session_lock` used above.

That leaves a concrete interleaving: chat passes `_session_owner_present()` while holding `session_lock`; a parent/direct CLI deletion acquires the runtime lock for this ID, evicts/tombstones it, and releases; chat then registers and starts a worker for the deleted owner. This is especially relevant to delegate-cascade IDs, because the route lock for the requested parent does not protect each removed child.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please serialize the decision, not only the file operations. A shared lifecycle lock must cover the chat-side final owner recheck through stream registration/start, and the delete-side active-state check through tombstoning/owner removal. The existing per-session runtime lock is a reasonable shared primitive if both paths use it with one documented lock order. The delete side should re-read runtime/cache state under that lock and refuse or defer removal when the session became active. For cascades, acquire per-ID locks in deterministic order or process each ID atomically without holding two session locks in conflicting order.

## Verification step

`tests/test_pending_runtime_state.py:316-371` toggles an in-memory owner flag inside `_prepare_chat_start_session_for_stream`; it proves the second check exists, but no deletion runs concurrently and no real lock interaction is exercised. Add a barrier-driven regression that races `_start_chat_stream_for_session()` against direct `models.delete_cli_session()` (including a cascaded child). Assert exactly one valid outcome: deletion wins and no stream/worker starts, or chat wins and deletion observes active state and leaves the owner intact. I did not execute PR-authored code; this finding is from read-only inspection, including the Agent session-deletion contract.

## Summary

Reading the complete `api/auth.py` at PR HEAD and on `origin/master`, plus the existing trusted-header suite in `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py`, the stale non-trusted-session precedence fix is in the correct auth-owner function. A trusted peer with an asserted identity now reaches reconciliation instead of returning the password/passkey/OIDC-style session. I found one blocker in the companion wildcard behavior, and the PR currently adds no regression tests for either behavior.

## Code reference

At `api/auth.py:723-729`, the first matching configured group still wins:

```python
for group, profile in mapping.items():
    if group in groups:
        return None if profile == "*" else profile
return "default"
```

That conflicts with the stated admin escape-hatch semantics when a user belongs to both an ordinary bound group and a wildcard admin group. With an insertion-ordered map such as `{"devs":"dev", "admins":"*"}` and headers containing both groups, this returns `dev`, so the admin remains bound. Reversing the map order makes the same identity unbound. The existing contract test at `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py:185-197` explicitly pins mapping-order precedence for concrete mappings, so wildcard precedence needs an intentional rule rather than inheriting that behavior accidentally.

The stale-cookie branch at `api/auth.py:865-882` correctly limits the override to trusted peers with a non-empty asserted identity. At `api/auth.py:895-907`, however, reconciliation invalidates the incoming session and creates a replacement during request authentication. That transition also needs an unsafe-request regression because CSRF validation later sees the original request cookie while the replacement cookie is only queued for the response.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Make a wildcard match dominate concrete matches while retaining mapping order among concrete profiles:

```python
matches = [profile for group, profile in mapping.items() if group in groups]
if "*" in matches:
    return None
return matches[0] if matches else "default"
```

Please also add the changes to `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py`; a security-sensitive auth change without executable coverage is not ready to merge.

## Test plan

Cover both wildcard map orders for a user in `devs,admins`, a concrete-only multi-group case preserving current order, a stale non-trusted cookie replaced on a trusted GET, and the first trusted unsafe request with the old cookie and CSRF token. The last test should pin the intended policy explicitly: either the write succeeds safely during rotation, or it receives a deliberate retryable rejection while the replacement cookie is emitted. Also retain negative cases for untrusted peers and requests without an asserted identity. I reviewed the source and assertions statically and did not execute PR-authored code.


This equality check does not require `info["auth_type"] == "trusted"`. A non-trusted record carrying the same username and bound profile therefore returns unchanged: the old cookie is not invalidated, no trusted cookie is issued, and `_remember_trusted_auth_session()` at `api/auth.py:842-851` does not populate the trusted-session handler fields because its own type check fails. The wildcard addition at `api/auth.py:723-729` makes the `bound_profile is None` equality case especially easy to reach for an unbound/admin identity.

`create_session()` at `api/auth.py:604-622` explicitly supports records with arbitrary `auth_type`, `username`, and `bound_profile`, so this is not merely a malformed-store scenario. It can occur when another authentication flow has identity metadata matching the proxy assertion.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Make reuse conditional on the session already being trusted:

```python
if (
    info
    and info.get("auth_type") == "trusted"
    and info.get("username") == username
    and info.get("bound_profile") == bound_profile
):
```

All non-trusted sessions on a valid trusted request should then fall through to invalidation and trusted-session creation. That matches the comment at `api/auth.py:868-875` and avoids carrying the old session security context across authentication mechanisms.

## Test plan

The existing tests at `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py:430-524` cover rotation between two trusted identities, but this PR adds no regression for the stale non-trusted case. Please add parameterized cases for:

1. a legacy/password-style session with no identity metadata,
2. a non-trusted session whose username/profile differ,
3. a non-trusted session whose username/profile exactly match, including wildcard/unbound profile,
4. an untrusted network peer presenting the same header, which must not gain trusted-session rotation.

For the first three, assert the old cookie is invalid, the replacement has `auth_type == "trusted"`, and exactly one new auth cookie is queued. I reviewed PR-authored code statically and did not execute it.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @SamsGuamejy — this is a real, well-diagnosed production security bug (a stale/leftover non-trusted session cookie silently overriding the proxy-asserted identity and bypassing the group→profile binding), and the **core auth-boundary fix is sound**. I gated the current head `63dc8a55` with an adversarial Codex pass (focused on spoofing, wildcard fail-closed, and rotation) + the full suite (13,949 passed).

Good news on the security core: the spoof surface is **closed correctly** — the trusted header only wins when `is_trusted_auth_enabled()` **and** `_raw_peer_is_trusted_proxy(handler)` **and** an identity is actually asserted, so a header from a non-proxy peer can't override a session. That's the right shape.

Holding for a revision — the CSRF/session-rotation machinery introduces **three regressions on the exact stale-cookie path this PR targets**, all reproduced:

### 1. BRICK — stale-cookie page load renders an empty CSRF token (`api/routes.py:12056`)
Reconciliation invalidates the request cookie, but the shell only uses `_trusted_auth_session_cookie_value` when the old cookie is **absent** — not when it's **present but invalid**. So `parse_cookie(handler)` returns the stale value, `csrf_token_for_session(...)` yields `""`, and `static/index.html:35` then disables CSRF injection. Result: every send, new-chat, profile switch, and other unsafe request returns **403 until a manual reload** — for exactly the user this PR is meant to help. Verified against the real `check_auth()` → `handle_get()` order (replacement cookie valid, shell body `csrfToken:""`). **Fix:** prefer the reconciled replacement cookie before `parse_cookie(handler)`, and add a stale-cookie shell regression test.

### 2. CORE — the advertised immediate retry can't succeed in an open tab (`api/routes.py:5524`)
The browser still holds the old page token captured at `static/index.html:34`; the rotation response doesn't hand back a new one. The new test at `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py:969` manufactures a replacement token directly — which production JavaScript can't do — so it masks the bug. Verified: first write gets the retryable 403, and a second request with the replacement cookie + the unchanged page token gets **another 403**. **Fix:** return the replacement CSRF token on the rotation response and update the fetch wrapper's token before the user retries (covering POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), then adjust the test to exercise the real client path.

### 3. SILENT — rotating an unbound session drops the profile binding (`api/auth.py:942`)
Rotating an unbound session (no group map, or a `*` mapping) doesn't re-sign the currently valid profile cookie. The first request keeps the request profile, but the next request rejects that profile cookie against the replacement session and **silently falls back to the process/default profile**. Verified with an isolated signed `devops` profile cookie. **Fix:** capture the authenticated profile selection before invalidating the old session and reissue it signed to the replacement unbound session.

**Net:** the security boundary itself is correct — no spoof hole, and the original stale-cookie override is genuinely fixed. The gap is that the rotation/CSRF handling wasn't carried through the present-but-invalid-cookie case, which bricks the same flow. Once those three land (and the retry test exercises the real client path), this should be a strong fix. Ping me when it's re-pushed and I'll re-run the adversarial gate on the exact head.

<sub>Gate: Codex (adversarial reproduction — spoof surface verified closed; three rotation/CSRF regressions reproduced against the real request order) + full suite (13,949 passed). Verdict: SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES. This is a security/auth-boundary PR, so the final merge decision stays with a maintainer even after the fixes land.</sub>
