payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the fast turnaround @SamsGuamejy — real progress. I re-gated the new head `255952b1` with another adversarial Codex pass + full suite (13,952 passed), and the three regressions from the last round are addressed: the 403 path now hands back a replacement CSRF token, `index.html` adopts it on `session_rotated`, and unbound rotation re-signs the profile cookie. The security core also still holds — the spoof guard (header wins only when trusted-auth is enabled + peer is the trusted proxy + identity asserted) is intact after the churn.

One more revision needed — the fix covers the **403 rotation path** but rotation also happens on **safe GETs**, and that trigger still bricks the tab:

### CORE — rotation on a safe GET leaves the page token stale (`api/auth.py:959`, `api/routes.py:5523`, `static/index.html:51`)
The token handback is gated on the CSRF-failure path: `routes.py:5523` only attaches `csrf_token` when `_CSRF_FAILURE_ATTR == "session_rotated"`, and `index.html:54` only adopts it when `body.reason === 'session_rotated'`. But a **normal GET — e.g. the 30-second session poll — rotates and installs the replacement cookie without ever going through that failure path**, so its response carries no `csrf_token` and the page keeps the old token. The next POST then reuses the (now-current) trusted session, so it's *not* flagged `session_rotated` and returns a plain `token_mismatch` with no recovery token → every unsafe action fails until a manual reload. Same brick as round 1, reached through the poll instead of the first write.

Two coupled issues on the same path:
- **Concurrent rotation race:** two concurrent stale-cookie requests create two valid replacement sessions; response ordering can leave cookie B paired with token A.
- **Async adoption gap:** the fetch wrapper resolves before async token parsing finishes — the new test masks this with `setTimeout(0)` at `tests/test_trusted_header_auth.py:1113`, so it passes without exercising the real client timing (same pattern as the round-1 test that manufactured a token).

**Exact fix:**
1. Atomically reuse **one identity-scoped replacement** for concurrent rotations (so a given identity can't spawn two replacement sessions with mismatched tokens).
2. Expose the replacement's CSRF token **whenever its cookie is flushed — including on safe GET responses** (the session poll), not only on the 403 failure path.
3. **Synchronously adopt** the token from every same-origin fetch response before the wrapper promise resolves, and update the test to exercise that real timing instead of `setTimeout(0)`.

The direction is right and the security boundary is sound — this is the last mile: make rotation-token propagation cover the GET/poll path and the concurrent case, with a test that follows the real client flow. Ping me on re-push and I'll re-run the adversarial gate on the exact head.

Verdict: SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES. Security/auth-boundary PR — final merge stays a maintainer decision even once this lands.</sub>

## Summary

I read the full PR-head and `origin/master` versions of `static/extension_settings.js`, `tests/test_extension_settings_runtime.py`, and `docs/EXTENSIONS.md`, and cross-checked the injected runtime inventory in `api/extensions.py`. The handle identity and no-write failure cases are well covered. There is one contract mismatch around registration after a status refresh: the docs define eligibility from the immutable initial-boot inventory, but the implementation gates uncached registrations against the mutable current schema map.

## Code reference

`static/extension_settings.js:99-128` seeds `trustedExtensions` only once, while clearing and rebuilding `schemas` on every `primeFromStatus` call. `static/extension_settings.js:310-325` then uses `schemas` for registration:

```js
const existing=registrations.get(clean);
if(existing) return existing;
if(!schemas.has(clean)) return null;
const handle=Object.freeze({
  id:clean,
  settings:settingsForExtension(clean),
  storage:storageForExtension(clean),
});
```

The text at `docs/EXTENSIONS.md:285-301` says eligibility comes from the effective-enabled inventory present at initial page boot and that status refresh does not implement runtime unload. The regression at `tests/test_extension_settings_runtime.py:221-243` refreshes away `alpha.ext`, but it registered alpha before the refresh, so the `registrations` cache masks this distinction.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Consider this sequence: alpha is present at boot, its injected script defers registration, a status refresh removes alpha from `schemas`, then the script calls `register("alpha.ext")` for the first time. The call now returns `null`, even though alpha is in the initial trusted inventory and the documented page-lifetime contract says reload is the enable/disable boundary.

I recommend choosing one invariant explicitly:

1. If identity is boot-snapshot based, gate on `trustedExtensions.has(clean)` and make the factories use the corresponding immutable trusted metadata when current `schemas` no longer contains the ID.
2. If first registration is intentionally current-status based, update the docs to state that and keep the present gate.

The first option seems more consistent with the one-time `trustedSeeded` design and the no-runtime-unload wording.

## Test plan

Add a case that boots with alpha, calls `primeFromStatus` without alpha **before any alpha registration**, then asserts the chosen result and settings/storage behavior. Keep the existing cached-handle case as a separate assertion. No PR-authored code was executed during this review.

@nesquena-hermes, you were right about the executable bypass. `_drain_webui_process_notifications` could settle fresh current-turn completions outside the durable receipt path.

For fresh events, the direct async claim and ACK and the direct ordinary consume are gone, so claim, ACK, and consume happen only after durable incorporation.

I reran the hostile receipt-path probe with `claim_completion_delivery` wired to raise. On `84861209`, the async event is not ACKed: its `delivery_state` stays `pending`, and its claim is released for durable retry. The ordinary event is not consumed and lands as one deferred recovery entry. Nothing is lost. The same probe method on pre-fix base `57452650` reproduces the original symptom: the async event is marked delivered and the ordinary event consumed without the receipt path being called. That baseline reproduction is what makes the fixed result meaningful.

- `tests/test_async_delegation_webui_bridge.py::test_current_turn_async_drain_crash_restart_executes_once_via_receipt` covers async acceptance, a crash before provider execution, restart, one eventual execution, and no loss or duplicate.
- `tests/test_background_process_restart_recovery.py::test_current_turn_ordinary_drain_waits_for_durable_incorporation_before_consume` keeps ordinary completion consumption false until durable incorporation.
- `tests/test_notify_on_complete_webui.py::test_current_turn_fresh_process_and_async_choose_same_root_and_tip_owner` verifies that fresh process and async events select the same lineage root and current delivery tip.
- `tests/test_background_process_restart_recovery.py::test_named_profile_current_turn_completion_restart_is_fully_isolated` covers both process and async-delegation completions and keeps the receipt, sidecar, journal, model scope, and resumed execution on the named profile's current tip.

Each regression is mutation-sensitive at the current call locations. Restoring the direct ordinary consume makes the ordinary-incorporation, root/tip convergence, and named-profile process cases fail. Restoring the fresh async claim and ACK makes the async crash/restart, root/tip convergence, and named-profile async cases fail. With both bypasses restored, all five parameter cases fail.

Your point about `test_drain_orders_converge_on_one_completion` was also correct. It entered through the canonical receipt path and never exercised the drain. That test is unchanged because it covers the teardown/idle lane; the gap you identified is now covered by tests that run through the drain itself.

I composed 21 conflict hunks across 6 files hunk by hunk, preserving cancelling-run non-attachability (`92c790ffe551`), atomic regeneration (`4d035781924459772864d5e0ffc06c31ae1e9898`), compression transcript fencing (`c27f3d67a80c`), and SILENT control-turn ingress suppression (`6d6560f286c4`).

## Summary

I re-reviewed the current head and the new commits after the earlier comment. The earlier concern about a separate poller and `messages.js` does not apply to this implementation: the current branch dispatches Codex IDs through `api/models.py:9365-9369`, and the existing generic read-only session flow in `static/sessions.js:2485-2515` is the relevant client path. This pass found two concrete issues that should be fixed before merge.

## Code reference

The first is a test-isolation bug in `tests/test_codex_session_bridge.py:348-382`. The test replaces `_parse_codex_rollout_impl`, but its cleanup restores a different attribute:

```python
        assert calls == 2
        assert [m["content"] for m in third] == ["changed"]
    finally:
        codex.parse_codex_rollout = real_parse
```

The assignment at `tests/test_codex_session_bridge.py:354` mutates `codex._parse_codex_rollout_impl`; line 382 must restore that same symbol. As written, later tests keep the closure-backed `counting_parse` wrapper for the remainder of the process. Use `monkeypatch.setattr` or restore `codex._parse_codex_rollout_impl = real_parse` in the `finally` block.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

There is also a deployment regression in `docker-compose.yml:29-35`. The new Codex bind is unconditional and uses Compose short bind syntax. When the host Codex directory does not exist, short bind syntax has create-host-path behavior on normal Docker Compose installations. A user who does not have Codex can therefore get a newly created directory, often owned by the Docker daemon user, instead of the documented clean no-op. That can later prevent Codex itself from initializing its state directory.

Please keep the base Compose file safe for hosts without Codex. The cleanest option is an opt-in Compose override for the Codex mount and matching environment setting. A long-syntax bind with host-path creation disabled avoids silent creation, but it would make the base deployment fail when Codex is absent, so an optional override better matches `docs/codex-sessions.md:35-67` and the additive behavior promised by `api/codex_sessions.py:477-506`.

The rollout containment check at `api/codex_sessions.py:148-177`, UUID validation at `api/codex_sessions.py:130-145`, and the read-only SQLite path otherwise look appropriately defensive in static review.

## Test plan

I did not execute code from the PR worktree. After the fixes, CI should run the entire Codex bridge module in process order, with another parser test after the cache test to prove global state is restored. Deployment verification should cover both a host with a populated Codex directory and a host where that directory is absent; the absent case must neither create the path nor fail an otherwise valid WebUI Compose startup.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading all three changed files at PR head **56c9307fa**, plus the corresponding **origin/master** files, the rewind detection itself is useful. I found one behavior blocker in the new suppression mechanism: the silent-prefix count lives in the raw source-text coordinate space, while both consumers live in rendered-text space. That mismatch means the PR can suppress the first genuinely new words after a rewind.

## Code reference

**static/messages.js:4350-4366** computes the budget before rebuilding, while renderer **add_text** receives only rendered text chunks:
~~~javascript
_streamFadeSilentPrefixChars=_silentCommon;
let silentLeft=_streamFadeSilentPrefixChars||0;
if(silentLeft>0){
  silentLeft-=match[0].length;
}
~~~
The common length includes Markdown delimiters, link destinations, and MEDIA token bytes. Smd does not pass those bytes to **add_text**: it emits token callbacks or media nodes and passes only visible prose. The same mismatch exists in **static/messages.js:4536-4573** and **static/messages.js:4864-4889**.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

A concrete case is old prose **alpha** beta rewritten to **alpha** gamma. The source common prefix includes the four strong-emphasis delimiters, but the renderer consumes only alpha and the separating whitespace. The leftover budget then writes gamma as plain text. That contradicts the intended contract that only the already-visible prefix is muted and the changed tail fades. A common prefix containing a MEDIA token has the same problem because the token becomes a node and does not reach **add_text** at all.
Please scope suppression to the owning parser or renderer, as the existing media-tail state is scoped, and calculate the boundary in rendered-text space. One practical option is to snapshot the old node text before rebuild, rebuild, compare it with the new node text, then remove **is-new** only from spans covered by that rendered common prefix. Whichever approach is used, clear the state on reduced-motion, safe-renderer, empty-text, and parser-finalization paths. The current stream-global counter can otherwise survive a rebuild that has no fade consumer and affect a later append.

## Verification

The new tests at **tests/test_smooth_text_fade.py:589-688** use plain text, and the self-heal test stubs parser writing, so they cannot expose this coordinate mismatch. Add a real vendored-smd regression for strong emphasis, links or code, and MEDIA before the changed tail. Assert the old rendered prefix is plain while the first changed word has exactly one **stream-fade-word is-new** span. Also cover reduced motion during rebuild followed by motion being enabled, and two concurrent anchor/main parsers to prove suppression cannot cross owners. I did not execute PR-authored tests; this review used read-only source, diff, and assertion inspection.

payload.author: silent-reader-cn
payload.body:
Addressed the coordinate-space blocker — rewind mute now runs in RENDERED-text space.

**What changed (commit `a6d37b22`):**
- Replaced the source-space `_streamFadeSilentPrefixChars` budget with `_streamFadeMuteRenderedPrefix()`: snapshot the OLD rendered node text before the rebuild, then after `parser_write` compare it against the NEW rendered text and strip `is-new` only from spans inside the rendered common prefix.
- Markdown delimiters / link destinations / MEDIA token bytes never reach the fade `add_text` hook, so they no longer inflate the mute budget — `**alpha** beta` → `**alpha** gamma` now fades `gamma` correctly (source-space counted 10 chars and muted it).
- Scoped to the owning node (main `assistantBody` and anchor `.msg-body` handled separately) — no stream-global counter that could survive a rebuild without a fade consumer.
- `_rewindPrevRendered` is a local variable consumed right after the rebuild; nothing persists across reduced-motion / safe-renderer / empty-text / parser-finalization paths.

**Tests:**
- `test_stream_fade_mute_rendered_prefix_plain_words` — plain-word prefix mute
- `test_stream_fade_mute_rendered_prefix_markdown_and_media_bytes` — the exact blocker regression (source-space budget bug)
- `test_stream_fade_mute_rendered_prefix_scoped_per_root` — concurrent main vs anchor nodes stay independent
- `test_stream_fade_smd_write_self_heal_sets_silent_prefix_on_rewind` — updated for the rendered-space snapshot flow

Gate: `node -c` OK; `test_smooth_text_fade.py` + `test_smd_media_in_stream.py` + `test_svg_audio_video_rendering.py` + `test_insights.py` → 83 passed, 18 subtests.

One note: the strong-emphasis/link/MEDIA-before-changed-tail behavioral test you asked for lives at the unit level (`_streamFadeMuteRenderedPrefix` with a fake DOM) rather than driving the real vendored smd parser — the full node-driven harness for this renderer doesn't mount a real DOM. Happy to add a vendored-smd round-trip if you want it.

payload.author: vduke
payload.title: feat(sidebar): add show_kanban_sessions toggle to hide kanban worker sessions

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for this — hiding kanban worker sessions from the default sidebar is exactly the right annoyance to fix, and the core mechanism is solid: an authoritative gate confirmed both cache-key implementations correctly separate toggle OFF/ON, the settings persist and round-trip, project-assigned kanban rows survive as `default_hidden`, and the source match is exact (doesn't hide `kanban-worker`). Full suite is green. Three behavioral edges need to match how the existing cron/webhook toggles already behave before it ships:

### Must fix

**1. An explicit kanban source filter should OVERRIDE default hiding — `api/routes.py:2407`.** When a request explicitly filters for kanban sessions (e.g. a source/kanban view), the default-hidden treatment should not apply — the user asked for them. Mirror the cron/webhook source-filter handling so an exact kanban filter returns those rows even when the toggle is off.

**2. Preserve PINNED kanban rows when the toggle is off — `api/models.py:4992`.** A kanban session the user has pinned should stay visible regardless of the hide toggle (same as pinned cron/webhook rows). Right now the flat `source == 'kanban'` hide in `_hide_from_default_sidebar` drops pinned kanban rows too.

**3. Don't let hidden kanban rows consume the general initial-fetch budget — `api/models.py:7551`.** Hidden kanban rows shouldn't eat slots in the general 20-row query (they'd crowd out visible sessions from the first page), but keep a bounded kanban-only retrieval path for the toggle-on case — again mirroring the cron/webhook mechanism.

### Not blockers
Suite is green; the two shard failures I saw (`test_issue2513_custom_provider_remote_models`, `test_ttl_cache::test_mtime_invalidation`) are pre-existing environment flakes on our CI box, identical on clean master.

Once these three match the cron/webhook behavior I'll re-gate the exact head (Codex + full suite) and ship it — the settings toggle renders cleanly (verified). Attribution preserved.

I applied maintainer fixes (Co-authored-by @vduke) for the cron/webhook-parity gaps the last review flagged:

- **Source-filter override:** `_dedupe_cli_sidebar_sessions_for_api` now takes `source_filter`, normalizes it (`strip().lower()`), and reveals the matching background source when explicitly filtered — so an explicit kanban view shows those rows even with the toggle off. Scoped to the matching source only. Bite-tested regression (fails if reverted).
- **Filtered-view cap:** `KANBAN_PROJECT_CHIP_LIMIT` (200) bounds a filtered kanban-only view, mirroring `CRON/WEBHOOK_PROJECT_CHIP_LIMIT`.

The other two findings are confirmed **out of parity scope** (verified against the code + Codex):
- *Excluding kanban from the general query budget* would break the toggle-ON case (kanban would never load) unless a bounded kanban-merge is added — which cron/webhook don't do either. Deferred as a separate cross-cutting optimization.
- *Pinned-survives-hide* and *revealing project-assigned rows at the `all_sessions()` layer*: `all_sessions()` hides cron, webhook, and kanban identically (project-assigned rows are `default_hidden` for all three, pinned affects only sort). Making kanban behave differently here would make it inconsistent with its siblings. Kanban is at correct parity.

## Summary

I read the complete changed backend helper files, the full test file at PR HEAD and on `origin/master`, and the route/UI diffs. I also checked the producer contract on the agent side: `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:9021-9028` stamps worker subprocesses with the canonical `kanban` session source. The WebUI filter therefore targets the actual persisted source rather than a guessed label. I do not see a code-level blocker in the current head.

## Code reference

The source is normalized and made read-only at `api/agent_sessions.py:59-100` and `api/agent_sessions.py:218-224`. The actual visibility gate is narrow at `api/models.py:4956-4975`:

```python
if not show_cron and (source == "cron" or sid.startswith("cron_")):
    return True
if not show_webhook and source == "webhook":
    return True
if not show_kanban and source == "kanban":
    return True
```

The flag is also part of cache identity at `api/route_session_list_cache.py:119-157`, then threaded through both cache lookup and rebuild calls at `api/routes.py:13132-13180`. That is important: otherwise toggling could keep serving a payload built under the opposite setting.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The implementation follows the cron/webhook contract consistently: default off, subordinate UI state, server-side filtering, settings-triggered cache invalidation, and non-CLI classification. The agent-side source contract confirms that `source == "kanban"` is the right layer.

My remaining recommendation is test quality rather than implementation correctness. `tests/test_issue2841_show_cron_sessions_toggle.py:132-224` mostly proves wiring through broad source-string searches. Those checks can still pass if a future edit leaves the string in one call site but disconnects the request path. A behavioral test around `_build_session_list_cache_payload` should feed one ordinary row and one kanban row, assert exclusion with the default, inclusion with the flag, and distinct cache keys for false versus true.

## Verification

The direct unit cases at `tests/test_issue2841_show_cron_sessions_toggle.py:31-57` do verify the core predicate, including isolation from the cron/webhook flags. I did not execute PR-authored code because this review path is read-only. Source inspection indicates the current head is internally consistent; the suggested route-level regression test is non-blocking.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @starship-s — exact-head warm-up at `dcf3069f0791` found objective blockers that need correction before another gate.

### Finding

**Yes — three current-head correctness gaps remain.**

### A. Profile-bearing references are not profile-addressed

`_transformBareSessionReferences()` recognizes `@session:<profile>/<id>` but deliberately drops `_profile` and emits only `[<id>](session://<id>)` (`static/ui.js:290-336`). Both settled and SMD rendering then rewrite that to the ordinary ID-only `/session/<id>` URL (`static/ui.js:7568-7578`; `static/messages.js:4374-4384`). The delegated click handler extracts only the ID and calls `loadSession(id)` (`static/ui.js:2507-2517`). No profile survives in the href, dataset, or navigation call.

The existing cross-profile recovery makes the common unique-ID case appear to work: `loadSession()` first GETs by ID, then reacts to a server `409 session_profile_mismatch` by switching to the owner returned by the server and retrying (`static/sessions.js:1618-1643,1820-1844`; `api/routes.py:12611-12623`). That is an ID-discovery fallback, not the semantics of an explicit `@session:<profile>/<id>` reference. It cannot assert that the named profile is the target; a stale/mistyped profile silently opens whichever owner the backend reports, and an ID that already resolves in the active profile never produces the mismatch needed to honor the named profile. The new test explicitly codifies the loss (`test_cross_profile_reference_uses_only_id_and_short_label`, `tests/test_renderer_js_behaviour.py:218-223`) instead of exercising a profile switch or verifying target ownership.

### B. User references remain plain text under the default rendering mode

`renderMd()` now calls the transformer (`static/ui.js:7168-7174`), so assistant messages and user messages with the opt-in Markdown setting enabled can link. The production dispatch does not always use `renderMd`: `_getCachedRender(text, true)` selects `_renderUserFencedBlocks(text)` whenever `window._renderUserMarkdown` is false (`static/ui.js:1556-1563`). That setting is explicitly **off by default** (`static/index.html:1082-1086`). `_renderUserFencedBlocks()` escapes ordinary user prose and never calls or restores `_transformBareSessionReferences` (`static/ui.js:359-443`). Therefore a user who pastes `@session:profile/id` into a normal sent message sees no link under the default product configuration.

The new renderer tests call `renderMd()` directly; they do not pass a user row through `_getCachedRender` in both settings states. This allows the default-path omission to pass.

### C. The token boundary rejects common valid prose punctuation/Markdown wrappers

The ID alphabet correctly matches the canonical safe WebUI alphabet `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` (`static/ui.js:334`; `api/models.py:202-218`), and the optional profile alphabet matches the canonical lowercase profile rule (`api/profiles.py:29-30`). Leading boundaries also correctly avoid emails, URL/path embeddings, and token concatenation. However the trailing boundary allows only whitespace/end or a small punctuation set (`.,;:!?()[]{}`) and omits closing single/double/curly quotes and Markdown emphasis delimiters. Thus ordinary prose such as `“@session:abc123”`, `'@session:abc123'`, or `**@session:abc123**` remains literal even though `abc123` is a complete valid ID and the wrapper unambiguously terminates it. The hostile test only covers a quote followed by more token text (`@session:abc123"tag`), which should remain literal; it does not cover a closing quote followed by whitespace/end.

### What is sound at this head

- Fenced blocks, the renderer's supported single-backtick code spans, raw `<pre>/<code>`, raw anchors, flat Markdown links/images, and bare `http(s)` URL spans are stashed before replacement (`static/ui.js:293-333`). This is aligned with the repository's current renderer grammar; no direct new script/URL-scheme injection was found.
- Settled `renderMd()` routes generated `session://` mar

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @starship-s. The force-push substantially improves the previous implementation, but exact-head static re-gating at `90a19116b805` found two prior correctness requirements still incomplete, plus one unbounded main-thread path.

### 1. Keep explicit profile ownership in the final session URL

`_navigateInternalSessionLink()` now passes the requested profile to `_openSessionReference()`, and `_openSessionReference()` switches profiles before loading. However, it calls:

```js
loadSession(sessionId, {skipProfileResolve:true, force})
```

without carrying `targetProfile`. The final URL promotion is still:

```js
_setActiveSessionUrl(S.session.session_id, opts.clearProfileIntent ? null : undefined)
```

`undefined` retains whatever profile was already in `window.location`, rather than the profile named by the clicked reference. The boot path similarly creates explicit-profile `loadOptions` without passing the target profile. A clicked `@session:profile/id` can therefore load from the right profile while leaving a missing or stale profile in the shareable/reload URL.

**Fix-spec:** carry the validated explicit profile through `_openSessionReference()` and `_profileScopedUrlSessionState()` into `loadSession()`, and use that exact value for every same-session and completed-load `_setActiveSessionUrl()` call. Add a production-path test that clicks a profile-bearing link, observes the real load completion and URL, then reloads from that URL and proves the same profile owns the session. Do not stop at a mocked `loadSession()` call.

### 2. Finish ordinary emphasis/punctuation support

The broadened boundary expression covers quotes, curly quotes and `**...**`, but `_` remains excluded as a leading boundary and is accepted greedily inside the ID. Canonical Markdown forms such as `_@session:abc123_` and `__@session:def456__` still cannot link. Entity-quoted prose is transformed before entity decoding, so `"@session:abc123"` also remains literal. The new punctuation test does not cover these cases.

**Fix-spec:** tokenize the reference independently from Markdown delimiters, support `_..._` / `__...__` and encoded/ordinary quote boundaries without absorbing delimiters into the session ID, and add positive tests for underscore emphasis, entity quotes and common guillemet/CJK closers, alongside negative identifier/URL/code/link tests.

### 3. Bound the transformer on malformed and growing input

`stashMarkdownLinks()` restarts a suffix scan for each unmatched `[`, and stash restoration rescans the full string once per token. The live incremental paths also call the transformer on accumulated prose after each append. This creates quadratic main-thread work for repeated unmatched openers or long growing streams.

**Fix-spec:** use a single-pass/bounded tokenizer and linear restoration, and avoid re-transforming the full accumulated prefix on every streaming append. Add adversarial malformed-input and growing-stream operation/time-budget tests that scale linearly.

The mandatory Layer-1 threat scan returned `SUSPICIOUS` on the PR's added `eval(extractFunc(...))` test-harness forms, so policy required a static-only NO-RUN review. No PR code or tests were executed. This scan verdict is an execution boundary, not itself a defect; the corrected head still needs an authorized sandbox run after it can clear the gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the substantial rework. I re-gated the exact current head `529f3941618228b5af990e35e4d7ede3f518708b` against the prior SQLite-authority findings. The metadata-only `#1558` guard is now correctly ahead of the SQLite save path, and the submitted SQLite tests pass, but the authority/lifecycle blockers are only partially closed.

### Blocking findings

1. **Session deletion still fails open when SQLite deletion fails.** In `api/routes.py`, `/api/session/delete` unlinks the JSON sidecar and prunes the index before calling `_session_store.delete_session(sid)`. Any SQLite exception is caught and logged, after which the route still returns `{"ok": true}`. A locked, corrupt, or otherwise failing database can therefore retain the authoritative row and full transcript while the user is told deletion succeeded. The retained row remains eligible for later SQLite-aware index discovery.

2. **The SQLite representation is still not lossless.** `_write_session_row()` persists only the closed `_SESSION_SCALAR_FIELDS` whitelist. Current session fields including `created_workspace` and `intentional_shrink_generation` are absent, as are runtime identity fields such as `user_id`, `chat_id`, `session_key`, and `platform`. There is no forward-compatible `extra_json`, so migration and subsequent saves silently discard unknown or newly added top-level session state.

3. **SQLite-only lifecycle parity remains incomplete.** `_preserve_pre_compression_snapshot()` still returns immediately when `<old_sid>.json` is absent, even though migrated sessions are expected to be SQLite-only. Clear verification and recovery/index-repair paths still inspect JSON sidecars rather than the active store. This leaves compression, clear, cleanup, and recovery behavior dependent on whether a stale sidecar happens to exist.

4. **The persisted-session-ID cache still uses only the session directory mtime.** `_persisted_session_ids_snapshot()` returns its cached JSON+SQLite union before querying SQLite when the parent directory mtime is unchanged. WAL commits to an existing `sessions.db` do not provide that invalidation signal, so SQLite row creation/deletion can remain stale in list/index projections.

5. **The backend still has no durable cutover marker or stale-writer fence.** The mere existence of `sessions.db` activates SQLite authority, including after a partial migration. Full writes remain unconditional delete-and-reinsert transactions with no per-session generation/CAS, so a stale recovered sidecar can overwrite a newer SQLite generation.

### Required fixes

- Make delete one fail-closed lifecycle transaction at the store boundary. Do not report success or remove the fallback/index/tombstone state if authoritative SQLite deletion fails. Add a route-level regression that injects a SQLite delete failure and proves the transcript remains visible/retryable rather than falsely deleted.
- Make SQLite round-trips lossless for every current `Session` field and preserve unknown top-level keys, with schema versioning/migrations.
- Route compression snapshot preservation, clear verification, background/ephemeral cleanup, recovery, and index repair through one canonical store abstraction for JSON and SQLite-only sessions.
- Tie list/index cache freshness to a SQLite revision changed by every write/delete transaction, not directory mtime alone.
- Add a validated migration-complete marker and a per-session generation/CAS or equivalent stale-write protocol before enabling SQLite-only authority.

### Verification

The mandatory security scan is CLEAN. Sandboxed targeted runs passed:

- `tests/test_webui_session_sqlite.py`: **29 passed**
- `tests/test_metadata_save_wipe_1558.py`: **18 passed**

Those results confirm the new happy paths and the repaired `#1558` guard, but the submitted tests do not cover the fail-open delete, SQLite-only compression/clear/recovery paths, cache invalidation, lossless migration, or stale-writer cases above.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Re-gate at `fbaab94abc69`: partial convergence, persistence blockers remain

Thanks for the substantial follow-up. I re-gated the five commits after `529f39416182`. The user-delete path now fails closed before sidecar/index mutation, the metadata-only save guard remains correctly ordered, and the persisted-session ID cache now follows the store revision. Those parts are fixed.

The current head still has objective authority and data-retention blockers:

1. **The stale-writer fence does not fence real stale `Session` objects.** `api/webui_session_sqlite.py::_write_session_row()` compares `updated_at`, but `api/models.py:Session.save()` replaces a stale object's timestamp with `time.time()` immediately before writing. A writer loaded before another writer can therefore save later, receive the newer timestamp, pass the guard, and replace the newer row and child collections. Please use a durable per-session generation loaded with the object, compare-and-bump it atomically, and add a two-reader test: load A and B, save A, then prove stale B is rejected or safely reconciled.

2. **Migration can publish unintended authority.** `WebUISqliteSessionDB.__init__()` commits a fresh database as `created_by=app` before the migration script can mark it incomplete; the script also stamps `migration_complete=1` without `--commit`. An interruption or dry run can therefore leave an activatable empty/partial database. Build a staged database marked `created_by=migration,migration_complete=0` from creation, publish it only after verified completion, make dry-run non-mutating, and fail closed on unreadable/missing markers. Add crash-point tests around creation, copy, verification, and publication.

3. **DB-only lifecycle paths still bypass the canonical store.** Ephemeral cancel/success cleanup still unlinks only `session.path`; hidden-background cleanup suppresses SQLite deletion failures; `/api/sessions/cleanup` scans JSON sidecars and can classify DB-only index rows as ghosts; recovered-workspace persistence rejects DB-only sessions because `<sid>.json` is absent. Route these through one store contract, retain retryable ownership when authoritative deletion fails, and cover DB-only cancel/success/background/cleanup/recovery with failure injection and restart.

4. **The claimed lossless/store abstraction contract remains incomplete.** `_row_to_metadata()` collapses explicit SQL `NULL` into key absence, migration comparison skips `None`, and JSON fallback nests `extra_session_fields` instead of restoring unknown top-level keys. Preserve key presence as well as values. The Postgres class is also not runtime-substitutable yet: production paths still branch on `_get_sqlite_session_store()`, the protocol/concrete `force` contract differs, and configured Postgres setup errors are caught as skips. Route all backends through `SessionStore`, use one metadata contract, and make a configured backend failure fail its contract tests.

Sandboxed targeted evidence was green for the submitted cases: **18 passed, 5 skipped**, plus **6 passed, 5 skipped** in the focused contract rerun. All five skips were Postgres because no DSN was configured. The missing discriminators above are the ones needed to prove the authority boundary.

Please re-push with these invariants covered and I will re-gate the new head.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the substantial persistence rework. I re-gated exact head `31ae8e5282f1611e72d7e843abd25e784eab1b71` against the five blockers from `fbaab94abc693d67cd53c2e08fba34c3721fb811`.

Several important pieces are genuinely fixed: the ordinary two-reader `Session` CAS now uses a loaded generation and has a faithful A-save/B-stale-write test; dry-run migration is outside the session directory; explicit-null and unknown top-level fields round-trip; SQLite marker reads fail closed; configured Postgres setup failures are no longer converted to skips.

The current head is still objectively unsafe to ship:

1. **A stale loaded session can recreate a deleted SQL row.** In both SQL stores, `_write_session_row()` treats `row is None` as unconditional generation 1 even when the writer supplied a non-null `expected_generation`. A `Session` loaded before delete can therefore save after delete and resurrect the retired transcript. Deletion does not retain/bump a durable per-SID incarnation outside the deletable row.

2. **The unreadable-row heal bypass launders stale sidecar state over SQL.** `Session.save()` turns the process-local `unreadable_sids` mark into `write_session(..., force=True)` after a failed full-row probe. That bypass replaces the row and child collections from an unversioned sidecar. `test_save_heal_bypasses_fence_for_marked_session` explicitly seeds a newer SQL row and an older sidecar, then requires the bypass; its equal transcript fixture cannot detect rollback of newer SQL messages.

3. **Migration still builds in the final selector-visible path before authority is crash-safe.** Commit mode constructs `sessions.db` in place and “publishes” by changing a marker in the same file. `_ensure_schema()` creates the schema before inserting `created_by=migration,migration_complete=0`, leaving a crash window where a later normal app open can stamp the unmarked final-path DB as `created_by=app` and activate it. The crash hooks run only after the constructor returns, so they do not exercise that window. A long-lived WebUI that probes while migration is incomplete also caches `_sqlite_session_store_instance=False`; flipping the marker later does not invalidate that process-local negative cache.

4. **Cleanup still splits authority and reports success after authoritative failure.** `_handle_sessions_cleanup()` unlinks JSON first, separately scans SQL, pops the cached owner before SQL delete, catches every delete failure, and returns unconditional `{"ok":true}`. A dual-representation session can lose the sidecar before SQL deletion fails; a DB-only failure loses its cached retry owner and is still reported as successful cleanup. The background and ephemeral cleanup paths log retention but do not create durable retry ownership.

5. **Postgres substitutability remains incomplete.** Recovered-workspace binding, index/existence/rebuild paths, and compression-parent classification still contain concrete SQLite branches. Metadata policy also differs: JSON rejects unknown metadata fields, while SQLite/Postgres store them in `extra_json`; Postgres `is_active()` fails open on marker-read errors. payload.author: sportsculture
payload.body:
Response to the `a3b0dfc` re-gate — the check→publish race is closed at head `2b6170b` with a cutover protocol live sidecar writers honor.

**The window.** The finding was exactly right: the preimage CAS and `os.replace()` were separate steps, live writers took no lock, and a save landing between them was left as post-publish drift evidence (exit 3) that the next `Session.load()` would never read. The fix makes the check→publish pair atomic against live writers instead of relying on the CAS alone:

**1. A second lock with one job: the live-writer handoff (`2b6170b`)**

`.migrating.lock` keeps its original job (whole-run, migration-processes-only; live writers never touch it). A new `.cutover.lock` (`api.session_store.CUTOVER_LOCK_NAME` — one canonical constant, imported by both the server and the script) is the handoff:

- `api.models._sidecar_write_guard()` holds it **SHARED** around every JSON sidecar write — `Session.save()`'s writer (extracted verbatim into `_write_json_sidecar`) and `save_metadata()`'s read-modify-write fallback — with the store-selector re-probe **inside the same hold**. The re-probe cannot be a separate step from the rename: a "probe said JSON, then publish, then rename" gap is precisely the flagged window.
- The script's publish window (`_publish_window_lock`) holds it **EXCLUSIVE** across the preimage CAS → `os.replace` → fsync → sidecar retirement (retirement moved inside the window so a compliant writer can't interleave with the move loop either).

So a live save lands in exactly one of the review's accepted outcomes:

- **completes before the CAS observes the file** → drift → the run refuses exit 1 *before* `sessions.db` becomes active, bytes stay canonical in the sidecar for the next run (outcome 1); or
- **starts inside the window** → blocks on the shared lock → publication completes → the in-hold re-probe finds the published store and the save is **durably applied to the published SQL generation** (outcome 3). It never renames a sidecar the next load will never read.

Both acquisitions are deadline-bounded (`HERMES_CUTOVER_LOCK_TIMEOUT` / `HERMES_MIGRATE_PUBLISH_LOCK_TIMEOUT`, default 120s) and fail closed; a process crash on either side releases its kernel lock. POSIX `flock` SH/EX; Windows uses the same exclusive byte the window holds with a retry loop (unit-tested msvcrt branches for both sides); no primitive → refuse.

**2. Cutover adoption (`2b6170b`)**

A blocked writer that wakes post-publication is a sidecar-lineage owner (`_persisted_generation/incarnation = None`) whose row now exists — a plain CAS write would deterministically refuse forever, stranding it behind a row the next load prefers. `Session.save()`'s SQL fast path now adopts the **current durable token fresh** for such owners, fenced by the store's guarded CAS against any writer that moved it in between. Scoped deliberately:

- The lineage is flagged **at load time** (`_cutover_sidecar_lineage`): only owners built while *no SQL authority existed for the sid* adopt — the published row was copied from this owner's own sidecar chain, so its write is the continuation of the authority it was loaded under, with the sidecar store's own last-writer-wins semantics now fenced by the durable token.
- **Marked-fallback owners keep failing closed exactly as before** — `test_recovery_demotes_mark_and_carries_draft` and `test_marked_recovered_save_fails_closed_on_divergent_transcript` pass unchanged; their sidecar view predates a row that was authoritative all along.
- Absent/retired rows adopt nothing, so the store's first-create / `DeletedSessionWriteError` / `RetiredSessionWriteError` fences keep their exact semantics, and SQL-loaded owners (real tokens) remain under strict CAS.

`save_metadata()`'s fallback gained the same in-hold re-probe (routing through the already-accepted token-less-owner adoption in `_save_metadata_via_store`), so the composer's 400ms draft autosave has the identical guarantee.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @AlexeyDsov — exact-head warm-up at `31c95c707ace` found objective blockers that need correction before another gate.

### Finding

**YES — current head has a concrete stale-height path.**

- `static/ui.js:554-556` introduces `_messageVirtualPrevMeasuredSet`, keyed only by `rawIdx`.
- `static/ui.js:1461-1498` makes `_updateMessageVirtualMeasurements()` skip the DOM read whenever that raw index is already in the set, reusing `_messageVirtualHeightCache[visibleIdx]` without checking content, DOM generation, disclosure state, or observed element size.
- The first synchronous measurement occurs at `static/ui.js:17767`, but asynchronous post-processing is merely scheduled one line-path earlier with `requestAnimationFrame(()=>_postProcessWithAnchorSuppression(inner))` at `static/ui.js:17740-17741`. That post-process subsequently highlights and loads/renders diff, CSV, Excalidraw, PDF, HTML, Mermaid, KaTeX, and tree views (`static/ui.js:18950-18976`), all of which can change a row's height after it has already been added to the measured set. Lazy message images (`static/ui.js:2717-2816`) and disclosure/worklog expansion are additional post-measurement height changes.
- No transcript-row `ResizeObserver`, image-load invalidation, disclosure-toggle invalidation, or content/version key clears the affected raw index. The `ResizeObserver` around `static/ui.js:6969-7036` is a short-lived bottom-follow settle observer; it does not update `_messageVirtualHeightCache`/`_messageVirtualPrefixSum` and does not protect an unpinned reader.
- Therefore a later settled scroll/render reaches `prevSet.has(entry.rawIdx)` and keeps the old height. `_messageVirtualWindow()` then binary-searches prefix sums built from those stale heights, and top/bottom spacers no longer equal the DOM height they replace. The visible consequence is a discontinuous scroll position/window jump when an expanded or asynchronously grown row is virtualized out and later remounted.
- The tip fix in `static/messages.js:2186-2195` clears the set only when owner inflight state is removed. That addresses streaming-to-settled reuse, but it does not address height changes after a settled row's synchronous measurement (nor user expansion of already-settled content), so the defect remains at exact head.

### Required fix

In `static/ui.js`, make delta-measurement validity track **actual row size/content generation**, not raw index alone:

### Focused verification

- **Local execution:** zero tests collected or run, by mandatory SUSPICIOUS / STRICT STATIC NO-RUN policy. No green/red runtime claim is made.
- **PR-added behavioral tests:** static diff inspection found three new test functions: sparse `_isRenderableRawIdx` membership in `tests/test_issue500_message_list_virtualization.py`, plus render-cache collision and capacity tests in `tests/test_render_cache_collision.py`. The remaining modified tests primarily adjust existing assertions/harnesses.
- **Missing regression test:** add a behavioral virtual-scroll test using production measurement/window helpers that:
  1. renders and measures a settled row at height A;
  2. changes that same raw index's DOM height to B after initial measurement (cover at least one async post-process/media case and one disclosure/worklog expansion case);
  3. triggers the normal invalidation/observer callback and a virtual-window recalculation;
  4. asserts `_messageVirtualHeightCache` and prefix sum now use B, spacer totals change by `B-A`, and an unpinned viewport anchor remains at the same visual offset as the row crosses the virtual boundary.
- Add a negative/control assertion that an unchanged observed row is not remeasured on ordinary scroll, preserving the optimization's purpose.
- Add a settled-row test proving this works when `INFLIGHT[sid]` is absent; otherwise a test can falsely pass solely because the streaming branch clears the entire set.

This is review-only warm-up: no contributor code or branch was changed.

nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I re-read the full current ui.js, the complete modified test files, and the diff against origin/master. The latest binary-search change fixes the sparse-index problem raised in review. I found a separate correctness blocker in the expanded markdown render cache: long messages can deterministically share a cache key and display the wrong message body.

## Code reference

static/ui.js:1624 raises the cache from 300 entries to 10,000. static/ui.js:1626-1634 deliberately drops the middle of every string over 500 characters, while static/ui.js:16346 uses the cached HTML as the visible message body.

~~~javascript
if(text.length <= 500) return p + ":" + text;
return p + ":" + text.length + ":" + text.slice(0,20) + ":" + text.slice(-20);
~~~

Two messages with equal length and identical first and last 20 characters but different middles receive the same key. The second call returns the first rendered HTML without calling renderMd. This is easy to hit with long templated outputs, fenced code, repeated headers and footers, or generated records. Expanding the retention window by more than 30 times makes the existing collision shortcut much more likely to affect a long session.

## Diagnosis and recommendation

Please make cache identity exact before increasing the limit. The simplest correct version uses the complete text in the key. If retaining another copy of the text is unacceptable, keep a compact lookup key but store the original text beside the rendered value and verify full equality before treating it as a hit. A bucket is needed if two full texts share the compact key.

There is also a small capacity off-by-one at static/ui.js:1646: eviction runs while size is greater than the maximum before insertion, so the map stabilizes at 10,001 entries. Evict while size is greater than or equal to the maximum before adding a new key, or insert first and then trim while over the maximum.

## Test plan

Add a behavioral test that renders two strings longer than 500 characters with the same length, prefix, and suffix but different middle content, then assert that both HTML results are distinct and that the renderer is called twice. Add a capacity assertion after maximum plus several unique inserts. The new sparse visWithIdx test at tests/test_issue500_message_list_virtualization.py:1150-1225 covers the latest binary-search fix, but it does not exercise this cache path.

payload.body:
Thanks @silent-reader-cn — exact-head warm-up at `fbc6810928bd` found objective blockers that need correction before another gate.

### Finding

**Yes — a current-head mobile nested-scroll defect applies.**

Concrete evidence from a sandboxed Playwright layout probe using the real `static/style.css`, the actual Insights class hierarchy, long unbroken model strings, and light/dark themes:

- **390px current head:** document overflow remained contained (`document scrollWidth - clientWidth = 0`), but the Models card had **32px outer overflow** and `.insights-model-table` had **42px inner overflow**. Scrolling the inner table to its maximum did **not** make the final Share cell reachable inside the card; a second scroll of the outer card was required. That second scroll shifted the `Models` title **32px left**.
- Root cause is the cascade between the new base rule `.insights-model-table{overflow-x:auto;display:block}` and existing mobile rules `.insights-usage-grid .insights-card{overflow-x:auto}` plus `.insights-model-table{min-width:360px}`.
- **641px / 768px / 900px current head:** the intended fix works. The card itself has no horizontal overflow; the table has respectively **133px / 70px / 4px** of local overflow, its head and row both measure **402px**, and the last column becomes reachable by scrolling the table alone. This closes the intermediate-width parent bug.
- **1280px and 1600px:** no document/card/table overflow; the grid expands normally and no visible desktop layout change is induced.
- **Long strings:** the first column remains bounded by `.insights-model-name` ellipsis; it does not enlarge the 402px row floor.

payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full `static/style.css` at the PR head and the generated skill-usage markup in `static/panels.js:4659`, this is the right containment fix. The table and its rows are inside an `.insights-card`, and that card can itself be a shrinkable grid item. Adding `min-width:0` at `static/style.css:6629` removes the grid-item intrinsic-width floor; adding overflow to the table at `static/style.css:6651` then keeps any remaining width inside the intended local scroller rather than widening the Insights panel. I do not see a code-level blocker in the patch.

## Code reference

The important part is that the shrink and scroll responsibilities are split across the card and table:

```css
.insights-card{background:var(--surface-2);border:1px solid var(--border);border-radius:8px;padding:14px;margin-bottom:16px;min-width:0;}
.skill-usage-table{overflow-x:auto;display:block;}
.skill-usage-table .insights-table-head,
.skill-usage-table .insights-table-row{grid-template-columns:minmax(90px,1.5fr) 60px 60px 58px 52px;gap:8px;align-items:center;min-width:352px;}
```

The markup at `static/panels.js:4659` applies both `insights-table` and `skill-usage-table` to the wrapper, with `.insights-table-head` and each `.insights-table-row` as direct descendants. The selector therefore reaches both the header and data rows, preserving column alignment while the wrapper scrolls.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

This is preferable to putting overflow on `.insights-card`: the title, summary grid, and footer remain stationary, while only the five-column data area scrolls. The explicit row minimum also avoids each numeric column collapsing independently on very narrow screens. Existing wide layouts remain unchanged because the minimum matters only when the available width is smaller.

The PR has no regression test, so I would add a small source/markup contract to `tests/test_insights.py` asserting all three pieces remain together: `.insights-card` has `min-width:0`, `.skill-usage-table` owns `overflow-x:auto`, and both header and row share the same minimum-width rule. That will prevent a later CSS cleanup from removing one half of the fix.

## Verification step

Browser verification should cover a narrow phone viewport with a long skill name and enough rows to make the horizontal scrollbar visible. Confirm the main Insights panel and page do not gain horizontal overflow, the footer remains fixed to the card width, all five headers stay aligned with their values while scrolling, and the existing desktop two-column Insights layout is unchanged. I reviewed the PR statically and did not execute code from its worktree.

The new branch in `api/providers.py:2818-2826` copies every string key verbatim:

```python
elif isinstance(cp_raw_models, dict) and cp_raw_models:
    cp_models = [
        {"id": str(k), "label": str(k)}
        for k in cp_raw_models
        if isinstance(k, str)
    ]
```

By contrast, `api/config.py:1379-1397` has `_configured_model_ids`, which strips whitespace, drops empty IDs, and de-duplicates while preserving order. That helper is already the source of truth for custom-provider catalogs in the picker, including the call at `api/config.py:5379`.

As written, a valid YAML mapping containing an accidental blank key or whitespace variants can produce empty-looking or duplicate pills in the Providers card while the model picker reports a cleaned catalog. For example, keys `Best`, ` Best `, and a whitespace-only key become three card entries here, but `_configured_model_ids` collapses them to one usable ID.

```python
model_ids = _configured_model_ids(cp_raw_models)
cp_models = [{"id": mid, "label": mid} for mid in model_ids]
if not cp_models and cp.get("model"):
    mid = str(cp["model"]).strip()
    cp_models = [{"id": mid, "label": mid}] if mid else []
```

This also avoids maintaining subtly different list and dict semantics in two endpoints.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full route diff and `api/auth.py:_is_loopback`, the security change is correctly fail-closed. The debug paths now require two independent conditions, an explicit opt-in and a socket peer that `_is_loopback()` accepts. Exceptions, a missing address, malformed peers, and unset flags all return false. The route wiring at `api/routes.py:13366-13380` and `api/routes.py:13507-13526` returns 404 before either simulation or injection runs. I do not see a security blocker in that part.

There is, however, a concrete gap in the added A-tier smoke: its advertised title-update step is currently a no-op and has no assertion.

## Code reference

The shared gate at `api/routes.py:5782-5798` has the right shape:

```python
if not _env_flag_enabled(env_var):
    return False
try:
    from api.auth import _is_loopback
    peer = str(address[0] or "")
    return _is_loopback(peer)
except Exception:
    return False
```

`tests/test_inject_test_guard.py:32-139` covers disabled defaults, remote denial, both loopback families, allowed approval injection, and update simulation. `tests/conftest.py:1041-1047` enables only the inject routes in the isolated test-server subprocess, which avoids changing production defaults.

The title portion in `tests/test_a_tier_stream_ui_smoke.py:126-149` is different. It checks `window.S` before assigning the smoke title:

```js
if (window.S) {
  window.S.session = window.S.session || {};
  window.S.session.title = "A-Tier Smoke Title";
}
if (typeof syncTopbar === "function") syncTopbar();
```

But `S` is declared as a top-level `const` at `static/ui.js:7`, so it is a global lexical binding, not a property on `window`. `window.S` is therefore normally undefined. `syncTopbar()` at `static/ui.js:10438-10462` runs against the unchanged lexical `S`, and the test never checks `#topbarTitle` or `document.title`. The smoke can pass even if title rendering is broken.

## Recommendation

Keep the endpoint gate as written, but make the smoke exercise and assert the title contract. In the page main world, access the lexical binding directly after guarding with `typeof S !== "undefined"`, set `S.session.title`, call `syncTopbar()`, then assert both:

```python
assert page.locator("#topbarTitle").inner_text() == "A-Tier Smoke Title"
assert page.title().startswith("A-Tier Smoke Title")
```

Alternatively, update the session through the production session API and then call the normal refresh path. The direct lexical-binding route is closer to the current test and keeps this focused on rendering.

I would also add two small route cases to complete the security matrix: update simulation with its flag enabled but a non-loopback peer must return 404, and a handler without `client_address` must fail closed. The generic helper already appears to behave correctly in both cases, but observable route tests would prevent future wiring regressions.

## Verification step

The security tests should prove that the protected handlers are never invoked for all denied cases, not only that the response is 404. The browser smoke should fail if either the topbar title or browser document title remains unchanged. I reviewed the five modified files and `api/auth.py` statically and did not execute code from the PR worktree.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading `api/passkeys.py` in full on both the PR head and `origin/master`, the proxy fix has the right target but introduces a trust-boundary problem: an unauthenticated request header now selects both the WebAuthn RP ID and the expected client-data origin. The later verification is therefore circular. It proves that the credential response matches the same caller-provided value, not that the value is an origin this WebUI deployment trusts.

This matters most for registration. A logged-in browser reaching the WebUI through an explicitly allowed cross-origin frontend may be legitimate, but an arbitrary `Origin` must not become a valid RP identity solely because it parses as a hostname.

## Code reference

The new branch at `api/passkeys.py:186-194` is:

```python
origin_header = self._request_header(handler, "Origin")
if origin_header:
    parsed_origin = urlparse(origin_header.strip())
    if parsed_origin.hostname:
        rp_id = parsed_origin.hostname
        origin = origin_header.strip().rstrip("/")
        return rp_id, origin
```

That result flows into option generation at `api/passkeys.py:211-227`, then into `_client_data` verification at `api/passkeys.py:265-278`. The repository already has same-origin and allowlisted-origin policy in `api/routes.py:5360-5426`, including CORS preflight handling at `api/routes.py:5409`; this passkey branch does not reuse that policy.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please validate the parsed origin before accepting it. The accepted set should be either the request host origin or an origin explicitly configured for this deployment. If it is not accepted, fail closed with a clear response rather than silently deriving an RP ID from it. Keep the existing Host fallback for requests with no browser Origin only where that path is already supported.

Also restrict the scheme to WebAuthn-capable schemes and normalize through one URL routine. Reusing the same origin policy as the route layer avoids creating a second, looser definition of trusted origin.

## Test plan

Add direct regression tests for: a trusted reverse-proxy frontend origin; a hostile but syntactically valid origin; malformed and `null` origins; a non-default HTTPS port; and registration plus login verification using the chosen RP context. The hostile-origin test should prove rejection before option issuance or credential verification. This PR currently changes authentication semantics without adding any passkey tests, so I would treat that coverage as required before merge.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I reviewed the current PR head against origin master and read the complete passkey helper plus the route security context. The URL parsing is better than splitting on a colon, but the current change still trusts any syntactically valid Origin header.

## Code reference

At api/passkeys.py:184-195, every parseable Origin replaces the server-derived relying-party context. At api/routes.py:5431-5438, both passkey options and login are CSRF exempt. The POST dispatcher at api/routes.py:13951 therefore does not run the normal same-origin gate for these requests.

~~~python
origin = handler.headers.get("Origin", "").strip()
if origin:
    parsed = urlparse(origin)
    if parsed.hostname:
        return parsed.hostname, origin.rstrip("/")
~~~

## Diagnosis and recommendation

Origin is client input, not proof that the request came through the configured public host. The existing same-origin helper already knows about Host, explicitly trusted forwarded-host headers, ports, and the configured public-origin allowlist. The passkey routes should validate provenance with that policy before rp_context consumes Origin. Because WebAuthn is browser-only, requiring provenance on both the options and completion requests is appropriate; malformed or foreign Origin values should be rejected rather than silently converted into relying-party IDs.

A small route-level fix keeps passkeys.py independent of routes.py:

~~~python
if not _check_same_origin_browser_request(handler, require_provenance=True):
    return bad(handler, "Invalid passkey origin", status=403)
~~~

## Test plan

The current diff changes only api/passkeys.py and adds no regression test. Please add route-level cases for a same-host Origin, an explicitly allowlisted public Origin, an opted-in forwarded host, a foreign Origin, and a malformed Origin. The accepted cases should assert both the returned RP ID and exact expected origin; the rejected cases should assert that challenge generation is never reached. This also protects the reverse-proxy behavior from later CSRF refactors.

payload.title: fix(sse): drop Connection: close from long-lived SSE responses (#3103)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @cabluvsmkm2009-source — the diagnosis is right (`Connection: close` does break the persistent gateway/session-list SSE streams #3103 is about), but a Codex re-gate with a live HTTP/1.1 socket probe found that removing the header **without replacing the socket-closure mechanism** introduces a connection-lifetime regression. It's a small, precise fix.

### The regression (verified with a real socket probe)
`BaseHTTPRequestHandler.send_header("Connection", "close")` was doing double duty: it's harmful as a *header* on a persistent stream (the proxy/browser sees it and tears down), but it was also the thing that told the handler to **close the socket at stream end**. Removing it entirely means nothing closes the socket now. The probe confirmed it: `origin/master` produces clean EOF right after the terminal frame, but this branch **keeps the connection open until the 30s timeout** (`server.py:296`). `sse_chunked.py` doesn't rescue the default path (chunking is opt-in and emits no terminal zero-length chunk), so deterministic closure is still needed.

### The fix (3 lines)
At each of the 3 sites you patched, set the closure at the HTTP layer instead of via the header — add `handler.close_connection = True` immediately before `end_sse_headers(handler)`:
- `api/routes.py:17467`
- `api/routes.py:17547`
- `api/routes.py:17911`

That gives you both halves of #3103: no `Connection: close` header racing the stream, *and* a deterministic socket close at stream end (no hung connection held to the 30s timeout).

### Two things that are already correct — leave them
- **`api/routes.py:17531`** (the `_handle_sse_stream` journal-replay branch) should **keep** `Connection: close`. I initially thought it was a missed sibling, but it isn't: `_replay_run_journal()` iterates a *finite* journal snapshot and returns, so the header correctly delimits that bounded response and can't cut it short.
- **`api/routes.py:19329`** (ZIP download) must **keep** `Connection: close` — no `Content-Length`, no transfer encoding, body ends at FIN. You correctly left it.

### One test note
`tests/test_issue3103_sse_no_connection_close.py` only asserts that *at least one* `Connection: close` remains, so it doesn't catch the EOF/socket-closure regression. Worth adding an assertion that the three persistent handlers set `close_connection = True` (or a socket-level EOF check) so this stays fixed.

Net: right bug, right 3 sites — just swap the header removal for `handler.close_connection = True` at those three spots and it's a clean, complete fix for #3103. Ping me when it's pushed and I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete PR diff and the surrounding SSE helper, this change is directionally correct for the default non-chunked path: the WebUI handler uses HTTP/1.1, and the standard library handler treats a `Connection: close` response header as a request to set `close_connection`. That gives the otherwise unframed SSE response a valid close-delimited end. I do not see evidence for the claim that a reverse proxy can strip this header before the upstream handler updates its own close state; that state transition occurs while the WebUI builds the response.

The remaining gap is regression coverage. This PR changes three endpoints but adds no assertion that the handler actually closes after each terminal SSE event.

## Code reference

The same change appears at `api/routes.py:17676-17679`, `api/routes.py:17949-17952`, and `api/routes.py:20639-20642`:

```python
handler.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
handler.send_header("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
handler.send_header("Connection", "close")
end_sse_headers(handler)
```

`server.py:295` explicitly selects HTTP/1.1. `api/sse_chunked.py:50-63` confirms that the default branch sends neither `Content-Length` nor `Transfer-Encoding`; only the optional chunked branch installs explicit framing.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Keep the header placement before `end_sse_headers()`. Please add a focused regression test for all three call sites. The important assertion is not merely that the serialized header exists. It is that the real HTTP handler has `close_connection == True` after the response headers are sent and that the final SSE event is readable before EOF.

A table-driven test around the completion, busy, and error paths would prevent one endpoint from losing the close behavior during later edits. The existing `tests/test_sse_chunked.py` covers chunk formatting and the helper branch, but it does not exercise these route-level terminal paths.

## Verification step

Run each endpoint in default non-chunked mode through a real local HTTP connection, consume until EOF, and assert: one terminal SSE payload arrives, EOF follows without a timeout, and no second request is accepted on that upstream connection. Repeat once with chunked mode enabled to ensure this unconditional header does not cut off the terminating zero chunk.

**NEEDS CONTRIBUTOR REWORK:** the persisted `model_override` / `provider_override` wiring is internally consistent and well tested, but the card UI presents that mutable *next-dispatch override* as the task's **execution model**; for an already-running task the worker was spawned from the earlier values, so editing the override makes the visible claim false for the active run.

### (2) RE-PUSH since last bounce?

**No known re-push — 2026-08-13.** No prior-bounce state was supplied and this bounded pass intentionally did not consult or modify GitHub. The review is pinned to exact head `722db76787ea7f0acbacab2f1a91ecdf99ac4a30` and the supplied worktree was clean.

### (3) FINDING STILL APPLIES?

**Yes. Concrete current-head evidence:**

1. `api/kanban_bridge.py::_task_dict()` serializes the task dataclass directly, so the UI receives the authoritative persisted `model_override` and `provider_override` fields.
2. The bridge create/patch path writes those same fields via `kanban_db.set_model_override()`; provider-without-model is rejected and clearing the model clears both fields. This is correct configuration-source wiring.
3. Hermes Agent explicitly defines these fields as dispatch-time inputs. `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py::set_model_override()` documents that the change applies when the worker is next dispatched; the CLI's `kanban set-model` help/output likewise says **“takes effect on the next dispatch.”** The dispatcher passes `-m <model> [--provider <provider>]` when it spawns the worker.

Example: a worker starts with provider/model A, the running card is edited to B, and `_task_dict()` immediately returns B while the live worker remains A. The card then reports B as the execution model even though B only applies to a retry or later dispatch.

- **Inherited/default:** no override is represented as the profile default rather than inventing an effective model. That is honest because the profile can be resolved only at dispatch time.

payload.title: fix(queue): persist queued turns server-side

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Strong work, @starship-s — this is a well-architected fix for a real data-loss bug, and a deep Codex re-gate confirmed most of the hard parts are genuinely safe: local and gateway teardowns share one drain path; the thread-start rollback deep-copies and prepends the claim without clobbering a concurrent same-object enqueue; queued attachments/model/provider survive sidecar reload **and** compression; crash-after-claim is recoverable through the persisted `pending_*` stale-stream repair; and the legacy browser storage correctly never auto-submits. 261 targeted tests pass, full suite 13,935/0. The durable-queue contract in CONTRACTS.md is clear and the ownership move is the right call.

Three defects to close before it ships — two are CORE (a data-loss edge and a lock/eviction gap):

### 1. (CORE) Claim isn't fully under the session lock + queued sessions can be evicted — `api/routes.py:21641`, `api/models.py:4505`
The head-of-queue resolution and the claim mutation aren't performed as one atomic unit under the session lock, leaving a TOCTOU window, and a session that still holds a non-empty queue can be **evicted** from the in-memory cache — dropping the pending work. **Fix:** perform resolution + claim entirely under the session lock, and prevent eviction of any session whose queue is non-empty.

### 2. (CORE, data-loss) An unrelated new start bypasses a retained queue — `api/routes.py:21257`
When a session has a retained queue, an incoming unrelated start can begin directly, skipping the head claim — so the queued item is jumped (and can be stranded). **Fix:** enqueue the incoming turn at the **tail** and trigger the head claim, so all starts go through the one ordered claim path rather than racing around it.

### 3. (UI correctness) The dispatched user turn isn't reconciled into the live view — `api/routes.py:21616`, `static/messages.js:7818`
`server_turn_started` carries only stream id / timestamp / source; its handler neither removes the claimed queue head nor inserts the item's user prompt + attachments. The old browser drain did both by going through `send()`. So after a server-side claim, the live UI can fail to show the dispatched user turn (or the queue head lingers). **Fix:** fan out the claimed item identity, display text, attachments, and the authoritative remaining queue in **both** the normal and subscribe-recovery events; on the client, hydrate the queue and append/dedupe the pending user turn before attaching the live stream so it renders exactly once.

Net: the persistence, rollback, attachment durability, and crash-recovery are all sound — these three close the lock/eviction window, the queue-bypass on unrelated starts, and the live-view reconciliation of the claimed turn. Because this is a larger cross-cutting change with a visible surface, I'm routing it to Nathan for the merge call alongside these fixes; I'll re-run the full concurrency + UI-reconciliation gate once they land.

Nice performance win, @starship-s — letting supported browsers size the composer natively via `field-sizing:content` (with the JS fallback preserved) is the right direction, and the gate verified content growth, the 200px cap, shrink, stale-inline-height cleanup, IME, ResizeObserver re-pin, and forced-fallback parity (22 focused tests pass). One real edge to fix first:

### Must-fix — empty composer grows to fit the placeholder (SILENT)

**`static/style.css:2596`.** `field-sizing:content` includes **placeholder text** in intrinsic sizing, so on supported browsers an *empty* composer grows to fit a long placeholder. Reproduced in the real app at 320px: the busy hint expanded the empty composer 44→71px, and a long clarification placeholder pushed it to the full 200px cap — stealing transcript/card space during the busy, compression, and clarification flows (these paths swap the placeholder without going through the old JS resizer, so nothing clamps it).

**Fix:** add, right after the composer rule:
```css
textarea#msg:placeholder-shown{field-sizing:fixed;}
```
That keeps native sizing only when actual draft content exists; an empty composer (placeholder showing) stays at its fixed base height. Please verify at 320px that a long busy/clarification placeholder keeps the composer at 44px while typed multiline content still grows, caps at 200px, and shrinks.

With that one rule this is a clean ship. Re-push and I'll re-gate.

## Summary

I read the complete three-file diff at `c0bd28806`, the full changed files at PR HEAD, and their `origin/master` versions. I do not see a blocking correctness issue. The change is narrowly scoped: native-capable browsers leave textarea sizing to CSS, while unsupported browsers continue through the existing geometry-based path unchanged.

## Code reference

The branch at `static/messages.js:6917-6926` performs an exact `CSS.supports` capability check, clears a stale inline height, updates `_composerLastResizeValue`, refreshes the send button, and returns before any geometry read. At `static/style.css:2592`, `field-sizing:content` is paired with the existing `min-height:44px` and `max-height:200px`, plus `overflow-y:auto`.

The corresponding contract at `tests/test_issue5514_composer_grow_scroll_pin.py:590-593` is:

```python
def test_composer_declares_native_field_sizing_and_capped_overflow():
    composer_rules = [part.split("}", 1)[0] for part in STYLE_CSS.split("textarea#msg{")[1:]]
    required = ("field-sizing:content", "overflow-y:auto", "min-height:44px", "max-height:200px")
    assert any(all(declaration in rule for declaration in required) for rule in composer_rules)
```

Unsupported engines ignore the unknown CSS declaration and reach the old JS fallback because the same support query returns false. The stale inline-height cleanup is also important: it lets a browser that enters the native path after an earlier fallback measurement return control to intrinsic sizing.

The native branch deliberately does not call the synchronous re-pin helper. That is consistent with the existing composer wrapper `ResizeObserver` at `static/boot.js:2293-2298`, which observes actual net growth and preserves the pinned-reader contract without putting geometry work back in the input handler.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

The implementation matches the intended split and preserves button updates, shrink behavior, the 200px cap, and unsupported-browser behavior. No code change requested.

## Verification

`tests/test_issue5514_composer_grow_scroll_pin.py:596-665` executes the extracted live `autoResize()` body with both support outcomes. The assertions cover zero geometry reads on the native path, stale inline-height removal, send-button updates, the exact feature query, and continued geometry/height work on fallback. I did not execute code from the untrusted worktree; the repository CI should remain the runtime verification source.
