## Re-gate request — rebased onto current master, plus tests that actually bite (`41727069`)

The branch was 193 commits behind master; it is now rebased cleanly onto `a00b02fc` with no conflicts. CI is **23/23 green**.

The substantive part of this push is a new test file. While preparing the rebase I reverse-verified the existing suite and found it does not cover this PR's changes at all.

### The existing 11 tests were vacuous for this PR

`tests/test_send_key_preference_live_update.py` was written for the *previous* review round — it proves the removed inline interceptor no longer shadows the live `window._sendKey` value. That is a real regression guard and it stays. But reverting each of this PR's three production changes individually leaves all 15 pre-existing tests green:

| Production change reverted | Pre-existing tests |
|---|---|
| `_isTouchOnlyDevice()` → upstream media-query-only detection | 15 passed |
| synchronous `window._sendKey` bootstrap removed | 15 passed |
| `enterkeyhint="enter"` removed | 15 passed |

The reason is that the harness always runs under a desktop UA with real media queries, so `_mobileDefault` is false on every path and the mobile branch is never entered. Nothing in the suite asserted the behaviour named in the PR title.

### New file: `tests/test_mobile_enter_newline.py` (8 tests)

Same technique as the existing file — the composer handler and helpers are extracted verbatim from `static/boot.js` — but driven under a mobile UA plus an init script that reproduces the iOS Safari quirk this PR exists for: `(pointer:coarse)` **and** `(any-pointer:fine)` both reporting true on a plain iPhone.

Reverse-verify, each change reverted on its own:

| Reverted | Tests that turn red |
|---|---|
| `_isTouchOnlyDevice()` | `test_iphone_reporting_fine_pointer_still_treats_enter_as_newline`, `test_android_phone_treats_enter_as_newline` |
| synchronous `window._sendKey` bootstrap | `test_stored_shift_enter_preference_applies_before_settings_fetch`, `test_send_key_bootstrap_precedes_composer_handler` |
| `enterkeyhint="enter"` | `test_composer_textarea_declares_enterkeyhint`, `test_enterkeyhint_reaches_the_dom` |

Restored tree is byte-identical to the pushed tree and all 23 tests pass.

Two design notes:

- **The harness degrades with the code, deliberately.** `_available_helpers()` extracts whichever of `_isTouchOnlyDevice` / `_hasFinePointerCoexisting` exist, and `_extract_send_key_init()` returns `""` when that line is absent. That is what makes reverting a change alter what the harness runs, rather than raising a `ValueError` and producing a red result for the wrong reason.
- **Each mobile test asserts its own premise first.** The iPhone test checks both media queries really report true before pressing Enter, and the `shift+enter` test checks `localStorage` was actually seeded. Without those, a shim that silently stopped applying would leave a test that passes for no reason.

Inverse cases are covered too, so the fix cannot be read as "mobile users lost the keyboard send path": `test_desktop_enter_still_sends`, and `test_mobile_ctrl_enter_still_sends` (Ctrl+Enter and Numpad Enter both still send on the iPhone UA).

### `enterkeyhint` — what the test does and does not prove

The rendered keycap is a native-keyboard behaviour with no DOM-observable effect in headless Chromium. So the two tests assert what is actually checkable — the attribute is present on the composer `<textarea>` in `index.html`, and it survives parsing as the `enterKeyHint` DOM property. Whether iOS then draws a return key instead of "Go" is not something I can verify in CI, and I am not claiming these tests do.

### Verification

- CI: **23/23 SUCCESS** on `41727069`
- Full local suite, CI sharding (`--timeout=60 --num-shards=5`): shards 0-3 green (3023 / 3011 / 3011 / 2904 passed). Shard 4 showed two failures, both flakes confirmed on a clean `origin/master` worktree at the same tip:
  - `test_sprint1.py::test_upload_too_large` — fai

payload.author: luckrucksack
payload.title: fix: resolve pre-compression snapshot ids on /api/chat/start

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @luckrucksack — this targets a real brick (a stale pre-compression bookmark can't append after the session is sealed), and the core approach is sound: Codex confirmed non-snapshot ids keep the unchanged downstream path, resolved sessions still get profile validation (no cross-profile auth bypass), and the shared resolver is read-only. A Codex regression gate found the **error paths** are incomplete — the fix fails *open* on ambiguity and returns the wrong status on a read-only continuation. Needs one more pass.

### Findings
1. **(CORE) Fail-open on missing/ambiguous continuation — `api/routes.py:22152-22163`.** When the snapshot has no uniquely loadable continuation, both a `None` result **and** a `KeyError` fall through to `_start_run`, so the append still starts on the **sealed snapshot** (probes returned 200 targeting the snapshot — the exact brick this PR set out to fix, just relocated). Worse, the new test at `tests/test_chat_start_resolves_pre_compression_snapshot.py:155` **enshrines** that unsafe fallthrough. Fix: return a clear **409** before `_start_run` whenever a snapshot lacks exactly one loadable continuation, and rewrite that test to assert **no run starts**. The resolver should also exclude forks/child sessions and reject ambiguous candidates (don't guess when >1 continuation exists).
2. **(CORE) Read-only continuation → 500 instead of 403 — `api/routes.py:22154-22158`.** The second `_get_or_materialize_session()` on the resolved id can raise `PermissionError`, but only the *initial* load catches it; the exception escapes and `server.py:416` turns it into a **500**. Directly supplying the same read-only id returns **403**. Fix: apply the same `PermissionError` handling to the resolved-continuation load so it returns 403 (consistent with the direct-id path).

### Why the tests didn't catch it
The focused 29-test run passes, but the new test *asserts the fail-open behavior as correct* (a run starting on the snapshot), so it can't catch finding #1 — it needs inverting to assert a 409 with no run started. Add a read-only-continuation case asserting 403 (not 500) for finding #2.

The decide-vs-act split here is the classic one: the code that *resolves* the id and the code that *acts* on it must agree that a unique, writable, authorized continuation exists before `_start_run` — on any uncertainty, fail closed (409/403), never fall through to the sealed snapshot. Once the ambiguity path returns 409 and the read-only path returns 403 (with tests asserting both), I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the fast re-push @luckrucksack — your two cycle-4 fixes are **confirmed resolved**: Codex verified missing / ambiguous / deleted / unloadable continuations now return 409 before `_start_run` (no more fall-through to the sealed snapshot), initial **and** resolved read-only loads return 403, and non-snapshot start behavior is unchanged. That layer is done. ✅

Re-gating the current head found the fork-exclusion you added over-corrected into two **new** CORE regressions (the suite caught one of them too — 2 failures on this branch, both passing on clean master A/B):

### 1. Compressed **fork** sessions can no longer continue/restore — `api/routes.py:9583`
The new filter excludes continuations via `session_source == "fork"`, but **compression reuses the fork's session object** — `/api/session/branch` sets `session_source="fork"` (routes.py:15218), and the compression transition (`api/streaming.py:9777-9825`) changes only the ID/parent, so `Session.save()` persists the inherited `"fork"` source onto a legitimate compression continuation. Result: a compressed fork returns **409 despite having a valid live continuation** (a production-shaped probe 409'd without calling `_start_run`; `origin/master` resolves it fine). The two suite failures (`test_mobile_reload_compression_recovery::test_stale_index_with_existing_candidate_falls_back_to_newer_sidecar` and `...multihop_falls_back_to_missing_descendant_sidecar`) are this regression. The new test at `tests/test_chat_start_resolves_pre_compression_snapshot.py:311` masks it by omitting `session_source="fork"` from the continuation fixture.
**Fix:** distinguish forks/child sessions from compression continuations via **explicit persisted lineage/relationship metadata**, not the `source` string. Build the test through the *real* production compression transition (so the continuation retains `"fork"` and still resolves).

### 2. Canonicalized snapshot leaves approval/clarify prompts owned by the stale id — `static/messages.js:1830`
When `/api/chat/start` **succeeds** and canonicalizes a stale snapshot, the server returns the continuation id (`routes.py:21312`), but the client ignores `startData.session_id`: it attaches the stream under the old `activeSid` (line 1900) and keys the prompt UI to it (lines 5706/5714). Approval/clarify responses then send the **stale** id (lines 7352/8399) while the backend does exact session-key lookups (`routes.py:24122`, `clarify.py:225`) — so approval is silently treated as stale, or clarification 409s, while the continuation run stays **parked** (a brick of the exact flow this PR is trying to unblock).
**Fix:** consume `startData.session_id` as the canonical run owner and **atomically migrate** `S.session`, `INFLIGHT`, stream ownership, prompt polling, URL/localStorage, and approval/clarify session keys **before** `attachLiveStream`. Add focused approval + clarify tests where the start-response id differs from the submitted snapshot id.

The error-status layer is right now — this is the identity layer underneath it: *which* lineage counts as a continuation (structural metadata, not the `source` string), and migrating client-side run ownership to the resolved id. Once both land with tests through the real compression path, I'll re-gate.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading `api/routes.py` on `origin/master` and the PR diff, resolving the stale snapshot before model and workspace setup is the right layer. I found one error-contract gap that can turn this recovery path into a 500, and the current fallback can still run the paid turn against the known-closed snapshot.

## Code reference

`api/routes.py:4996-5014` documents and implements two failure modes from `_get_or_materialize_session`: `KeyError` and `PermissionError`. The new block at `api/routes.py:22145-22163` handles only the first:

```python
if continuation_sid:
    try:
        s = _get_or_materialize_session(
            continuation_sid, refresh_cli_messages=True
        )
    except KeyError:
        logger.warning(
```

Because this call occurs after the outer `except PermissionError` at `api/routes.py:22143-22144`, a read-only or subagent-marked continuation propagates out of `_handle_chat_start` instead of preserving the existing 403 contract.

The added regression file has chat-start cases at `tests/test_chat_start_resolves_pre_compression_snapshot.py:112`, `:134`, and `:155`. Those cover success, multi-hop success, and no continuation. They do not cover the load failures described in the PR body.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please fail before `_start_run` for both continuation load failures:

1. Catch `PermissionError` locally and return the same read-only 403 used by the original session load.
2. When lookup produced a continuation id but materialization raises `KeyError`, do not continue with the snapshot. That fallback recreates the reported defect: the request can spend a full agent turn and then fail because the snapshot is closed by compression. Return a retryable 409 or 404 carrying the stale snapshot id and resolved continuation id so the client can reload safely.

The no-continuation branch can retain current behavior if compatibility requires it; the important distinction is that a resolved-but-unloadable child is evidence of a race or stale lineage, not permission to append to the archived parent.

## Test plan

Add two handler tests that force `_pre_compression_continuation_session_id` to return a child while `_get_or_materialize_session` raises `KeyError` and `PermissionError`. In both, assert `_start_run` is never called and assert the intended 409/403 response. Keep the existing successful test assertion that the returned `session_id` is the continuation id.

payload.author: luckrucksack
payload.body:
Thanks for the thorough gate — both findings are correct, and finding #1 was a fair hit: my original no-continuation test *enshrined* the unsafe fallthrough. Round 2 addresses all of it.

## Finding 1 — fail-open on missing/ambiguous continuation (fixed)

`/api/chat/start` now refuses to start a turn whenever a pre-compression snapshot lacks **exactly one loadable continuation**:

- No uniquely resolvable continuation → **409** (retryable, message names the archived session)
- Continuation resolves but materialization raises `KeyError` → **409** (carries both the snapshot id and the resolved continuation id)
- The old test asserting the fallthrough is inverted: it now asserts 409 and that `_start_run` is never reached

The resolver also no longer guesses: the `max()` "newest candidate" heuristic is gone. A snapshot with several non-fork children now resolves to `None` (ambiguous lineage → 409 at chat/start; the GET /api/session hint is simply omitted — fail closed rather than redirect to a wrong target).

## Fork/child exclusion — `session_source == "fork"`

I verified against real sidecars before choosing the discriminator: gateway-created continuations on this deployment carry `compression_recovery_source_session_id = None` (that field is only written by the WebUI's own recovery flow, routes.py:21875, not by gateway compression), and webui sidecars have no `end_reason`/`ended_at` (so `agent_sessions._is_continuation_session`'s compression gate can't evaluate them). The field that *is* populated on real data is `session_source` — forks are created with `session_source="fork"` (routes.py:15224-15225) and continuations carry `None`. So the resolver excludes `session_source == "fork"` children; real continuations pass through unchanged. If gateway-created continuations start carrying a positive marker in the future, this filter can be tightened.

## Finding 2 — read-only continuation → 500 (fixed)

The resolved-continuation load now catches `PermissionError` and returns the same 403 contract as the direct-id path.

## Proof

- 8 tests in `test_chat_start_resolves_pre_compression_snapshot.py`: canonicalization, multi-hop chain, no-continuation 409, KeyError 409, PermissionError 403, ambiguous 409, fork-exclusion (fork saved after the continuation so the old newest-wins resolver would pick it), fork-only 409
- **Red without the fix: 6 failed / 2 passed. Green with it: 8/8.** Adjacent suites (`test_compression_recovery_action.py`, `test_issue5532_clear_truncation_watermark.py`): 23/23.
- One test-harness note: the error-path assertions read the real status via `handler.send_response` (a minimal BaseHTTPRequestHandler-shaped fake), since `bad()` doesn't route through the `j` seam the success-path tests stub.

payload.author: greptile-apps
payload.body:
Greptile Summary

 The PR canonicalizes archived pre-compression snapshot IDs before starting chat turns and rejects unresolved, ambiguous, or inaccessible continuation lineages. - Filters user-created fork children when selecting a continuation. - Requires exactly one loadable continuation and preserves read-only-session errors. - Adds regression coverage for direct, multi-hop, ambiguous, missing, forked, and inaccessible lineages.

Confidence Score: 4/5

 The PR is not yet safe to merge because compressed user-fork lineages can still be rejected as having no valid continuation. Automatic compression mutates the existing fork session into its live continuation without clearing `session_source="fork"`, while the updated resolver excludes every live child carrying that value; the resulting empty candidate set makes `/api/chat/start` return 409 for an otherwise valid compressed-fork lineage. The added test avoids this production state by creating the continuation without the inherited source. **Files Needing Attention:** api/routes.py; tests/test_chat_start_resolves_pre_compression_snapshot.py

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | api/routes.py | Canonicalizes snapshot IDs for chat starts, filters fork candidates, and fails closed when continuation resolution or loading is unsuccessful. | | tests/test_chat_start_resolves_pre_compression_snapshot.py | Adds focused handler tests for continuation selection, refusal paths, multi-hop compression, and fork-related lineage cases. |

Flowchart

 ```mermaid %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%% flowchart TD A[POST /api/chat/start with session ID] --> B[Load requested session] B --> C{Pre-compression snapshot?} C -- No --> D[Start turn on requested session] C -- Yes --> E[Resolve continuation lineage] E --> F{Exactly one eligible child?} F -- No --> G[Return 409] F -- Yes --> H[Materialize continuation] H --> I{Loadable and writable?} I -- No --> J[Return 409 or 403] I -- Yes --> K[Start turn on continuation] ```
Reviews (3): Last reviewed commit: ["test: pin compressed-fork lineage resolu..."](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/commit/d153a86327805eb50095fbdc5add4fd6380ee2cf) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=49745468)

payload.author: luckrucksack
payload.body:
@greptile-apps[bot] — I checked the P1 against the actual data model, and the inheritance mechanism it assumes doesn't exist here. Evidence from the deployed stack:

1. **The gateway has no `session_source` column.** `state.db`'s `sessions` table schema has `source`, `source_tag`, `parent_session_id`, `end_reason` — no `session_source`. Verified on the live DB for a real compression lineage (`db6f…` → `023130…` → `031616…`): the continuation row carries `source="webui"` and `parent_session_id`, and nothing else that a fork marker could survive in.

2. **The webui materializer reads `session_source` exclusively from gateway metadata** (`s.session_source = cli_meta.get("session_source")` — routes.py:5076, 16000, 16025). Since state.db has no such column, materialized continuations always get `None`.

3. **The only writer of `session_source="fork"` in the codebase is `/api/session/branch`** (routes.py:15225), which stamps the fork's *own* sidecar at creation. Compression creates a *new* gateway session for the continuation; the webui then materializes that new sidecar from gateway metadata → `session_source=None` → the resolver's fork filter never sees it.

Additionally, the branch endpoint already **detaches forks from compression snapshots** (routes.py:15043-15047: `if _parent_is_compression_snapshot: s.parent_session_id = None`), so a fork-of-snapshot doesn't even link to the snapshot as a child.

The one scenario where a `session_source="fork"` child *does* exist — a fork created before its parent was compressed — is exactly the case the filter is meant to reject (writing there would fork the archived conversation instead of continuing it).

To pin this so it can't regress silently, I added `test_chat_start_compressed_fork_lineage_still_resolves`: a fork sidecar sealed as a snapshot (session_source="fork", pre_compression_snapshot=True) with a materialized continuation resolves to the continuation. 9/9 tests green, pushed as d153a86. If the gateway ever grows a session_source column and starts copying it onto continuations, that test will go red and the filter can be revisited — until then, the exclusion is safe.

payload.author: luckrucksack
payload.body:
Correction to my earlier Greptile reply: the claim that "the only writer of `session_source="fork"` is /api/session/branch" is not quite right — `_handle_session_compression_recovery_start` (routes.py:21856) also stamps `session_source="fork"` when it creates a recovery fork of a sealed snapshot.

The core refutation is unaffected: the gateway has no `session_source` column and the materializer maps it to NULL, so a *compression continuation* can never inherit the marker. But the fork filter does conservatively exclude recovery forks too — a snapshot whose only child is a recovery fork now resolves to 409. That's fail-closed (never a run on a snapshot) and consistent with the "exclude forks" ask, but it's a consequence worth naming: it's now in the PR body, with a tracked follow-up to distinguish recovery forks via `compression_recovery_source_session_id`.

payload.author: webtecnica
payload.title: fix(streaming): forward MoA reference outputs as labeled blocks (#6743)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

The SSE forwarding in `api/streaming.py:8699-8737` is scoped correctly, but the browser side currently stores each reference only in the live DOM. That makes the fix transient: the cards appear during aggregation, then disappear when the terminal event settles the transcript. The same loss occurs after recovery or reload. This still leaves the requested labelled reference output unavailable once the final answer is shown.

## Code reference

Reading `static/messages.js:2408-2468`, `_upsertMoaReference` only creates elements under `liveAssistantTurn`. The handler at `static/messages.js:5647-5654` snapshots that live HTML, but it does not put reference data in `S.messages`, `INFLIGHT`, or the assistant-turn anchor registry.

```css
.moa-reference .thinking-card-label{
  overflow:visible;
  white-space:normal;
}
```

The styles in `static/style.css:22184-22200` are fine for the live card. The lifecycle is the problem. On completion, `static/messages.js:6016-6100` replaces state from `d.session.messages`, and `static/messages.js:6171-6175` calls `renderMessages` twice. Since no MoA field or anchor event is attached to the settled assistant message, that render removes the cards.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please carry each `moa.reference` through the settled-turn path before replacing the live DOM. The cleanest fit is the existing assistant-turn anchor flow used by reasoning and tool events: teach it a MoA reference activity, call `_applyToAnchor` from the listener, and let `_attachProjectedAnchorSceneToLastAssistant` preserve it at done. Another workable design is a dedicated assistant-message field plus render support and inclusion in `_EPHEMERAL_TURN_FIELDS`; if cold reload durability is required, the server session also needs that metadata.

Also use `index` as the identity when present. `static/messages.js:2427-2434` upserts by label, so two reference slots with the same model label collapse into one card even though the event contract supplies distinct indexes.

## Test plan

The tests at `tests/test_6743_moa_reference_output.py:108-135` are source-string checks, so they cannot catch either lifecycle bug. Please add a DOM-level test that emits two references, emits `done`, and asserts both labels and bodies remain in the settled transcript. Include duplicate labels with different indexes, plus a session reload or stream-recovery case. I reviewed the worktree read-only and did not execute contributor code.

payload.author: twunji
payload.body:
Thanks for this fix — this is exactly the gap we filed #6743 for. We hit the same issue in our setup and implemented a local fix; here are a few field observations that may be useful:

1. **Index is 1-based (confirmed).** The agent side emits `moa.reference` with `index` from `enumerate(..., start=1)` (`agent/moa_loop.py`). Your backend passes `moa_index` through verbatim and the frontend renders `d.index/d.count` as-is, which is correct. (Our first local attempt added `+1` and produced `Ref 2/3 … Ref 4/3` on a 3-reference run; removing the `+1` fixed it.)

2. **Cleanup on turn end / error paths.** With our first implementation (a separate `#moaFanout` container outside the live assistant turn), the reference blocks stayed on screen after the turn completed — `renderMessages()` rebuilds the turn but not our container. We added explicit removals on `done`, `apperror`, `stream_end`, new send, and session switch. Your approach renders inside `liveAssistantTurn`, so the normal `renderMessages()` rebuild on `done` should clean them up — but it's worth double-checking the error paths (`apperror` / `stream_end` without a preceding `done`) still clear the blocks, since that's where ours got stuck and left reference cards occupying the screen.

3. **Long-session context can make references fail upstream.** MoA fan-out sends the full context to each reference advisor, so in a long WebUI session the reference requests can get very large (we measured ~80K–113K estimated tokens hitting our proxy's rate limits and the fallback model returning 400). Not a WebUI bug, but users running MoA from long sessions may see references fail or time out; a short/fresh session is more reliable.

## Summary

I checked the new field report against current head `4eed1ef48` and re-read the terminal paths. The observation about terminal cleanup is useful, but the intended fix should not be explicit removal of the reference cards. Normal completion already removes them, and that is the unresolved blocker: the reference output is lost precisely when the final answer settles.

## Code reference

`static/messages.js:2411-2439` creates MoA references only under `liveAssistantTurn`, and `static/messages.js:5644-5653` snapshots that DOM after each reference. On `done`, however, `static/messages.js:6016-6020` replaces browser state from the persisted session:

```js
S.session=d.session;
S.messages=_carryForwardEphemeralTurnFields(
  S.messages||[], d.session.messages||[]
);
```

The only terminal metadata projected onto the settled assistant message is the anchor scene at `static/messages.js:6100`; the MoA cards never enter that scene. The following renders at `static/messages.js:6171-6175` therefore discard them.

I also checked the paths raised in the new comment. `apperror` starts at `static/messages.js:6362` and projects the existing anchor scene at `static/messages.js:6431-6448`; `stream_end` starts at `static/messages.js:6221` and converges through `_restoreSettledSession`. Neither path has MoA data to project. A session switch can temporarily restore the DOM snapshot, but it remains an in-flight display cache rather than settled transcript state.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please preserve references first, then clean up only transient status UI. The existing anchor path is still the smallest fit:

- Send each `moa.reference` through `_applyToAnchor` with an identity based on `index` when present, not label alone.
- Render that activity in the live worklog and let `_attachProjectedAnchorSceneToLastAssistant` carry it across `done`, `apperror`, and `stream_end` settlement.
- Remove or hide `.moa-status` at terminal state; do not remove the settled reference activities.

This also resolves duplicate labels correctly. The Agent contract in `agent/moa_loop.py:2154-2163` emits 1-based `index` and `count`, and the WebUI backend forwards them at `api/streaming.py:8709-8715`; using label as the key at `static/messages.js:2425-2427` throws away that identity.

The current source tests at `tests/test_6743_moa_reference_output.py:108-135` still cannot observe lifecycle behavior. [project.scripts]

payload.author: AlexeyDsov
payload.title: perf: optimize message virtualization with incremental caching, windowed render scans, and programmatic scroll guard

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete PR diff at `d95df17a3`, the full `static/ui.js` on PR HEAD and `origin/master`, and all three changed tests, I found one correctness regression in the bounded question-to-assistant map. A virtualized render has two disjoint slices, the viewport head and the always-mounted recent tail. The new single pass concatenates them but carries question state across the omitted middle, so jump-to-question can target the wrong user row for the first assistant turn in the retained tail. I would treat this as a blocker for the current optimization.

## Code reference

The disjoint shape is explicit at `static/ui.js:15779-15784`:

```js
const renderHeadVisWithIdx=visWithIdx.slice(windowStart, windowEnd);
const renderTailStart=Math.max(windowEnd, virtualWindow.tailStart);
const renderTailVisWithIdx=virtualWindow.virtualized&&renderTailStart<visWithIdx.length
  ?visWithIdx.slice(renderTailStart)
  :[];
const renderVisWithIdx=renderHeadVisWithIdx.concat(renderTailVisWithIdx);
```

At `static/ui.js:15939-15957`, the question map seeds only from before `_visScanStart`, scans the head, and then immediately scans the tail. It never checks the final user in the gap `[windowEnd, tailStart)`. For example, if the head ends with user 20, the omitted gap ends with user 100, and the retained tail starts with assistant 101, assistant 101 is incorrectly mapped to user 20.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Build the map per contiguous slice, seeding the head from `windowStart - 1` and the tail from `tailStart - 1`. A small helper that accepts a slice and its visible-array start index would preserve the bounded work. Keeping the original full `visWithIdx` scan would also be correct, but gives back this part of the optimization.

## Test plan

The update at `tests/test_issue500_message_list_virtualization.py:105-127` changes source-string assertions but does not test this invariant. Please add a behavior test with disjoint head and tail slices where a user in the skipped gap owns the first tail assistant. Assert that `questionRawIdxByAssistantRawIdx.get(101)` equals the gap user raw index, not the last user in the head. I did not execute PR-authored code, per the read-only review boundary.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete five-file diff at `744366941`, all changed files on PR HEAD and `origin/master`, plus the existing read-only and session-shortening contracts, I found two correctness blockers. The more serious one exposes deletion on branchable read-only cron sessions even though delete is a mutation, not a branch. The second leaves the browser transcript unchanged after deleting from a partially loaded session.

## Code reference

The branchable exception is specifically a cron exception in `static/sessions.js:2485-2497`:

```js
function _isBranchableReadOnlySession(session) {
  if (!_isReadOnlySession(session)) return false;
  const sources = [
    session && session.source_tag,
    session && session.raw_source,
    session && session.source,
  ].map(v => String(v || "").trim().toLowerCase());
  return sources.includes('cron');
}
```

At `static/ui.js:16211-16220`, the PR uses `(readOnlySession&&!branchableReadOnlySession)` for `deleteBtn`. That gate is appropriate for `forkBtn`, because forking does not mutate the source, but it makes the trash button visible for read-only cron sessions. `deleteMessage()` at `static/ui.js:18525-18556` has no read-only guard. The server handler at `api/routes.py:15091-15131` rejects subagent views and invalid counts, but does not reject a read-only session before calling `truncate_session_at_keep()` and `s.save()`.

The partial-history bug is at `static/ui.js:18534-18554`: the server count correctly uses `_oldestIdx + msgIdx`, but the same absolute count is used to slice the window-relative `S.messages`. With `_oldestIdx=100`, 20 loaded rows, and `msgIdx=5`, the server keeps 105 messages while `S.messages.slice(0,105)` keeps all 20 loaded rows, including the deleted tail.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

1. Hide delete whenever `readOnlySession` is true. Keep the branchable exception only for fork. Add the same guard inside `deleteMessage()`, and preferably enforce read-only in the shortening endpoint as defense in depth.
2. After a successful shortening request, either slice locally with `msgIdx`, preserving `_oldestIdx`, or consume the authoritative `session.messages` returned by the endpoint and reset the offset consistently.

## Test plan

The new tests at `tests/test_6737_delete_edit_messages.py:76-111` are source-structure checks and currently assert the faulty branchable gate. Add behavior coverage for a read-only cron session and for `_oldestIdx > 0`. The first must render no trash action and refuse direct deletion; the second must remove the selected loaded row and every loaded row after it while sending the absolute keep count to the server. I did not execute PR-authored code, per the read-only review boundary.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @ruizanthony — this correctly diagnoses the root cause (the branch route sliced `keep_count` against the raw sidecar while the frontend counts against `GET /api/session`'s merged display transcript), and the direction is right. A Codex regression gate found the new merge doesn't match GET's display merge *exactly* in two spots, and those divergences reintroduce the same coordinate-shift for large/messaging sessions (both SILENT), so it needs one more pass.

### Findings (both SILENT — the fork silently ends before the conclusion for edge sessions)
1. **`api/routes.py:15192` — missing state.db backstop limit.** `GET` reads state.db with `limit=_state_db_backstop_limit_for_display(source, None)` (50,000). The new branch else-path reads **without** a limit. For a session exceeding the 50k backstop, the two lists differ → `keep_count` coordinates shift again (the exact bug this PR fixes), and it reintroduces an unbounded-memory read on large sessions.
2. **`api/routes.py:15179` — messaging-empty fallback copies undisplayed rows.** For a messaging-classified session with an **empty** CLI transcript, `GET` leaves `state_db_messages=[]`, but the branch path falls through to the generic state.db reader → the fork can include rows GET never displayed, again shifting `keep_count`.

### Fix-spec
Route both paths through **one shared full-display builder** so the fork's `source_messages` is byte-for-byte what GET builds:
1. `api/routes.py:15179-15199` — the messaging-empty fallback must use sidecar lineage **plus an empty state.db list** (matching GET), not the generic reader.
2. `api/routes.py:15192-15195` — construct the non-messaging reader kwargs exactly like GET, **including** the gated `limit=_state_db_backstop_limit_for_display(source, None)`.

Ideally extract GET's display-transcript construction into a single helper and call it from both the GET handler and the branch route, so they can't drift again. Add a test for a >50k-row session and a messaging-empty session asserting the fork keeps the displayed conclusion. Codex verified everything else is intact (merge ordering, dedup, truncation params, inactive-row filtering, `keep_count=None` path; 42 branching + 4 reconciliation + 2 lineage + 11 backstop tests pass). Once both paths go through the shared builder, I'll re-gate.

payload.title: fix(cron): mark running cron sessions as active in sidebar

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @webtecnica — the cron-liveness plumbing here is correct and Codex verified the hard parts (state copied under `_RUNNING_CRON_LOCK`, overlaid after every cache read, cleared before the completion invalidation; profile-isolation intact; no hot-path cost). Two things need fixing before ship — one predicate gap and one regression against an existing test.

### 1. (CORE) `_isSessionEffectivelyStreaming()` ignores `cron_running` — `static/sessions.js:814`
Rendering, sorting, polling, and completion-transition tracking all key off this predicate, but it doesn't consider `cron_running`, so a running cron row renders **visually idle** and can lose its eventual completion/unread transition. A Node probe confirmed `predicateWhileRunning: false` and no completion mark after `cron_running` clears.

**Fix** — add `s.cron_running ||` to the predicate:
```js
function _isSessionEffectivelyStreaming(s) {
  return Boolean(s && (
    s.is_streaming ||
    s.cron_running ||
    _hasPendingUserMessageSignal(s) ||
    _isSessionLocallyStreaming(s)
  ));
}
```
Add a focused JS regression proving a running cron renders active and produces **exactly one** `true → false` completion transition when the flag clears. (I verified this exact fix locally — it passes and fails-closed correctly when reverted.)

### 2. (REGRESSION) The PR breaks `test_issue856_background_completion_unread` — full suite: **2 failed, 13898 passed**
These two tests pass on clean master but fail on this branch:
- `test_polling_transition_marks_completion_when_long_running_stream_snapshot_advances`
- `test_polling_snapshot_fallback_does_not_mark_first_seen_historical_sessions`

They're **structural** (source-string) assertions on `_markPollingCompletionUnreadTransitions`, and your (correct) `!cronRunning &&` guards shifted the exact strings they match. The behavior change is right — you just need to update the assertions to match the new source. Specifically:
- Line ~365 / ~386: `"const completedWithNewMessages = Boolean("` → `"const completedWithNewMessages = !cronRunning && Boolean("`
- Line ~369: `"const completedPersistedObservedStream = Boolean(observedStreaming && !isStreaming);"` → `"const completedPersistedObservedStream = !cronRunning && Boolean(observedStreaming && !isStreaming);"`

## Summary

The server overlay identifies the current cron session correctly, but the new flag is not connected to the code that renders or schedules active rows. As written, this suppresses an early unread-completion transition, yet the cron row still has no animated running indicator and is not treated as active for sorting or polling. That leaves the main symptom in issue 6728 unresolved.

## Code reference

The new overlay at `api/route_session_list_cache.py:445-506` stamps `cron_running`, and `api/routes.py:9811-9827` preserves it in the sidebar response. However, the backend active-sort predicate at `api/route_session_list_cache.py:536-547` still ignores that field.

```js
function _isSessionEffectivelyStreaming(s) {
  return Boolean(s && (
    s.is_streaming ||
    _hasPendingUserMessageSignal(s) ||
    _isSessionLocallyStreaming(s)
  ));
}
```

That helper at `static/sessions.js:814-820` controls all relevant behavior. `static/sessions.js:5437-5442` decides whether to keep the fast session-list poll running, `static/sessions.js:6524-6532` assigns the active sort rank, and `static/sessions.js:7973-7985` adds the `streaming` class that drives the green indicator. None of those paths sees `cron_running`. The only frontend read added by this PR is at `static/sessions.js:1216-1229`, where it merely blocks completion marking.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please include `s.cron_running` in `_isSessionEffectivelyStreaming`, and include `row.get("cron_running")` in `_session_list_row_is_runtime_active`. Then a running cron row will receive the same visual class, active-first ordering, and polling cadence as another live session. When the server changes the flag to false, the existing `wasStreaming` transition can produce the completion marker once, instead of needing three separate negated guards.

## Test plan

The new tests at `tests/test_6728_cron_running_sidebar.py:35-118` prove only that the backend flag survives the response. Add frontend behavior coverage asserting that a row with `cron_running: true` is effectively streaming, receives the running class, ranks ahead of idle rows, and keeps streaming polling active. Then flip the same row to false and assert one completion transition. A backend sort test should also place a running cron row ahead of a newer idle row. I reviewed the worktree read-only and did not execute contributor code.

payload.author: webtecnica
payload.title: fix(restart): don't SIGTERM the gateway when restart CLI becomes the gateway

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @webtecnica — this correctly diagnoses and fixes the single-container "Restart Service" kill loop (the CLI falls through to `run_gateway()`, becomes the gateway, and `_wait_and_release` then SIGTERMs the healthy replacement). The base fix is sound and well-tested (39 focused restart/health tests + full suite **13,902 / 0**, and the #6721-area PID-tracking suite stays green). A Codex regression gate found one edge in the exemption condition that needs tightening before ship.

### The defect (SILENT — leaks a wedged restart child) — `api/gateway_restart.py:89`
The termination exemption is too broad: it returns `True` (skip terminate) for a `starting` gateway state and uses raw same-PID equality. But the gateway writes `starting` **before** potentially-blocking plugin/MCP/platform initialization and only writes `running` once fully up. So a restart child that **wedges during startup** matches the exemption and is never cleaned up — lines 205–218 silently skip the existing 240s cleanup, leaking the process. Separately, raw PID equality has no process-generation proof, so a stale record + PID reuse can misclassify a genuinely-stuck supervised restart child as "the healthy replacement."

### Fix-spec
1. `api/gateway_restart.py:89` — exempt from termination **only** a confirmed `gateway_state == "running"` gateway (not `starting`), and validate the PID through the canonical `gateway.pid` / runtime-lock / start-time metadata rather than raw PID equality. Any `starting` or generation-mismatched record must still fall through to the existing 240s cleanup + terminate.
2. Add tests proving a same-PID **`starting`** record and a **stale-generation** record still terminate (the current 39 tests cover the happy exemption but not these two leak cases).

Everything else checks out — the 5s probe keeps its dynamically-expanded wait budget and single-flight behavior, and the multi-container/systemd path is unchanged. Once the exemption is gated on confirmed-`running` + canonical PID validation (with the two leak-case tests), I'll re-gate. Nice catch on the root cause — this is just about not over-exempting a startup-wedged child.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Deep-review gate: SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES — right fix for a real bug, but the takeover detection needs a true process-generation check

Thanks for this — the single-container restart kill-loop is a real, nasty bug (the CLI becomes the gateway, then the 240s timeout SIGTERMs the healthy replacement), and the overall approach (detect "the child became the gateway" and skip the terminate) is correct. The code is careful and well-documented. The adversarial gate (Codex, with end-to-end timeout-path reproductions) took this through two rounds; I applied the round-1 fixes myself on the branch and Codex confirmed them resolved, but a third, same-class defect remains that needs a design addition I don't want to make on your behalf without your call.

### Already fixed on the branch (round 1 — Codex-confirmed resolved)
I pushed two fixes to the exemption logic (feel free to keep or adjust):
1. **Missing `gateway.pid` now fails closed.** `_subprocess_became_gateway` gated the canonical-PID cross-check on `pid_file.exists()`, so an absent pid file fell through to `return True` — a hung child with a stale future-dated `running` record + PID reuse escaped `terminate()`/`kill()` and leaked. Since the real gateway writes `gateway.pid` before flipping to `running`, absence can't confirm takeover: now the canonical PID must always be read and must match (missing/None/mismatch → False → terminate).
2. **`_read_canonical_gateway_pid` now truly fails closed.** The `except ValueError: int(raw)` fallback accepted non-JSON forms like `+4242` / `0004242` as PID 4242, contradicting the documented strict contract. Removed the fallback (a legacy bare `4242` is valid JSON, so it's still accepted).
I also updated the three exemption tests to write a matching `gateway.pid` and added coverage for both fixes.

### REMAINING MUST-FIX (CORE) — PID equality isn't proof of process generation `api/gateway_restart.py:~127, ~210`
Even with the pid-file cross-check, a hung restart child can still be mis-exempted when a **stale runtime record AND a stale canonical `gateway.pid` both carry the child's REUSED PID**, plus a future-dated `updated_at`. Codex reproduced this on the timeout path: `terminated=False`, `killed=False`, lock released — the child leaks. The root cause is that identity is proven by PID equality + `updated_at` postdating, but neither survives PID reuse: the OS can hand the same PID to an unrelated stuck child, and a stale record's `updated_at` can be arbitrarily far in the future.

The robust fix is a real **process-generation fingerprint**: Hermes records a `start_time` (process start fingerprint) in both the runtime and canonical records — validate BOTH against the LIVE child's actual process-start time (e.g. from `/proc/<pid>/stat` btime, or `psutil.Process(pid).create_time()`), so a reused PID with a different creation time fails the exemption. For a legacy PID-only file, require positive proof the pid file was (re)written AFTER the subprocess was spawned before granting the exemption. Please also add an end-to-end timeout test proving that stale-but-matching PID records still call `terminate()`/`kill()`.

I stopped short of building the `start_time`-fingerprint check myself because it's a design addition (which record fields to trust, `/proc` vs psutil availability across the Docker base image, the legacy-file policy) rather than a mechanical fix — your call on the exact mechanism. The two round-1 fixes are on the branch; happy to re-gate the moment the generation-fingerprint validation lands. This is close — it just needs identity to survive PID reuse.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Gate on current master (exact head `33489b46`, staged): the restart-lifecycle intent is right and the fail-closed *design* is sound, but an adversarial gate (Codex, verified against the real isolated gateway writer, on a full 13,926-pass suite) reproduced **three CORE defects** — two would terminate the healthy single-container gateway, one fails open on a hung child. The current tests miss them (they use a plain-text PID fixture, not the real JSON shape). Holding for a revision:

### 1. CORE — the exemption can't read the production `gateway.pid`
Hermes writes `gateway.pid` as a **JSON object** (`{"pid":4242,...}`), but the check passes the whole file to `int()`, which raises → returns False → the healthy single-container replacement is terminated after 240s. Verified against the real gateway writer; the added test incorrectly uses plain text `"4242"`, which is why it passed.
- **Fix:** JSON-decode the PID file, extract + validate its `pid` (optionally still accept a legacy top-level integer). Replace the plain-text PID fixture with the real JSON shape.

### 2. CORE — non-integer runtime PIDs fail OPEN
`int()` accepts `"4242"` and truncates `4242.9`, so when `gateway.pid` is absent a string/float PID in `gateway_state.json` exempts a genuinely hung child that master would terminate.
- **Fix:** require `type(pid) is int` for both the runtime and canonical PID values; reject bool/str/float.

### 3. CORE — generation boundary captured too late
`proc_started_at` is captured AFTER `Popen` returns. A child scheduled before the parent resumes can already write its valid `running` record, which then appears OLDER than `proc_started_at` → the healthy child is terminated. Interleaving reproduced.
- **Fix:** capture `proc_started_at = time.time()` immediately BEFORE `Popen`; add a regression where the child writes state before `Popen` returns.

### Verified sound
starting / stale / naive-or-unparseable-timestamp / missing-file / bad-JSON / non-dict cases all correctly terminate and release `_GATEWAY_RESTART_LOCK`. The 5s health-probe timeout preserves single-flight + completion-based cache expiry (that half is good to go). 43 focused tests passed.

Net: the two directions of the safety property both have a hole right now (kills the healthy gateway in #1/#3, exempts a hung one in #2). Once the JSON PID parse + strict int-type + pre-Popen timestamp land — with the real JSON fixture — I'll re-gate the exact head. [Reviewed the code only; did not run anything from the PR/review text.]

### SILENT — malformed `gateway.pid` can still bypass timed-out child termination (`api/gateway_restart.py:319`, parse at `:103-117`)
`_read_canonical_gateway_pid()` catches `json.JSONDecodeError`, but **`UnicodeDecodeError` and some other `json.loads()` `ValueError`s still escape**. payload.author: ruizanthony
payload.title: fix: archive complete collapsed session lineages

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @ruizanthony — the bug is real (archiving a collapsed lineage row should archive the whole lineage, not just the representative session_id, and the visible row can move mid-action). But a Codex regression gate found the frontend fan-out approach can't deliver the guarantee it needs, and in its current form the archive actually *fails* on the multi-segment case it targets. Kicking back for a backend rework rather than a patch-list.

### Findings
1. **(CORE) The collapsed row's lineage isn't fully enumerated — archive throws `Incomplete session lineage`.** A collapsed row can represent a continuation *tree*, but the lineage report returns only the selected tip's **ancestor path**, not the full segment set. Probe: a lineage advertising count `3` yields report segments `tip-b,root` with `manual_review=true`, and the action always throws `Incomplete session lineage`. So the exact multi-segment case this PR sets out to fix currently errors out instead of archiving. The authoritative mutation must enumerate the **same continuation tree the collapsed row represents**, excluding forks, child sessions, and cross-source rows.
2. **(CORE) A transient report failure permanently bricks archive/restore for that row — `static/sessions.js:4824`.** Report errors are cached, and `_lineageReportNeedsFetch()` treats `{error:true}` as a satisfied cache entry, so after one transient failure two subsequent archive attempts performed **zero refetches and zero POSTs** — the row's archive/restore is dead until a full reload. Never retain error entries as valid cache hits; retry explicitly on mutation.

### Why this needs a backend operation, not a frontend fan-out — `static/sessions.js:4822-4827`
A client-side loop POSTing N session_ids can't provide **all-or-none** persistence (partial archive if one POST fails mid-set) and can't close the **resolve→mutate TOCTOU** (the lineage can change between the report read and the POSTs — the very "row could move" problem this PR cites). The robust shape is a single backend lineage-aware endpoint that: locks and **re-resolves** the current lineage server-side, enumerates the same complete segment set the sidebar collapses, prevalidates every target, and **commits or rolls back the whole set as one result**.

### Verified safe
Codex confirmed a single non-collapsed session still makes exactly one POST with byte-identical body `{"session_id":"single","archived":true}`; direct fork/child actions stay singleton; rename and delete are unchanged. 60 focused lineage/action tests + `node --check` pass. So the regression surface is contained to the collapsed-archive path — it's the *approach* that needs to move server-side. Happy to re-gate once it's a backend all-or-none operation.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @ruizanthony — the substantive rewrite closes the old frontend-fanout, incomplete-lineage, report-cache, and locked re-resolution blockers. Two objective exact-head gaps remain before this is safe.

### 1. The multi-session save is still not all-or-none

`api/routes.py` mutates and saves lineage members sequentially, and only appends a member to `saved` after `Session.save()` returns. But `Session.save()` can replace the sidecar before a later index publication fails. In that schedule, the failing member is already durable but is absent from `saved`, so rollback omits it and leaves both its in-memory value and sidecar changed. Rollback is itself a sequence of ordinary saves whose failures are only logged, so the route can still return an error with a mixed old/new lineage.

Please make this a recoverable batch transaction under the existing sorted locks: snapshot every in-memory and durable preimage, stage/validate the full new batch, publish through one durable transaction/journal authority with startup recovery (or equivalent), include the currently failing member in compensation, and never report generic failure after merely logging residual mixed state. Add production-composed tests for sidecar-replace → index failure on the current/later member, compensation failure, exact cold reload/index parity, and restore symmetry.

### 2. Literal profile equality regresses the renamed-root alias contract

`read_session_lineage_ids()` filters normalized profile strings by literal equality. WebUI’s canonical `_profiles_match()` contract treats missing/`default` rows and a renamed root profile as equivalent. A legitimate root-profile lineage can therefore false-404 after this remediation.

Please use canonical profile equivalence during lineage resolution while retaining the per-materialized-session visibility prevalidation, and add renamed-root + `default`/missing rows with a foreign named-profile control.

Thanks @ruizanthony. The re-push closes the two previously named implementation gaps in the ordinary request path: the batch now journals complete old/new images with rollback/roll-forward recovery, and lineage filtering uses canonical root-profile aliases. One objective startup-composition gap still breaks the core all-or-none guarantee.

### Legacy `.bak` recovery can split a committed lineage after batch recovery

The new startup order is:

1. `api/session_batch_transaction.py::_recover_pending_locked()` replays the batch's complete sidecar/index images and deletes `_session_batch_transaction.json` after a successful replay.
2. `api/session_recovery.py::run_startup_session_recovery()` immediately runs `recover_all_sessions_on_startup()`.
3. `recover_session()` copies an entire `<sid>.json.bak` over the live sidecar. It does not preserve the live `archived` value.

That makes this reachable: a committed two-member archive journal rolls A and B forward to `archived=true`; only A has a larger valid pre-archive `.json.bak`; the legacy pass replaces A with that backup (`archived=false`) while B stays `true`; index rebuild then publishes the mixed lineage. The same split can occur on a later ordinary restart after journal cleanup. Each recovery pass is internally consistent, but they do not compose with the PR's durable lineage invariant.

### Required fix

Make legacy backup restoration preserve the current archive authority instead of replacing it with stale backup metadata. A narrow safe shape is to restore the recovery-owned transcript fields from the backup while retaining the live `archived` value (and other metadata outside `.bak` recovery authority), then atomically publish the merged sidecar and rebuild the index. Do not replay the batch's full image afterward, because that would overwrite the longer transcript the backup recovery was meant to restore.

Please add a production-composed startup test with a two-member lineage where only one member has a larger valid backup carrying the stale archive value. After `run_startup_session_recovery()`, cold-load both sidecars and `_index.json` and prove both retain the committed archive state while the intended transcript recovery lands. ## Static re-gate: indexed lineage recovery is fixed, but ordinary backups can still replace current metadata

I re-gated exact head `b8f04f4fa7ef33c4f01bb4ca90df35190a94d16e` against the prior review at `34cc23b656da`. The rebased twin is patch-equivalent, so the response is the two-commit, four-file delta after `9b4295b1f`.

- missing/malformed lineage members now compose backup transcript fields onto a typed current index envelope, or leave an explicit residual;
- backup recovery and lineage commit now share one in-process, cross-process, and index-write transaction lock with a pre-replace byte recheck.

Two objective blockers remain.

### 1. The no-authority “ordinary” path restores the complete stale backup

When live is missing/malformed and `_read_index_metadata_authority()` cannot return a complete accepted row, `_recover_session_locked()` still reaches `recovered = dict(backup)` if `_backup_requires_current_metadata_authority()` says the backup looks ordinary.

That predicate checks `archived` and key names containing `parent`, `lineage`, `compression`, `delegate`, `branch`, `batch`, `revision`, or `archive`. It does not protect `title`, `workspace`, `model`, `profile`, `project_id`, owner/source fields, routing, or future metadata. A rescue backup predates the shrinking write, so publishing it wholesale can silently revive stale profile/title/project/source ownership. The new `test_backup_recovery_without_metadata_authority_restores_ordinary_backup` explicitly locks in whole-backup restoration.

A `.bak` is transcript authority only. Remove the wholesale fallback. Add stale ordinary profile/title/project/source matrices with complete, incomplete, and absent indexes.

### 2. Sidecar and index recovery still are not crash-complete

Recovery fsyncs a temp file and replaces only the sidecar. The index rebuild happens later, outside that publication. If the process crashes after sidecar replace but before index rebuild, the next startup sees equal live/backup message counts (`restored == 0`) and skips rebuilding an existing stale index. There is no durable recovery intent to finish the operation.

Journal sidecar plus index recovery as one intent, or persist and fsync a marker that forces exact index reconciliation on the next boot. Add crash injection after sidecar replacement and prove a fresh startup converges the sidecar and index even though no second transcript restore is needed.

## Static re-gate at exact head `ec9c5327afc8`

The new commit genuinely closes both blockers from the August 23 review:

- missing or malformed live sidecars no longer restore an “ordinary” backup wholesale when current metadata authority is unavailable;
- recovered sidecar and index images are now staged under one durable commit intent, and startup replays that intent.

One objective crash-recovery gap remains in the new publication path.

### Blocking: a leftover committed journal can overwrite successful later work

`api/session_batch_transaction.py::commit_session_recovery_locked()` publishes the recovered sidecar and full `_index.json` image, then tries to remove `_session_batch_transaction.json`. At lines 426–431, a cleanup failure is only logged and the function returns success while the replayable commit journal remains.

That journal contains complete `new` bytes for both the recovered sidecar and the full index. Ordinary `Session.save()` does not acquire `session_store_transaction_lock()` or reject a pending journal. The following sequence is therefore reachable:

1. manual or startup backup recovery publishes sidecar + index;
2. journal unlink fails, but recovery reports success;
3. the user continues the recovered session (or another session updates the index), durably writing newer bytes;
4. the next startup runs `_recover_pending_locked()`, which unconditionally replays the old journal’s `new` images before removing it.

Step 4 overwrites the target session’s post-recovery messages/metadata and replaces the index with the older snapshot. The current committed-journal test mutates an image *before* immediate replay; it does not cover successful ordinary writes after the transaction returned.

### Required fix

Do not return success while a replayable commit journal can coexist with later mutations.

- After journal cleanup failure, recover/remove the intent under the transaction lock. If it still cannot be consumed, surface `recovery_required=True` and make every ordinary session mutation fail closed on that pending authority (or use generation/preconditioned replay that cannot replace bytes written after the transaction).
- Apply the same invariant to the existing archive-batch cleanup path, which uses the same “log and return” pattern.
- Add a crash/cleanup injection test: leave a committed journal, then attempt a later append to the recovered target plus an unrelated index update, simulate fresh startup, and prove neither newer image is overwritten. If the design blocks those later writes instead, assert that fail-closed behavior explicitly.

This is a direct data-loss schedule, so it needs to be closed before the PR can return to the ship gate.

## Static deep re-gate at exact head `2d3f96d066c3`

The latest response closes the visible scope gap: individual and batch archive actions now send one backend-authoritative `lineage:true` request, and the previously approved cleanup-only journal/precondition behavior is unchanged.

One objective all-or-none race remains in the production store boundary.

### Blocking: an ordinary `Session.load()` self-heal can overwrite a committed archive member without updating the index

`commit_session_archive_batch()` holds `session_store_transaction_lock()` plus the sorted per-session locks at the route, but `Session.load()` has a write-capable path that participates in neither authority:

- `api/models.py:1569-1574` reads a sidecar and collapses adjacent duplicate partials.
- If it found duplicates, `api/models.py:1576-1583` calls `session.save(touch_updated_at=False, skip_index=True)` directly.
- `Session.save()` replaces the sidecar at `api/models.py:1519-1525`; it does not acquire the per-session agent lock or `_session_store_process_lock`.

That admits this deterministic schedule, including across WebUI processes:

1. A reader loads a lineage member while its durable payload says `archived:false`, collapses duplicate partials, and pauses before the self-heal save.
2. The lineage archive takes its locks, commits every member and `_index.json` as `archived:true`, disarms/removes the journal, and returns success.
3. The reader resumes and replaces that member with its stale pre-archive object (`archived:false`) using `skip_index=True`.

The durable sidecar is now unarchived while `_index.json` still reports archived. The transaction returned success, but the lineage is split. The new tests cover journal publication/replay and the frontend delegation, not an ordinary writer paused across the batch commit.

### Required fix

1. Put the write-capable `Session.load()` duplicate-partial self-heal under the same per-session and cross-process session-store authority as lineage publication.
2. After acquiring that authority, revalidate the exact sidecar snapshot (for example, with the existing pre-read signature plus a byte/stat CAS) before replacing it. If another writer changed the sidecar, skip/reload/retry rather than publishing the stale object.
3. Audit the remaining ordinary sidecar/index writers against the same rule. A lock described as cross-process store authority cannot protect the batch if writers that target the same files do not participate.
4. Add a production-shaped regression that pauses the real `Session.load()` self-heal after its read, commits a two-member archive, resumes the self-heal, and then cold-reads both sidecars plus `_index.json`. Require every member to retain the requested archive state and sidecar/index parity. Include a separate-process leg or equivalent proof of the advisory-lock contract.

This review is static-only. Layer 1 reported **SUSPICIOUS** on six `eval(extract(...))` test-harness lines, so no PR code or tests were executed; the scanner finding itself is not part of the requested fix.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @FlaBouy. The new exact-byte snapshot machinery addresses the two ordinary-path repros from the previous review, but the current head still has two objective blockers.

### 1. Leading-dot and ignored colliders can still be destroyed without a usable recovery snapshot

`_posix_relpath()` currently does:

```python
return Path(rel).as_posix().lstrip('./')
```

`str.lstrip('./')` removes every leading `.` and `/`, not one literal `./` prefix. A legitimate untracked path such as `.hermes-local` or `.github/local.json` is therefore rewritten to `hermes-local` / `github/local.json`. `_iter_worktree_files()` then looks up the wrong filesystem path and returns no captured entry. If this is the only local dirt, `_create_update_recovery_snapshot()` falls through to `_create_update_backup_branch()`, which records only `HEAD`.

That is destructive on both paths in this PR:

- normal Agent safe-reset can reach `reset --hard <compare_ref>` with the leading-dot collider neither identified nor snapshotted;
- force update runs `git clean -fd` and then `reset --hard <compare_ref>` after returning the misleading HEAD-only recovery ref.

There is a second form of the same gap: `_list_snapshot_paths()` and `_list_untracked_files()` use `--exclude-standard`, while the comment assumes ignored files always survive because clean omits `-x`. `reset --hard` can still replace an ignored local file when the target ref begins tracking that path. Such bytes are neither enumerated nor snapshotted.

Required fix:

1. Preserve exact Git-relative names. Remove only an explicit `./` prefix, not arbitrary leading dots, and use NUL-delimited output consistently for dirty, staged, and untracked names.
2. Fail closed when preflight reports dirty/untracked state but complete enumeration or snapshot verification fails. Do not silently downgrade to an HEAD-only branch in that case.
3. Account for ignored local paths that the target tree will overwrite, either by snapshotting those colliders or refusing before any checkout/clean/reset.
4. Add real-repo regressions for a leading-dot collider and an ignored collider that upstream begins tracking, through both normal Agent safe-reset and force update. Assert either exact bytes are readable from the returned recovery ref or HEAD/worktree remain completely unmodified.

### 2. `/api/updates/diagnose` exposes unsanitized secrets

The new route returns `diagnose_checkout()` directly. `_describe_checkout_sync()` puts `_normalize_remote_url(remote_url)` in `remote_url`, but `_normalize_remote_url()` only converts SSH syntax and strips `.git`; it preserves HTTPS userinfo and secret query parameters. `_list_checkout_processes()` also serializes each complete `ps ... command` string. A remote such as `https://user:token@host/repo.git`, or an updater process with `--api-key ...`, is therefore returned to the API caller.

Required fix:

- sanitize or omit remote credentials before the value enters the diagnostic payload;
- do not return raw process argv (PID plus a non-secret executable identifier is enough), or apply a fail-closed redaction contract that cannot expose arbitrary argument values;
- add route-level regressions covering URL userinfo/query secrets and a process command containing a secret.

### Verification status

The exact-head threat scan returned **DANGEROUS / NO-RUN** because the added `tests/conftest.py` content around `os.execv` / `_schedule_restart` matched the execution-obfuscation gate. Per policy, I did not execute any PR code or tests and did not bypass the sandbox gate. The findings above come from static exact-head tracing. After the fixes, the PR needs a clean threat scan and the focused real-Git suite through `warmup-safe-test.sh`.

This is a review-only warm-up; no contributor branch was modified.

The current focused test file contains an assertion that cannot pass at this head, and non-Linux hosts are reported as having a valid zero-throughput network collector instead of an unavailable metric.

## Code reference

The later boot fix at static/ui.js:9431-9441 correctly changed the DOMContentLoaded callback to _bootResourceStatusBar. The regression at tests/test_issue693_system_health_panel.py:475-485 still requires the superseded direct callback:

~~~python
assert "document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded',_mountResourceStatusBar)" in UI_JS
assert "_mountResourceStatusBar();" in UI_JS
~~~

That first string no longer exists in static/ui.js, so the PR's own targeted test should fail at the current head. This appears to have drifted when a84363950 introduced the deferred-script boot helper.

The backend has a separate portability problem at api/system_health.py:169-191:

~~~python
try:
    with _PROC_NET_DEV.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            if ":" not in line:
                continue
~~~

The matching except OSError at api/system_health.py:189-190 returns (0, 0). On macOS, Windows, or a restricted container without that procfs file, this feeds a normal network dictionary into build_system_health_payload(). The response remains ok rather than partial, and the bar displays zero traffic. The change to the unavailable test at tests/test_issue693_system_health_panel.py:97 implicitly confirms this: every other collector has to be forced to raise because the network collector otherwise makes available true.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

First, update the boot assertion to pin _bootResourceStatusBar, preferably with a behavioral DOM harness that fires DOMContentLoaded after panels.js is available and verifies exactly one footer plus one polling timer.

Second, make missing or unreadable network counters raise a coarse network_unavailable error, as the CPU and memory collectors do. A psutil fallback is also reasonable, but silently returning zeros is not. Add a non-procfs regression asserting network is null and the overall response is partial when CPU, memory, or disk still works.

Finally, _NET_SAMPLE at api/system_health.py:165 is mutable shared state in QuietHTTPServer, which is explicitly threaded at server.py:117-139. Multiple tabs can consume each other's sample baseline, and simultaneous requests can read and update the three fields without one coherent critical section. Protect the sample with a lock and test interleaved callers, or move sampling to one fixed-cadence server collector whose latest result is read by all requests.

## Verification step

After those changes, the focused health test should fail independently if the boot callback regresses or procfs is absent, and a two-client concurrency test should prove one caller's poll cannot distort the other caller's interval. I did not execute PR-authored code; this review is read-only.

## Summary

Reading the full two-file diff at bb34367c4 and both complete files on PR HEAD and origin/master, the core #6725 fix is correct: removing the inline background shorthand from static/index.html:282 lets the base select background-image survive, and static/style.css:2231-2234 restores the right-side spacing for the Insights control through .insights-period-select. payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @dss539 — the underlying bug is real (`@ollama-cloud:deepseek-v4-flash` reaching the API as the provider name → "Unknown provider"), and the direction is right. But I gated this at head `cc327e70` (rebased clean, red-before-green confirmed) and both Codex and a direct empirical trace found the `split(":", 1)` approach **mis-parses legitimate multi-segment custom provider IDs**, which would reintroduce the same "Unknown provider" break for named custom providers.

### The defect
`_clean_session_model_provider` splits on the **first** colon, but the codebase's canonical parser `_split_provider_qualified_model()` (api/routes.py:6376) splits on the **last** colon (`rsplit(":", 1)`) precisely because a custom provider ID can itself contain colons. Direct trace:

```
value                             _clean_session_model_provider (this PR)   _split_provider_qualified_model (canonical)
@ollama-cloud:deepseek-v4-flash   'ollama-cloud'                            'ollama-cloud'        ✅ agree
@custom:backup:model-a            'custom'                                  'custom:backup'       ❌ DIVERGES
@custom:backup:model-a:free       'custom'                                  'custom:backup:model-a' ❌ DIVERGES
custom:backup                     'custom:backup'                           (non-@, preserved)    ✅
```

So for a custom provider whose ID is `custom:backup`, `@custom:backup:model-a` would be stripped to `custom` — the wrong provider, causing exactly the "Unknown provider" failure this PR fixes, just for named custom providers instead.

The PR's own new test enshrines the wrong expectation: `test_strips_model_from_at_custom_named_provider` asserts `@custom:backup:model-a:free` → `custom`, but the canonical parser (and the rest of the routing path) treats the provider as `custom:backup:model-a`.

### Fix-spec
1. In `_clean_session_model_provider`, resolve the provider through the shared `_split_provider_qualified_model()` (or its `rsplit(":", 1)` + `_clean_session_model_provider(hint)` logic) rather than a first-colon `split(":", 1)`, so `@ollama-cloud:deepseek-v4-flash` → `ollama-cloud` **and** `@custom:backup:model-a` → `custom:backup`.
2. Correct the regression test: `@custom:backup:model-a:free` should expect the multi-segment provider (`custom:backup:model-a`), not `custom`. Add a `custom:<host>:<port>`-style case.

Everything else (non-`@` colon preservation, plain provider, empty/None/`default`) is correct. Once it routes through the canonical parser I'll re-gate. Nice catch on the root cause.

`_strip_provider_prefix_for_gateway()` does `value.split(":", 1)[1]`, so it sends the **wrong model name** to the gateway for any multi-segment custom provider:

`api/config.py:2555` already has `_parse_provider_qualified_model_id()`, the authoritative grammar that correctly handles `custom:<slug>`, `custom:<host>:<port>`, and `:free`-style model tags. Codex's concrete spec:
1. **`api/gateway_chat.py`** (lines ~550 and ~1039) — use `_parse_provider_qualified_model_id()` for gateway model stripping instead of `_strip_provider_prefix_for_gateway`; the gateway `model` field should be the parser's bare-model result and the provider its provider result.
2. **`api/routes.py:6360`** — route qualified-model parsing through `_parse_provider_qualified_model_id()`; remove the added heuristic block (≈lines 7332–7351) and consume the authoritative `(model, provider)` tuple at the two call sites (≈7783–7788).
3. **`tests/test_issue1855_resolve_model_provider_fast_path.py:364`** — change the expectation to `custom:backup` (not `custom`), and add named-custom tagged-model + `custom:<host>:<port>` assertions for both the routes path and **both** gateway request bodies.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the re-push @franksong2702 — the shared-parser adoption is exactly right: `_split_provider_qualified_model` now delegates to `config._parse_provider_qualified_model_id()`, the `rsplit(":", 1)` heuristic is gone, and Codex confirmed the 12 new tests genuinely fail-before/pass-after on the multi-segment case (the old splitter returned `("free", "custom:backup:model-a")`; the parser now handles it correctly). ### Finding — premature qualifier strip breaks provider-switch repair — `api/routes.py:7784`
The new `model_value = _bare` assignment strips the qualifier **before** `_resolve_compatible_session_model_state()` runs, so a session pinned to an unavailable/removed provider no longer gets repaired to the active default:

payload.author: dss539
payload.body:
## Update: added a third fix for the gateway boundary

The initial PR only addressed `_clean_session_model_provider` (fix 1) and `_session_model_state_from_request` (fix 2). During local testing I found a third leak path that required an additional commit.

### Why a third fix was needed

Fixes 1 and 2 handle the `model_provider` field and the `model` field at the `/api/chat/start` and `/api/session/update` boundary. But `_resolve_compatible_session_model_state` intentionally keeps the full `@provider:model` string for internal routing (per #1253 — it needs the prefix to distinguish duplicate model IDs across providers). The model value is then passed through to `_run_gateway_chat_streaming`, which sends it verbatim as `body["model"]` to the Hermes API server.

The Hermes gateway then forwards `model: "@ollama-cloud:minimax-m2.7"` to the upstream ollama-cloud API, which 404s: `model "@ollama-cloud:minimax-m2.7" not found`.

The fix: `_strip_provider_prefix_for_gateway()` in `api/gateway_chat.py` strips the `@provider:` prefix at the gateway request boundary — the last point where the internal routing string leaves the WebUI and enters the Hermes API. This is called at both gateway request sites (legacy chat completions and runs API).

### Commit summary

1. `cc327e7` — `_clean_session_model_provider`: strip model suffix from `@`-prefixed and poisoned non-`@` provider values
2. `bca2ac0` — `_resolve_compatible_session_model_state`: catalog-aware re-split on first colon when `rsplit` misparses colon-bearing model names like `deepseek-v4-flash:0731`
3. `a93e7f3` — `_session_model_state_from_request`: set `model_value` to the bare model name from `_split_provider_qualified_model`
4. `5355e4c` — `_run_gateway_chat_streaming`: strip `@provider:` prefix before sending to Hermes gateway

All 78 tests across 3 test files pass. Verified locally with minimax-m2.7, gemma4, and deepseek-v4-flash.
