payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full static-fallback regression file, the changed portions of `api/config.py` against `origin/master`, and the provider/model identity contract used by the agent catalog, this follow-up fixes the remaining false deduplication without flattening meaningful vendor namespaces. The provider-aware identity is the right unit: it treats only the active group prefix as decoration and retains every remaining slash component as part of the model ID. I do not see a code blocker in this revision.

## Code reference

The central normalization at `api/config.py:5271-5285` is deliberately narrow:

```python
def _provider_model_identity(model_id: object, provider_id: object) -> str:
    raw = str(model_id or "").strip().lower().replace("-", ".")
    pid = str(provider_id or "").strip().lower().replace("-", ".")
    slash_prefix = f"{pid}/"
    hint_prefix = f"@{pid}:"
    if pid and raw.startswith(slash_prefix):
        raw = raw[len(slash_prefix):]
    elif pid and raw.startswith(hint_prefix):
        raw = raw[len(hint_prefix):]
    return raw
```

That identity is used when collecting each target group at `api/config.py:5470-5478`, and again for active-provider default injection at `api/config.py:5501-5507`. This addresses the old `split("/", 1)[-1]` behavior without making `vendor-a/model-x` collide with `vendor-b/model-x`.

The tests map directly to the behavior: `tests/test_issue3928_models_budget_fallback.py:185` covers prefixed-default dedup, line 217 protects distinct vendor namespaces, and line 239 ensures an overlapping sibling group cannot suppress injection into an active named custom group. I also checked the agent-side catalog semantics in `hermes_cli/models.py`; provider selection and slash-bearing model IDs remain distinct there, so this WebUI-only identity helper is at the correct layer.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

No further runtime change is needed. Keeping `_provider_model_identity` local to the static fallback is preferable to reusing the broader resolver normalization, because this path must remain network-free and must not reinterpret an internal vendor namespace as a provider switch.

## Verification

The focused CI run should include the full `tests/test_issue3928_models_budget_fallback.py` file and the existing resolver suite in `tests/test_model_resolver.py`. The three new identity tests should be retained together; each guards a different failure mode. I did not execute code from the contributor worktree, per the read-only review policy.

payload.author: qxxaa
payload.title: fix(docker): use editable install for hermes-agent in docker_init.bash

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
The follow-up closes the marker-present / missing-directory case when an Agent source mount exists, but the new fast-path predicate regresses the script's supported source-unavailable mode.

At current HEAD, the decision is:

```bash
if [ -f /app/venv/.deps_installed ] && [ -d /tmp/hermes-agent-build ]; then
  # fast restart
else
  uv pip install -r requirements.txt ...
  ...
  if [ -n "$_agent_src" ]; then
    # create /tmp/hermes-agent-build
  else
    # explicitly supported: start with reduced functionality
  fi
  touch /app/venv/.deps_installed
fi
```

When neither Agent source path is mounted, the first boot deliberately takes the warning/reduced-functionality branch and writes `.deps_installed`, but it never creates `/tmp/hermes-agent-build`. Every later restart therefore fails the new `&& [ -d ... ]` guard, reinstalls all WebUI dependencies, upgrades pip/setuptools, warns, and writes the same marker again. This removes the documented fast-restart behavior for the source-unavailable configuration and makes every restart depend on package-network availability; an offline restart that previously reused the venv can now fail before `server.py`.

Please make the fast-path state-aware rather than requiring the staged directory unconditionally. It needs to distinguish at least:

1. dependency marker + no editable Agent installation expected: reuse the venv without requiring a staged source;
2. editable Agent installation expected: require a valid staged import target, and repair it when missing or incomplete;
3. Agent source newly appears after a prior reduced-functionality boot: run the editable-install path once.

A durable sentinel recording whether an editable Agent target was installed, or staging the target beside persistent venv state with equivalent mode tracking, would avoid conflating these states. Checking only that the `/tmp/hermes-agent-build` directory exists is also weaker than validating the import target inside it.

Please add regressions for both sides of the predicate: marker present + source unavailable + no staged directory must take the fast path, while marker present + editable install expected + target missing/invalid must take the repair path. Keep the existing first-boot and target-missing coverage.

I verified this by tracing the current-head branches and the explicit `source not found` fallback in `docker_init.bash`. I did not execute PR code: the mandatory threat scan returned `SUSPICIOUS` for the added `.pth` references, so policy required a static-only review. That scan verdict is not itself a defect in the PR.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Re-gate at exact head `7a9cab57903c30f941a00b4bd9006fc6d9f50c55`: the new predicate fixes the narrow **marker + source currently unavailable + no staged directory** case, but it still conflates current mount presence with the mode recorded in the persistent venv.

The remaining deterministic failure is:

1. Boot with Agent source mounted. The script stages `/tmp/hermes-agent-build`, performs `uv pip install -e`, and writes `/app/venv/.deps_installed`. The venv now contains a `.pth` link to the staged path.
2. Later restart with the source mount unavailable and `/tmp/hermes-agent-build` missing or incomplete (container/tmpfs recreation, cleanup, or partial stage loss).
3. `_has_agent_src=false`, so the new guard at `docker_init.bash:403` takes the fast path **without validating the editable import target**:

```bash
[ -f /app/venv/.deps_installed ] && {
  [ "$_has_agent_src" != true ] || [ -d /tmp/hermes-agent-build ]
}
```

The stale editable `.pth` remains in the reused persistent venv, but its import target is gone. The server can then start with broken Agent imports. A merely existing directory is also insufficient: an empty/partial `/tmp/hermes-agent-build` passes the same guard.

This is why the prior fix-spec asked for durable installed-mode state rather than inferring it only from the mount visible on the current boot. The patch also weakens the test to a source-string check; it does not execute any of the required state transitions.

## Required rework

- Persist whether the venv contains an editable Agent installation, or inspect the installed editable metadata/`.pth` target directly.
- Fast-path only when one of these is true:
  1. the venv is durably known to be reduced-functionality/non-editable; or
  2. the editable target is valid (not just a directory: require the expected `pyproject.toml` and import package/module).
- If Agent source newly appears after reduced mode, install/stage it once. If Agent source disappears after editable mode and the staged target is missing/invalid, fail clearly or repair from an available durable source; do not silently reuse a dangling editable install.
- Add behavioral shell-state tests for: reduced boot → reduced restart; reduced boot → source appears; editable boot → stage missing; editable boot → stage incomplete; and editable boot → source disappears + stage missing.

The Layer-1 scan remains SUSPICIOUS on benign `.pth` prose, so policy required a static-only re-gate. I did not execute the script or its tests, and the scan verdict is not itself a defect.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Maintainer exact-head re-gate

Rebased mechanically onto current `origin/master` with contributor authorship preserved. The contributor's net diff stayed byte-identical across the rebase; the only maintainer follow-up corrects stale wording in the test oracle.

### Root cause and chosen contract

Hermes Agent intentionally rejects wheel/sdist builds. The previous Docker bootstrap still attempted a normal project install, so Agent's `bdist_wheel` guard aborted multi-container startup. The final design uses Agent's supported editable-install contract from a writable staged source and keeps that source beside the WebUI venv/marker so the editable finder cannot outlive its target.

Independent packaging reproduction against Hermes Agent commit `46539eda28859106d7b28f42ad470d2fae7e3eaf` confirmed:

- normal install reaches the intentional wheel/sdist guard;
- editable install succeeds;
- the generated editable finder maps `agent`, `hermes_cli`, `tools`, and the rest of the runtime packages to the staged source;
- deleting that target makes `import agent` fail, proving the target lifetime requirement.

### Exact-head evidence

Proposed head: `32581913ba1660daa4fb170a825a20cd92cf3f85`
Base: `320789ae596a3963d726d90f6c7f3bc86f7f2d6d`

- Threat scan: CLEAN, score 0, on the exact live PR head.
- Focused Docker/bootstrap tests: 26 passed in 21.32s inside the no-network/no-secrets sandbox.
- Shell syntax/config checks: `bash -n docker_init.bash` passed; exact-head Compose config validation passed in GitHub CI.
- Full current sharded suite: all 15 exact-head GitHub shards passed across Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13.
- Codex independent static review: `VERDICT: SAFE TO SHIP`.
- Opus independent static review: `SHIP`; its footprint/invariant/restart-smoke suggestions are follow-up hardening, not regressions in this PR.
- GitHub required checks: 24/24 successful.
- Real Docker matrix: image build, Compose validation, and single/two/three-container smoke all passed on this head.

Local Docker daemon evidence is intentionally not claimed: this host has no `docker` binary. Runtime Docker proof comes from the exact-head GitHub matrix.

### Disposition

Gate-clean. Approving exact head `32581913ba1660daa4fb170a825a20cd92cf3f85` and moving it to the maintainer merge queue. This review/handoff pass does not merge, tag, or release it.

Thanks @qxxaa for iterating through both lifecycle review rounds.

payload.body:
Greptile Summary

 This PR fixes container startup failures caused by the upstream hermes-agent `setup.py` build guard that blocks `bdist_wheel` outside Nix builds. It replaces the standard `uv pip install` with `uv pip install -e` (editable), moves the staged source tree from `/tmp/` to `/app/` for persistence across restarts, and removes the post-install cleanup that would have dangled the `.pth` link. - **`docker_init.bash`**: Adds the `-e` flag to the install command, changes `_stage_src` from `/tmp/hermes-agent-build` to `/app/hermes-agent-src` (persistent alongside the venv), and drops the `rm -rf "$_stage_src"` that previously cleaned up the staged tree after install. - **`tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py`**: Adds three new text-based regression tests verifying the editable flag, the persistent `/app/` staging path, and that the staged source is not removed after install.

Confidence Score: 5/5

 Safe to merge — the one-line install flag change is tightly scoped, the staging path move to /app/ is consistent with the editable install's lifetime requirements, and the three new regression tests lock in all three invariants. The fix is mechanically correct: editable installs invoke build_editable rather than bdist_wheel, bypassing the Nix guard. Moving the staged source to /app/ keeps the .pth link valid across container restarts, and dropping the post-install rm -rf prevents dangling imports. The added tests verify each property directly against the script text, mirroring the project's existing test style for this file. No files require special attention.

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | docker_init.bash | Adds -e for editable install, moves staging path to /app/hermes-agent-src, removes post-install rm -rf; all three changes are consistent and well-motivated. | | tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py | Adds three text-pattern regression tests covering editable flag, persistent staging path, and no post-install source deletion; test logic is correct and edge cases are handled. |

Sequence Diagram

 ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant D as docker_init.bash participant FS as /app/hermes-agent-src participant UV as uv pip participant PTH as site-packages (.pth) participant PY as Python runtime D->>FS: rm -rf (clear stale staged copy) D->>FS: rsync / cp -a (stage fresh source) D->>FS: chmod -R u+w (ensure writable) D->>UV: uv pip install -e /app/hermes-agent-src[all] UV->>FS: build_editable (writes .egg-info in staged tree) UV->>PTH: write .pth pointing to /app/hermes-agent-src D->>D: touch /app/venv/.deps_installed note over D,PTH: Container restart (fast path) D-->>D: .deps_installed exists skip install block PTH->>FS: .pth still valid (source persists in /app/) FS->>PY: imports resolve at runtime ```

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete `docker_init.bash` at PR HEAD and on `origin/master`, plus the existing read-only-mount regressions, the two-line patch addresses the compatibility break correctly. The follow-up commit fixes the initial revision[0ms dangling editable target by retaining the staged source. The remaining gap is that the WebUI tests and comments still describe that directory as disposable build output, while it is now runtime state.

## Code reference

The source lifecycle begins at `docker_init.bash:448-450`:

```bash
_stage_src="/tmp/hermes-agent-build"
rm -rf "$_stage_src"
mkdir -p "$_stage_src"
```

At `docker_init.bash:467-470`, the PR changes the installer to editable mode and removes the cleanup that followed it. Both changes are necessary together because the editable installation records the staged source as an import target.

The current source-level coverage does not pin that new invariant. `tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py:158-165` still says the flow stages, installs, and then cleans up; `tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py:172-208` only proves that installation uses `_stage_src`; and `tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py:267-302` only proves the copy is writable before installation.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Keep the implementation shape, but update the contract around it before merge. The comments at `docker_init.bash:428-447` should call this a retained editable source rather than a temporary build directory. They should also avoid saying it is rebuilt on every container start, because the enclosing `.deps_installed` fast path at `docker_init.bash:407-484` skips the whole block on reuse.

Add a focused regression that requires editable installation and forbids removal of `_stage_src` after that point. Without such a test, a future cleanup refactor can restore the exact startup-success/runtime-import failure that the second commit fixes while all present structural tests remain green.

1. Extend `tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py` to assert editable installation and retained staged-source ordering.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I re-read the complete `docker_init.bash` and `tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py` at head `ff399ba2846ba5d03ac48e04aecbca71509f8b9f`, compared both with `origin/master`, and checked the two multi-container compose definitions. The follow-up correctly pins editable installation and prevents immediate deletion of its source target. One lifecycle gap remains: the dependency marker can survive while the editable source target does not, and the fast path never validates that target before starting the server.

## Code reference

The comments at `docker_init.bash:440-447` expose the conflicting lifecycle assumptions:

```bash
# supported. The staged copy is rebuilt on every container start (the agent
# source can change across volume re-init); cost is one rsync of ~10MB of
# Python source. The `.deps_installed` fast path skips this entire block on
# reuse, so the retained copy from the previous start serves imports until
# the next full rebuild.
```

`docker_init.bash:397-400` makes the dependency marker authoritative and skips the whole install branch when it exists. The editable target is created later inside that skipped branch at `docker_init.bash:456-476`, under temporary storage. Therefore it is not rebuilt on every start.

The new test at `tests/test_docker_docs_and_readonly.py:344-373` proves only that no source deletion text appears after the install line. It does not cover a restart where the marker exists but the editable target is absent.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

This is more than comment wording. An editable install resolves imports through the staged directory. If temporary storage is cleared independently, such as with a tmpfs-backed temporary directory or an external cleanup, a later restart sees the dependency marker, skips staging, and starts with a dangling editable link.

Please give the source target the same lifetime as the marker, preferably by staging under the application directory, or make the fast-path condition require both the marker and a valid staged source tree. If the second option is used, a missing target should force the existing staging and editable-install block to run again before server startup. Then rewrite the comments to describe the actual chosen lifecycle.

## Verification plan

Add a regression for the marker-present, target-missing state and assert that startup selects the repair path rather than the skip path. The Docker smoke should cover first boot, a normal fast restart, and a restart after removing only the staged target; the final case must restore imports before launching the server. I did not execute code from this PR worktree. The current CI rollup is green, but its structural tests do not exercise this lifetime split.

payload.author: qxxaa
payload.body:
The fast-path guard is now state-aware - it scans for mounted agent source and only requires the staged directory when an editable install was actually performed. Three states handled cleanly:

1. **Marker + no agent source**: fast path fires, no staged dir needed (reduced-functionality mode preserved)
2. **Marker + agent source + staged dir present**: fast path fires normally
3. **Marker + agent source + staged dir missing**: falls through to re-stage and re-install

This avoids introducing a sentinel file - the guard derives intent from the runtime environment rather than tracking installation history. Test updated to match.

payload.author: qxxaa
payload.body:
Taking a different approach that eliminates the entire class of concern at the root.

The prior commits tried to handle the `/tmp` lifetime mismatch with guards and validation. The real problem is simpler: an editable install's `.pth` target shouldn't live on ephemeral storage in the first place. Moving the staged source from `/tmp/hermes-agent-build` to `/app/hermes-agent-src` gives it the same lifecycle as the venv and `.deps_installed` marker - all three survive restarts, all three are lost on container recreation. No sentinel files, no state machine, no validation of partial targets.

I'll note that several of the scenarios raised (agent source disappearing after being mounted, partial stage loss, external `/tmp` cleanup) don't occur in any documented deployment mode - the compose files either mount the source or don't, and that doesn't change between restarts. Building compensating state machines for scenarios that require active user misconfiguration mid-deployment adds complexity without protecting real users. The persistent path approach sidesteps these theoretical states entirely rather than handling them one by one.

Force-pushed a clean single commit against upstream HEAD. The state transitions collapse into lifecycle equivalence:

| Scenario | Outcome |
|---|---|
| First boot (with or without agent source) | Stages + installs or warns, writes `.deps_installed` |
| Restart (same container) | `.deps_installed` + staged source both present - fast path |
| Recreation (new container) | Both gone - fresh boot, re-stages automatically |
| Source newly appears after reduced boot | `.deps_installed` absent for agent path - full install runs |
| Source disappears after editable boot | Staged copy persists independently - no dangling link |

payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full regression test, the `static/messages.js:5995-6008` settlement hunk, and the surrounding deferred-row machinery in `static/ui.js`, the in-place collapse removes the second transcript rebuild as intended. There is one state-preservation regression: it discards expanded/collapsed state for nested Worklog details when it removes the rendered rows.

## Code reference

`static/ui.js:13527-13565` stores the scene rows and then clears the list on the next frame, but it never captures the detail-disclosure map from those live DOM rows. The lazy materializer at `static/ui.js:11910-11921` explicitly expects that map:

```js
const disclosure=group._deferredWorklogDisclosure;
group._deferredWorklogDisclosure=null;
if(!rows||!rows.length) return false;
const ok=_renderAnchorSceneRowsIntoWorklog(group,rows,{settled:true});
if(!ok) return false;
```

The old second `renderMessages` pass preserved this contract. `renderMessages` captures the current detail state before rebuilding, restores it after rebuilding, and at `static/ui.js:16880-16889` stashes that map on every still-deferred group so `_materializeDeferredWorklogRows` can reapply it after expansion. The new successful `_collapsedInPlace` branch in `static/messages.js:5998-6008` bypasses that path entirely.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Before `list.replaceChildren()` can destroy the rendered detail elements, `_collapseJustSettledWorklogInPlace` should capture their state and assign it to `group._deferredWorklogDisclosure`. A minimal shape is to call `_captureWorklogDetailDisclosureState(group)` before scheduling row removal, then retain the returned non-empty map beside `_deferredWorklogRows`. This keeps the no-rebuild behavior while preserving the existing #5839 contract.

Without that, a user can have an individual tool detail open in the live Worklog, let the turn settle, collapse the Worklog, and find that detail closed when reopening it. payload.body:
Thanks @franksong2702 — the flicker-seam fix itself is sound (in-place collapse of the one settled Worklog instead of a second whole-transcript rebuild, with #5839 deferred-row recovery intact), and CI is green. But an adversarial re-gate on the exact head (`ca1e2d585f0a`) reproduced one real regression that the suite doesn't cover:

**The in-place collapse ignores the "Open Worklog details automatically" preference at settlement.**

`static/ui.js:13563` — the keep-open guard is:
```js
if(!(savedDisclosure==='open'||(errored&&savedDisclosure!=='closed'))){
  // ...collapse the settled Worklog in place...
}
```

With **"Open Worklog details automatically" enabled** and **no per-turn disclosure override** (`savedDisclosure` is neither `'open'` nor `'closed'`), the guard is false → the settled Worklog is force-collapsed: `collapsed=true`, `open` removed, `aria-expanded=false`. The previous full-render path honored that preference through `ensureActivityGroup()` (line ~13765), and `_worklogDetailsExpandedDefault()` (defined at 10856, consumed at 11007 / 17774 / 19288) is exactly the signal the render paths use. Your new helper is the one spot that drops it.

Net: a user who set "expand Worklog details by default" now sees the Worklog **collapse the moment the turn settles** — the flicker fix trades one settlement-seam annoyance for a preference violation.

**Fix (Codex-precise):**
`static/ui.js:13563` — include `_worklogDetailsExpandedDefault()` in the keep-open condition when `savedDisclosure !== 'closed'`, preserving the existing saved-open and errored-turn rules and an explicit per-turn `'closed'`:
```js
const keepOpen =
  savedDisclosure==='open'
  || (errored && savedDisclosure!=='closed')
  || (_worklogDetailsExpandedDefault() && savedDisclosure!=='closed');
if(!keepOpen){ /* ...collapse... */ }
```
Then add a regression asserting that with `window._worklogDetailsExpandedByDefault=true` and no per-turn override, the settled Worklog stays open (`open` present, `aria-expanded="true"`, rows NOT deferred), while an explicit per-turn `'closed'` still collapses.

Everything else looks good — this is the only blocker. Ping me when it's re-pushed and I'll re-gate on the fresh head.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
The base-refresh reconciliation fixes the six CI failures, but the 150 ms programmatic-scroll ownership contract still has one cross-file writer gap.

`static/sessions.js`, in `_loadOlderMessages()`'s `!restoredViaAnchor` fallback, sets `_programmaticScroll = true` and writes `container.scrollTop` without refreshing `_programmaticScrollSetAt`. That fallback can inherit the timestamp taken before `renderMessages({ preserveScroll: true })`; if the render takes more than 150 ms, the new `_freshProgrammaticScrollActive()` treats the fallback write as stale and clears the latch. The resulting native scroll event can therefore be misclassified as reader input.

I reproduced this on exact head `67279ae35c8e8f0b2628d6db2101d80f05384e45` through the mandatory sandbox, exercising the real `_loadOlderMessages()` fallback and production freshness helper with 200 ms of render work: the fallback wrote `scrollTop = 300`, but the latch age was 200 ms and `_freshProgrammaticScrollActive()` returned false. The contributor scroll slice otherwise passed 13/13.

Required fix:

1. In `static/sessions.js`, stamp `_programmaticScrollSetAt = performance.now()` on the same ownership edge as `_programmaticScroll = true`, immediately before the fallback `scrollTop` write.
2. Add a behavioral regression that runs the real fallback after render work exceeding 150 ms, proves the latch is fresh for that write, and proves it expires only 150 ms after the write. Please include a cross-file writer assertion or equivalent coverage so `ui.js` and `sessions.js` cannot drift independently.

Threat scan: CLEAN. No bare PR code was executed; all targeted tests and the diagnostic ran through the networkless/masked-home sandbox.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full new regression test plus the scroll-intent and native-scroll paths in `static/ui.js`, the capture-phase approach is the right layer for #6414: it records the real wheel input before the guarded `scroll` listener can return. One edge in the guard definition should be tightened before merge. The new branch treats any truthy `_programmaticScroll` as active, while the existing listener treats that latch as stale after 150 ms.

## Code reference

The new decision at `static/ui.js:5780-5794` computes `guardedWheelUp` from `wheelUp && _programmaticScroll` alone. By contrast, the native listener at `static/ui.js:6029-6032` already has stale-latch recovery:

```js
if(_programmaticScroll&&(performance.now()-_programmaticScrollSetAt)>150) _programmaticScroll=false;
if(_programmaticScroll) return;
_markMessageVirtualScrollActive();
cancelAnimationFrame(_scrollRaf);
```

This distinction matters because the document capture listener runs first. If an 80 ms clear timer is delayed by a busy main thread or input-task priority, a wheel event can observe `_programmaticScroll === true` after the 150 ms validity window. A small `deltaY=-5` gesture is then promoted to sticky unpin even though the ordinary path deliberately requires `deltaY < -30`.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Make `guardedWheelUp` use the same freshness contract as the scroll listener, ideally through one helper used by both call sites. At minimum, clear or reject the latch when `performance.now() - _programmaticScrollSetAt > 150` before applying the small-delta exception. That keeps the fix scoped to the timing gap described in #6414 rather than broadening low-delta unpin whenever a stale boolean survives.

The state is already timestamped at the programmatic writers (`static/ui.js:6713-6733` and `static/ui.js:6873-6878` on origin/master), so this does not need another timer or new state.

## Test plan

`tests/test_issue6414_programmatic_scroll_user_intent.py:29-80` covers only a truthy latch and does not define `_programmaticScrollSetAt`. Add two cases with an explicit timestamp: a fresh guarded wheel must unpin and block `scrollIfPinned`, while a stale guarded wheel with `deltaY=-5` must keep the ordinary threshold behavior. The existing fresh case should also assert that `_cancelBottomSettle` ran, since canceling late follow writers is part of the fix.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Review finding

The aggregate job and exit-code propagation are now sound, but two deterministic evidence gaps remain at exact head `a3b3a0ccacb5`.

### 1. The new Worklog negative canary can still false-green an unrelated exception

`tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:1113-1125` catches **every** exception from `_expand_settled_worklog()` and rewrites it to:

```text
NEGATIVE CANARY EXPECTED UNMARKED FAILURE: Worklog expansion failed after the reloaded Anchor group was present
```

The selector wait at lines 1095-1112 proves that a group existed earlier, but it does not prove that the exception caught at line 1118 is the deliberate `force_failure` exception. A page closure, route-specific timeout, group disappearance, or another Playwright error between those operations gets the same required marker. `.github/workflows/conversation-lifecycle.yml:127-155,173-178` then accepts nonzero + that marker + no mutation marker, so the negative canary can pass for the wrong reason.

This is the same arbitrary-failure masking class the canary is intended to rule out. The current green CI run does not distinguish it.

**Required fix:** give the injected Worklog failure a unique sentinel and translate only an exception proven to contain that exact sentinel. Re-raise every other exception unchanged. Check page errors/server liveness at that boundary, and add a discriminating case where the group disappears or the operation times out after the initial selector check; that case must not emit the required negative-canary marker.

### 2. Mutation artifacts are shared and can come from the wrong case

All four invocations use the same `LIFECYCLE_ARTIFACT_DIR` (`.github/workflows/conversation-lifecycle.yml:96-178`). Expected failures overwrite the fixed `failure.png` and `snapshot.json` names in `tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:1202-1219`. If a later canary unexpectedly exits 0, it writes no new failure snapshot, the step fails, and the upload can contain an earlier canary's screenshot/snapshot under the later failure.

## Re-gate at `612e50a90aaa`

The per-case artifact isolation is fixed, and the latest commit now routes the timeout discriminator past the persistence mutation. One deterministic blocker remains: the intended Worklog sentinel poisons the browser-error list that is supposed to validate it.

### Reproduced failure

At `tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:466`, every page error is appended to `errors`. `_expand_settled_worklog()` deliberately throws `FORCED_WORKLOG_EXPANSION_FAILURE` in page JavaScript, so Playwright records that exact expected sentinel as a `pageerror`. The catch at lines 1143-1160 then recognizes the sentinel in `exc`, but immediately rejects the run because `errors` contains the same injected page error:

```python
if errors:
    raise AssertionError(
        "unexpected browser errors before expected unmarked "
        f"Worklog failure: {errors!r}"
    ) from exc
```

I ran the exact current-head case only through the required no-network sandbox gate:

```text
LIFECYCLE_TEST_BITE=drop-anchor-persistence
LIFECYCLE_NEGATIVE_BITE=throw-reloaded-worklog-expand
python tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py
```

It exited 1 with:

```text
CONVERSATION LIFECYCLE GATE FAILED: unexpected browser errors before expected unmarked Worklog failure: [..., ('pageerror', 'hermes lifecycle negative canary: forced Worklog expansion failure')]
```

It did **not** emit the workflow-required marker:

```text
NEGATIVE CANARY EXPECTED UNMARKED FAILURE: Worklog expansion failed after the reloaded Anchor group was present
```

Therefore `run_unexpected_failure_without_marker` rejects the intended case and the mutation-canary job cannot pass for the reason it specifies.

### Required fix

Inject the reviewer-controlled failure outside page-error capture, preferably as a dedicated Python exception after the settled-group precondition. If the page-context throw is retained, remove exactly the one expected sentinel page-error entry before the unrelated-error check, require that it occurred exactly once, and reject every residual console/page error. Continue translating only the exact sentinel exception; re-raise all other exceptions unchanged.

Then rerun both Worklog rows and prove:

1. `throw-reloaded-worklog-expand` emits the required negative-canary marker and no mutation marker.
2. `timeout-reloaded-worklog-expand` preserves its unrelated marker and emits neither classification marker.

## Deep re-gate: changes requested at `9003956b9976`

The prior Worklog sentinel problem is fixed, and the concrete Playwright timeout check is now narrow enough. The new crash canaries still do not certify the classifier health guards they are meant to protect.

### Blocking finding

All four new crash modes bypass `_assert_canary_health()` and emit their discriminator directly from the exception handler:

- `tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:1159-1164` translates any exception for `close-reload-final-text` and `server-death-reload-final-text` before the Playwright-timeout and health checks at lines 1165-1177.
- `tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:1197-1202` does the same for `close-reloaded-anchor-group` and `server-death-reloaded-anchor-group`, before the classifier path at lines 1203-1225.

That means deleting or breaking the page-closed, browser-error, or server-dead checks in `_assert_canary_health()` leaves all four crash rows green. The rows prove only their bespoke `NEGATIVE_BITE -> discriminator` branches. They do not prove that the ordinary final-text and missing-Anchor classifiers reject crash false greens. For a PR whose deliverable is the proof workflow, this is an objective regression-net defect.

I ran 13 exact-head driver invocations through `warmup-safe-test.sh`. Layer 1 was CLEAN and every run entered the no-network sandbox. All four crash modes emitted their expected discriminator, and the real Playwright timeout paths reached `_assert_canary_health()`. The normal control could not complete because the sandbox correctly surfaced no-egress `ERR_INTERNET_DISCONNECTED` console events, so I am not using those runs as a clean-path or flake-rate claim.

### Required fix

Separate fault injection from classifier selection. Drive page-close/server-death through the same ordinary final-text, missing-Anchor, and Worklog classifier paths. Those paths must first reject the crash via `_assert_canary_health()` or an equivalent shared guard. Only an outer verifier should translate the exact rejected crash plus proved state (`page.is_closed()` or `proc.poll() is not None`) into the stable discriminator marker.

A counterfactual removal of each health guard must make its corresponding crash row fail. Also make each crash-row shell check reject every known positive and negative classification marker, not only its row-local pair.

No runtime or visual concern is involved. This is a narrow test-infrastructure rework request; the prior Worklog injection fix, timeout recognition, artifact isolation, marker parity, and aggregate status propagation can remain unchanged.

## Re-gate at `35d65adede7b`

The follow-up routes the four crash modes through `_assert_canary_health()` and broadens the shell-side forbidden-marker check. Those are real improvements, but the explicit guard-knockout acceptance condition from the prior review still fails.

### Remaining blocker

`_raise_rejected_crash_discriminator()` catches any `AssertionError` from `_assert_canary_health()` and then authorizes the crash discriminator from independent live state:

```python
except AssertionError as health_error:
    if bite.startswith("close-") and page is not None and page.is_closed():
        raise AssertionError(DISCRIMINATOR_FAILURE_MARKERS[bite]) from health_error
    if bite.startswith("server-death-") and proc is not None and proc.poll() is not None:
        raise AssertionError(DISCRIMINATOR_FAILURE_MARKERS[bite]) from health_error
```

The caught assertion is not proved to be the corresponding health rejection. If the page-closed branch is removed, another health assertion such as captured browser errors can enter this catch, after which `page.is_closed()` still emits the required discriminator. The server-death rows have the same provenance gap. The row therefore proves that *some* health assertion fired while the injected state exists, not that the exact shared guard rejected that state.

I ran the exact-head control and counterfactual only through `warmup-safe-test.sh` (threat scan CLEAN; no-network sandbox entered). The four current crash rows emitted their expected discriminators and no classification markers. I then removed each unique corresponding guard branch in temporary reviewer copies. All four rows still emitted their required crash discriminator:

- page-close guard removed: final-text page-close and Anchor-group page-close both survived
- server-exit guard removed: final-text server-death and Anchor-group server-death both survived

That is the exact false-green condition the prior review required these rows to catch.

### Required fix

1. Make `_assert_canary_health()` return a typed or reason-coded rejection, for example `page-closed`, `browser-errors`, or `server-exited`, rather than indistinguishable generic assertions.
2. Translate to `DISCRIMINATOR_FAILURE_MARKERS[bite]` only when the rejection kind exactly matches the bite *and* the corresponding state is independently present. Re-raise every mismatched rejection.
3. Add executable guard-knockout coverage for all four rows. Removing the page-close guard must make both `close-*` rows fail without their required marker; removing the server-exit guard must do the same for both `server-death-*` rows. Include a competing-browser-error case so a different health rejection cannot authorize the discriminator.

Please keep the improvements already present: the ordinary operation/catch routing, all-classification-marker rejection loop, typed Worklog injection, concrete Playwright timeout check, per-case artifacts, post-fulfillment mutation-event recording, and aggregate status propagation.

No full suite was run. This focused re-gate used the exact PR head and sandboxed lifecycle probes only.

## Re-gate at exact head `2d8b34ff` (release-manager pass) — one blocker on the PR's own proof

I picked this up as a low-risk Phase-1 ship, approved+updated the branch, and let the full CI matrix run on the up-to-date head. The **10 required checks are all green** (browser-smoke + the 9 `test` shards), and the 3 real lifecycle-proof jobs — `live-to-final` for `normal`, `terminal-error`, and `historical-transcript-hydration` — **all pass**. 

But the PR's own **`Lifecycle mutation canaries`** job **fails** (and `Lifecycle proof summary` inherits that failure):

```
##[error] anchor-group-page-close failed without required marker:
          NEGATIVE CANARY DISCRIMINATOR: page closed before reloaded Anchor-group classification
```

The `anchor-group-page-close` negative canary is invoked via `run_unexpected_failure_rejects_marker`, so the harness requires it to fail **and** emit the discriminator line `NEGATIVE CANARY DISCRIMINATOR: page closed before reloaded Anchor-group classification`. On this run it failed **without** emitting that marker, tripping `Wrong negative failure`. So the negative canary is failing at an earlier point than its discriminator is designed to catch — the discriminator isn't being reached/emitted on the CI browser timing.

Why this blocks: the entire point of this PR is to make the lifecycle proof's failures **reliable and visible**. A proof whose own mutation-canary discriminator doesn't fire deterministically isn't yet delivering that. Note the **same** "Conversation lifecycle (informational)" workflow passes cleanly on other branches (#6573, #7188) right now — so this is specific to this PR's canary rework, not a general environmental flake.

Make the `anchor-group-page-close` negative canary emit its `NEGATIVE CANARY DISCRIMINATOR: page closed before reloaded Anchor-group classification` marker deterministically before the run aborts (or classify the earlier abort so `run_unexpected_failure_rejects_marker` accepts it), then confirm the `Lifecycle mutation canaries` + `Lifecycle proof summary` jobs go green on your own PR run. payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the complete workflow and browser gate at PR HEAD, the aggregate job and scenario-specific marker check fix most of the masking problem. One broad exception-classification path still lets an unrelated hard-reload regression satisfy the `drop-anchor-persistence` canary. The mutation only suppresses Anchor-scene persistence; it does not remove the persisted final assistant text. A failure to reload that final text must remain an ordinary failure.

## Code reference

At `tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:1020-1040`, the first post-reload prerequisite is wrapped as an expected mutation failure:

```python
except Exception as exc:
    if TEST_BITE == "drop-anchor-persistence":
        _raise_expected_mutation_failure(
            EXPECTED_MUTATION_FAILURE_MARKERS["drop-anchor-persistence"],
            errors=errors,
            proc=proc,
            cause=exc,
```

The same classification is applied around `_expand_settled_worklog` immediately afterward (`tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:1041-1053`). `_raise_expected_mutation_failure` only rules out recorded console/page errors and a dead WebUI process (`tests/browser_conversation_lifecycle.py:681-702`). It does not establish that the missing Anchor scene caused the exception.

The workflow then accepts any nonzero run whose log contains that marker at `.github/workflows/conversation-lifecycle.yml:98-119`. As a result, a regression that loses `FINAL_TEXT` on hard reload, a Playwright timeout with a still-live process, or an unrelated Worklog expansion failure can emit the expected marker and make the mutation-canary job green. This is the exact arbitrary-failure masking class the second commit is trying to prevent.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Keep prerequisites outside the mutation classification. The final-text wait should run normally and fail normally. After it succeeds, inspect the specific mutated boundary: whether a settled Anchor group exists after reload. If no group exists, emit the expected marker. If a group exists, run `_expand_settled_worklog` normally; an expansion exception should not be reclassified. If rows materialize, report `Mutation survived` as the code already does.

That makes the marker evidence of the intended missing-persistence condition, not merely evidence that some later browser operation threw.

## Test plan

Add a negative canary-classification check alongside the existing two expected failures: force the hard-reload final-text prerequisite to fail while leaving the process and page-error list clean, and verify that the log does not contain the expected mutation marker. A second check should force Worklog expansion to throw after a group is present and require the wrapper to reject it as an unexpected failure.

## Review finding

The new browser row does not yet prove its stated strict ID-linked result ownership.

`tests/browser_historical_transcript_hydration.py::_historical_messages()` intentionally declares `terminal` then `read_file` while storing the two tool results in reverse order. That is a useful discriminator. However, `_assert_hydrated()` only checks the rendered tool names/order, row count, idle state, and final-answer uniqueness. It never checks either row's expected result text or `tool_call_id`. `_semantic_snapshot()` then compares the initial render with the reload, so a stable but cross-wired mapping would pass both phases.

Concretely, the test would still green if the `terminal` row consistently displayed `README historical contents` and the `read_file` row consistently displayed `/isolated/workspace`. The existing source-extraction unit test catches that mapping, but the new real-browser integration row does not, so it cannot establish the integration guarantee claimed by this PR.

## Required fix

In `_assert_hydrated()`, preserve the reverse-order fixture and assert the expected ownership in both directions:

- the `terminal` row contains `/isolated/workspace` and does not contain `README historical contents`;
- the `read_file` row contains `README historical contents` and does not contain `/isolated/workspace`.

Please also expose the real activity-row IDs in the browser snapshot (or a stable DOM ID attribute) and assert the expected IDs `historical-tool-first`, `historical-tool-second`. Keeping these checks inside `_assert_hydrated()` makes them run before and after the hard reload.

The workflow wiring, isolated credential-free setup, mutation bite, and reload path otherwise look sound. The sandboxed underlying hydration suite passed: `30 passed` in `5.80s`. I did not run the new browser script in this warm-up pass.

The previously reviewed historical-hydration proof remains sound, but commit `b87cd389861d` adds a new runtime path in `static/messages.js` with a stale-owner race.

At `attachLiveStream()`'s application-error settlement, the new `setTimeout(..., 0)` callback checks only that the visible session still has `activeSid`. That is not enough to identify the terminal stream or assistant turn:

- The callback closes over the old stream's `_anchorRegistry` and `streamId`.
- `_attachProjectedAnchorSceneToLastAssistant(S.messages)` resolves the last assistant **when the delayed callback runs**, not the assistant that received the application error.
- It then writes the old scene and old `_anchor_stream_id` onto that current assistant and persists the old `streamId` with the newly selected message ref/index.

A concrete counterexample is: application error for stream A schedules the callback; before that task runs, another already-queued task creates a local-command or replacement assistant in the same session; A's callback passes the SID guard and attaches/persists A's worklog on the newer assistant. Browser task sources do not guarantee that a newly scheduled zero-delay timer runs before every already-queued user or application task. The same callback is also not a deterministic barrier for “all queued EventSource activity drained.”

The enforced sandbox gate was CLEAN. Existing focused coverage passed: 30 historical-hydration tests, 6 Anchor-settlement tests, 5 terminal-error-preservation tests, and 3 tool-limit tests. Those tests verify the prior ownership work and the synchronous application-error attachment, but none retains this new callback and invokes it after a same-session assistant replacement.

### Required fix

Fence the retry to the exact terminal owner and target, not only the session:

1. Capture the exact assistant object/ref (after the synchronous settlement and any `d.session` carry-forward) that the retry is allowed to update.
2. Before the delayed retry, require that this captured target is still the intended terminal assistant and that the old registry/stream generation still owns the retry. Do not re-resolve an unconstrained “last assistant” from current `S.messages`.
3. Keep the retry idempotent. Avoid a second persistence POST when the projected scene is unchanged.
4. Add a production-composed fake-timer regression that retains callback A, appends/installs assistant B under the same SID, invokes A, and proves B's scene, stream ID, and persistence calls remain untouched. Keep positive controls for a genuine late Anchor row on A and for switching to a different SID.

This is limited to the new eight-line runtime follow-up. The original strict tool/result ownership assertions and reload proof do not need to be weakened or removed.

## The delayed retry still has a same-index wrong-owner path

The exact-object and registry-generation fences in `e4aab86b8c58` close most of the earlier race, but the new refresh exception uses `_messageIdentityKey()` as ownership authority. That helper is not unique: it is only `role | optional timestamp | first 160 content characters`.

A deterministic remaining schedule is:

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks @starship-s — the re-push is close and the helper itself is solid (strict shape validation: `role==='assistant'`, non-empty `tool_calls`, every call with a non-empty id/call_id **and** name/function.name). Full suite is green (13,898/0) and the focused branching/reattach tests pass. But a Codex regression gate reproduced a real **CORE** data-loss regression against master, so it needs one more pass before ship.

### The defect (CORE — drops a legitimately-repeated user turn)
The helper validates the envelope's *shape* but not its *turn ownership*. When an **older** turn ends with a canonical tool-call envelope + tool result but **no final assistant message**, both walkers (`_currentTailUserMessage` and `_pendingCurrentTailUserMessage`) now `continue` across that older tool tail, reach the older user message, and return it as the "current tail" — suppressing a **newer** optimistic/pending user row with the same text.

Reproduced against `origin/master` (A/B):
- master retained user timestamps **`[1, 10]`**; this branch retained only **`[1]`**.
- `getPendingSessionMessage()` changed from the timestamp-10 row to **`null`**.

This is reachable under default deferred persistence + writable CLI/TUI continuation — i.e. a real session-switch/reattach can silently discard a genuine repeated user turn.

### Fix-spec
Make both scans **candidate-turn-aware** and stop at envelopes/tool rows that predate the candidate turn:
1. `static/sessions.js:3280` — pass the candidate turn's identity/start time into `_currentTailUserMessage`; do **not** `continue` through an older or unowned tool-call envelope.
2. `static/ui.js:10380` — pass `session.pending_started_at` into `_pendingCurrentTailUserMessage` and apply the identical temporal/turn boundary before deduping.
3. Unknown ownership must **fail closed** (don't skip). Add a test with an older no-final-assistant tool-tail + a newer repeated user turn, asserting both timestamps survive (the `[1,10]` case above).

The dedupe intent is right — this is purely about scoping the skip to the current turn so it can't reach back and cannibalize an earlier one. Once both scans are turn-bounded, I'll re-gate.

After `await /api/chat/start`, the continuation writes session A's response into pane-global state without proving that A still owns the visible pane:

actual:   { sid: 'A', streamId: 'A-stream' }

## Re-gate: pending active-turn fallback still crosses tagged activity without authority

Thanks for the substantial response. I re-gated exact head `8bcba8085be7aea9f353291a7eedd78da245a3ee`. Three prior blockers are fixed: stale/background sends no longer reconcile another pane, send routing and transcript state are frozen before effectful awaits, and the regression suite now composes the production send/load/sidebar/generation paths. One deterministic ownership blocker remains.

### Must fix

`static/ui.js::_pendingActiveTurnUserMessage()` checks activity-row identity only inside `if (hasActiveToken)`. When the session has no `active_turn_token`, it crosses `_live`, canonical assistant tool-call, and `role: "tool"` rows even when those rows carry a non-empty `_active_turn_token` from another/unknown turn.

That disagrees with `_pendingCurrentTailUserMessage()`, which correctly rejects the tagged boundary when it cannot establish ownership. `getPendingSessionMessage()` then falls through to `_pendingActiveTurnUserMessage()`, selects a timestamp-matching earlier user row, and `_matchesPending()` / `_adoptExistingRow()` can move the current pending turn's attachments onto that older row.

The exact unsafe branch is around `static/ui.js:10757-10764`: with no session token, a tagged activity row is unconditionally crossed. The fallback then reaches and adopts the older user at `10780-10788` and `10839-10840`.

### Required fix

1. In `_pendingActiveTurnUserMessage()`, normalize the activity row's `_active_turn_token` for every live/tool boundary.
2. If the session has an authoritative token, retain the exact-equality requirement.
3. If the session has no authoritative token but the activity row has any non-empty token, fail closed (`return null`) instead of crossing it. A timestamp fallback may remain only for genuinely tokenless legacy activity, if that compatibility policy is intentional.

## Re-gate: exact turn-token identity is weakened by trimming

Thanks for the follow-up. I re-gated exact head `f95a3e135803f96ad1dd57618676ce3e9f47dd12`. The prior absent-authority/tagged-activity blocker is fixed, and the focused sandboxed slices pass, but the tip introduces one deterministic ownership walkback.

### Must fix

`static/ui.js::_pendingActiveTurnUserMessage()` now trims both the authoritative session token and each activity row's `_active_turn_token` before comparing them. These are opaque identity tokens. Trimming turns byte-distinct identities into a match, while the sibling `_pendingCurrentTailUserMessage()` and `_activeTurnTokenMatches()` still require raw exact equality.

This can make the strict scanner reject a raw-mismatched live/tool boundary while the active-turn fallback crosses it, selects an older user row, and lets `getPendingSessionMessage()` migrate the pending attachment onto that older row. The new “exact” positive fixture encodes the mismatch: the session/user token is `' exact-turn '`, while the activity token is `'exact-turn'`, yet it expects a match.

### Required fix

1. In `static/ui.js::_pendingActiveTurnUserMessage()`, use trimming only to classify a token as blank or nonblank. Compare the original opaque token strings byte-for-byte.
2. Preserve the newly correct rule that a nonempty activity token fails closed when the session has no authoritative token.
3. Change the exact-token positive fixture to use genuinely identical raw values.
4. Add inverse behavior-level cases for live, canonical tool-call, and tool-result boundaries where the activity token is only trim-equal. Both scanners must return `null`; the synthetic pending row must be materialized; the older user's attachments must remain untouched.

### Verification

Threat scan: CLEAN. All PR-code execution used the mandatory no-network/no-home sandbox wrapper. Focused submitted slices passed 9, 4, and 11 selected tests. A sandboxed reviewer characterization through the production helper chain reproduced the raw-token mismatch: the strict scanner returned `null`, the fallback selected the older user, and the pending attachment moved onto that row. The temporary diagnostic was removed and the contributor test file reran clean (9 passed).

This is an exact-head review. Re-gate after a substantive push.

## Summary

The correction is directionally right, but `setup/index.html:365` still describes the missing-Agent path in the wrong order. This PR targets `gh-pages`, so I compared the full PR-head and `origin/gh-pages` versions of `setup/index.html` and read the complete unchanged `install.sh`. The one-liner checks for the Agent before it clones or starts WebUI. If the Agent is absent, the first invocation exits and the user must install the Agent and run the WebUI one-liner again.

## Code reference

The missing-Agent branch ends at `install.sh:64-67`:

```bash
  say "  Agent docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/getting-started/installation"
  say ""
  exit 1
fi
```

Only after that block does the script clone or update the checkout at `install.sh:70-86`, and only then does it hand off to the server launcher at `install.sh:88-96`.

The new sentence at `setup/index.html:365` currently says the one-liner:

> Clones the Web UI ..., checks that Hermes Agent is installed ..., and starts the server ...

That sequence is false for the exact first-time case this PR is trying to explain: no clone occurs before the missing-Agent exit. It also does not tell the user that a second invocation is required.

## Recommendation

Please make the two-run flow explicit and preserve the real order. For example:

```text
Checks for Hermes Agent first. If it is missing, the installer prints the Agent install command and exits. Install the Agent, then run this WebUI command again; it will clone or update WebUI and start the server on 127.0.0.1:8787.
```

I would also tighten `setup/index.html:358` and `setup/index.html:379-382` with the same rerun instruction so all three edited passages agree. The current wording at line 379 says the one-liner points the reader to the Agent installer, but the nearby primary flow should not leave the required second run implicit.

## Verification

No runtime test is needed for this documentation-only diff, but the final copy should be checked against these three observable branches in `install.sh`: Agent missing means print and exit; Agent present with no checkout means clone and start; Agent present with an existing checkout means update and start. That gives the page a direct source-of-truth check rather than only replacing the prior automatic-install claim.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the focused follow-up. The projected-scale clamp and navigation reset are improvements, and the submitted Node test plus the existing focused lightbox tests pass in the sandbox. I found three remaining gesture-lifecycle defects at the current head that need to be fixed before visual review.

## Must fix

1. **A completed mouse pan can close the lightbox, and a lost release can leave a stale drag active.**

   In `_attachImgZoom`, `mousedown` is stopped, but the window-level `mouseup` only clears `mDown`. There is no moved/drag-click suppression. If a press starts on the image and the release lands on the exposed backdrop, the browser can target the resulting `click` at the common ancestor, `.img-lightbox`; its `onclick` immediately calls `_closeImgLightbox(lb)`. Stopping the earlier `mousedown` does not stop that later click. Also, `mousemove` does not check `e.buttons`, so a release outside the window can leave `mDown` live and a later buttonless move can continue the stale drag.

   Please accept only the primary button, track a small movement threshold, cancel the drag when `e.buttons` no longer contains the primary button (and on blur/cancel), and consume only the click generated by the completed drag. The next intentional backdrop click, nav controls, and close button must still work. Pointer Events with pointer capture is also fine if it has equivalent cancellation and cleanup.

2. **A pan or pinch contact can become the first half of a double-tap.**

   `lastTapTime/lastTapX/lastTapY` are recorded on every one-finger `touchstart`, before the code knows that the gesture ended as a tap. Movement does not invalidate the candidate, the two-touch branch does not invalidate it, and there is no `touchcancel` handling. A short moved contact or quick pinch followed within 300 ms and 30 px by one contact can therefore trigger the 2.5x double-tap toggle even though no first tap completed.

   Promote a contact to `lastTap*` only after a one-finger touch ends within time and movement thresholds. Invalidate it on a second touch, movement beyond the threshold, and `touchcancel`; include the new fields in navigation reset.

3. **Pan bounds are stale after viewport/orientation changes.**

   `clampPan()` depends on `window.innerWidth/innerHeight`, but it runs only during zoom/pan. Rotating from landscape to portrait or resizing the viewport can leave the transformed image mostly outside the new viewport until another gesture occurs. Re-clamp or reset on resize/orientation change, store the handler on `lb`, and remove/cancel it in `_closeImgLightbox` alongside the mouse listeners.

## Regression coverage

Please extend the integration-level harness to cover:

- zoom, primary-button drag, release/click over backdrop: the dialog stays open; a later intentional backdrop click closes it;
- lost release (`mousemove` with `buttons === 0`) and blur/cancel: no stale pan;
- true double-tap versus moved-contact→tap, first-contact→pinch→tap, and `touchcancel`;
- landscape→portrait resize: bounds are recomputed and the resize listener is removed on close;
- `_navigateLightbox` itself while a gesture is active. The current test calls `st.reset()` directly, so deleting the production navigation call would not make it fail.

Sandboxed checks at this head:

- `tests/test_lightbox_zoom_fixes.js`: **4 passed**
- `tests/test_composer_chip_lightbox.py tests/test_issue4075_mermaid_lightbox.py`: **15 passed**
- `node --check static/ui.js`: **passed**

Those checks confirm the submitted fixes, but they do not exercise the paths above.

payload.body:
Thanks for the review — both P1s were real. Fixed in 49c4c432:

**1. Pan bounds used the previous scale.** `clampPan()` called `getBoundingClientRect()` (current/old rendered size) before `apply()` painted the new scale, so the first zoom step from 1x clamped against the un-scaled size and discarded the cursor-anchoring offset (center-zoom instead of point-zoom). `clampPan(projectedScale)` now projects the rendered size to the target scale and clamps against that, so the anchor survives. `st.scale` is assigned after the clamp so the projection math stays correct.

**2. Navigation retained active gesture state.** `st.reset()` only cleared `scale`/`tx`/`ty`, leaving `mDown`, `panning`, pinch distance and tap timing live — so navigating with an arrow key mid-drag applied the previous image's drag to the new one. `reset()` now also clears all in-flight gesture state via a `_clearGestures()` helper.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Summary

I reproduced four objective blockers at exact head `ed5416c627e48c71b2e7298fcec98dc20c44a533`. The submitted focused tests pass, but they do not exercise session ownership, autocomplete races, server-side inventory authorization, or the server-busy fallback.

## Blockers

### 1. Plugin selections are page-global, not session/draft-owned

`static/plugin_mentions.js` stores all selected plugins in one module-global `mentions` array. Session switching and composer draft persistence save/restore only text and files. Selecting a plugin also removes the literal `@token` from the textarea.

The result is wrong-owner behavior: select a plugin in session A, switch to session B, and `getPluginMentions()` still returns A's plugin for B. Reload has the inverse failure: the text is restored without either the removed token or the structured mention.

### 2. Delayed plugin results can replace a newer slash-command popup

`updatePluginMentionAutocomplete()` awaits inventory without a generation or shared popup owner. Its continuation checks only whether the same `@token` is still at the caret, then unconditionally calls `hideCmdDropdown()`.

A deterministic delayed-promise probe opened the command popup while inventory was pending, resolved inventory, and observed the newer command popup close and the plugin dropdown take over.

### 3. `/api/chat/start` treats URI shape as authorization

`_normalize_codex_plugin_mentions()` accepts any bounded, whitespace-free `plugin://...` value. It never reconciles the submitted path/name with the current plugin inventory, canonicalizes the name, or binds inventory to the runtime that will execute the turn.

A direct-client probe supplied authoritative inventory containing only `plugin://known`; the chat-start normalizer still accepted `plugin://not-in-inventory`. The same client-controlled value reaches local, runner, and gateway paths. This is a capability boundary, not only input formatting.

### 4. The authoritative server-busy fallback drops plugin intent

The early client-side busy checks correctly refuse to queue plugin mentions. But if the client believes the session is idle and `/api/chat/start` returns `session already has an active stream`, `static/messages.js` queues plain `msgText` with `files: []` and no plugin metadata, rather than restoring the failed draft and chips. The selected plugin intent is silently detached from the queued turn.

## Required changes

1. Make plugin selections owner-scoped and draft-durable. Save, restore, clear, and render mentions by session/draft owner together with text and files. New Chat, reload, rapid session switching, and failed sends must not leak or lose them.
2. Give autocomplete a single owner plus a monotonic generation. Plugin, slash, and path completion must invalidate one another; every async continuation must verify generation and current owner before rendering.
3. Keep syntax normalization separate from authorization. At chat start, resolve the current inventory from the runtime that will execute the turn, reject unlisted/stale paths and spoofed names, canonicalize identity, and deduplicate by canonical path. If runner/gateway inventory contracts do not exist yet, fail closed for those backends rather than trusting local inventory.
4. On the server-busy 409 path, do not queue stripped text. Restore the captured draft, attachments, and owner-scoped chips, then ask the user to retry after the active turn finishes.
5. Add executable regressions for session switch/reload/new-chat ownership, both popup completion orders, unlisted/stale/spoofed plugin submissions, backend inventory mismatch, and the client-idle/server-busy race. Source-string assertions are not enough for these paths.

## Verification

All PR-code execution used the mandatory no-network/no-home sandbox gate after a CLEAN threat scan:

- submitted plugin slices: **19 passed**
- reviewer current-behavior probes for findings 1–3: **3 passed** (they assert the unsafe behavior an

payload.body:
## Summary

Reading the full PR-head and `origin/master` versions of `api/streaming.py`, the complete one-file diff, `tests/test_title_gen_reasoning_extra_gate.py`, and the current Agent auxiliary client, the proposed docstring is ahead of the runtime contract. The WebUI change says correctness no longer depends on the reject list because Agent retries every strict-provider reasoning rejection. The checked Agent source does not implement that retry, so merging this wording now would document a guarantee that users do not have.

## Code reference

The new claim appears at `api/streaming.py:3238-3244`:

```python
Correctness does NOT depend on this list being exhaustive — the generic
compatibility retry in ``agent/auxiliary_client.py`` (call_llm) strips
``reasoning`` on 400 ``unsupported_parameter`` / ``unknown parameter`` and
retries once.
```

That guarantee matters because `generate_title_raw_via_aux()` still constructs and forwards the parameter at `api/streaming.py:3451-3478`:

```python
reasoning_extra = {}
if not _route_rejects_reasoning_extra(provider, model, base_url):
    reasoning_extra["reasoning"] = {"enabled": False}
# ...
extra_body=reasoning_extra or None,
```

The current Agent implementation has `call_llm()` at `agent/auxiliary_client.py:6909`; its compatibility branches handle temperature and `max_tokens`, but there is no reasoning-parameter branch. The generic parser exists, yet the call path does not invoke it for `reasoning`. This is a contract mismatch, not merely missing WebUI test coverage.

## Diagnosis / recommendation

Please do not make the unconditional correctness claim until the companion Agent change is merged and the WebUI support policy can name the first Agent version or commit that provides it. Two safe options:

1. Keep the existing docstring for now, then land this PR after the Agent retry is present, with the merged Agent reference in the comment.
2. Reword this as a future/version-qualified guarantee and retain the reject list as correctness-critical for older supported Agent installs.

The current PR description names a branch-like companion reference rather than a merged PR or commit, so it is not enough to establish the runtime contract.

## Verification step

`tests/test_title_gen_reasoning_extra_gate.py:19-56` only checks which WebUI routes are reject-listed; it cannot prove the claimed Agent fallback. The companion Agent change should include a focused test where the first strict-provider response rejects `reasoning`, the second request omits only that field, exactly one compatibility retry occurs, and an unrelated 400 still propagates. After that lands, cite its commit and minimum compatible Agent version here. I did not execute code from the untrusted PR worktree.
